Reports  of  Brigadier-General  Walter  Gwynn,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  at  Norfolk. 

Norfolk,  Va.,  May  20 ,  1861. 

The  enemy  fired  on  the  unfinished  battery  at  Sewell’s  Point  on  the 
18th,  but  did  no  damage.  There  were  at  that  time  no  guns  mounted 
or  nearer  than  Norfolk.  I  sent  forward  three  guns  immediately  and 
two  of  the  rifled  cannon.  Got  them  in  position  at  5  p.  m.  on  the  19th. 
Soon  after  the  enemy  opened  fire,  which  was  returned  and  kept  up  one 
and  a  half  hours,  when  the  vessel  from  which  the  guns  were  fired  with¬ 
drew.  A  fuller  report  will  be  made  to  morrow.  Just  returned  from 
Sewell’s  Point.  Reports  in  from  the  pickets  at  all  points. 

No  immediate  attack  apprehended.  Troops  thrown  forward  and  in 
position.  Confident  of  making  defense  good.  I  am  strengthening  to 
some  extent  my  position.  Want  COO  laborers,  and  am  reenforcing  the 
batteries,  which  takes  off  so  many  men  that  additional  troops  are 
required. 

Walter  Gwynn. 

R.  S.  Garnett, 

Adjutant- General  Virginia  Forces. 


Headquarters  Forces  of  Virginia  around  Norfolk, 

May  20,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  late  in  the  evening  of  the 
18th  instant  I  received  intelligence  of  an  attack  made  by  the  enemy’s 
steamer  Monticello  on  the  unfinished  works  at  Sewell’s  Point.  This 
battery  was  not  sufficiently  advanced  at  the  time  to  receive  its  arma¬ 
ment  and  garrison.  The  Monticello  carried  three  guns,  one  of  which 
was  a  heavy  10  inch  Dahlgren.  With  these  she  kept  up  a  constant 
fire  with  solid  shot  and  shell  for  more  than  an  hour,  when  a  steam  tug 
from  Old  Point  carrying  one  gun  came  to  her  aid,  and  the  two  vessels 
continued  the  cannonade  until  the  close  of  the  day  without  any  serious 
injury  to  the  works.  The  tug  then  returned  to  Old  Point,  and  the 
Monticello  moored,  with  broadside  on,  with  the  intention,  apparently, 
of  continuing  the  attack,  in  order  to  demolish  the  works  or  prevent 
their  progress.  Early  on  the  morning  of  the  1 9th  I  hurried  on  the  guns 
and  equipment,  and  repaired  to  Sewell’s  Point,  to  expedite  the  works 
for  their  reception,  and  by  5  p.  m.  succeeded  in  getting  three  32- 
pounders  and  two  small  rifled  guns  into  position,  while  detachments  of 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


647 


infantry  and  artillery,  ordered  from  neighboring  posts,  occupied  the 
battery  and  contiguous  points.  During  all  this  time  the  Monticello, 
apparently  not  suspecting  the  operations  going  forward,  was  engaged 
in  preparing  for  another  effort,  by  calculating  the  range  and  distance 
and  adjusting  her  guns  to  suit.  With  instructions  to  Captain  Colquitt, 
of  Georgia,  to  whom  I  gave  command  of  all  the  forces  and  guns  at  the 
post,  to  continue  the  preparations,  reserving  his  tire  until  the  enemy 
renewed  the  cannonade,  I  returned  to  Norfolk.  At  5:30  o’clock  the 
Monticello  again  opened  tire  from  all  her  guns,  and  with  much  greater 
precision  than  on  the  preceding  day.  it  was  instantly  returned  and 
with  such  effect  that  she  was  driven  off  and  returned  to  Old  Point.  The 
engagement  continued  for  an  hour  and  a  half  without  intermission  on 
either  side,  and,  though  the  enemy’s  fire  was  well  directed,  one  shell 
bursting  within  an  embrasure  and  several  others  directly  over  the  bat¬ 
tery,  while  solid  shot  repeatedly  passed  through  the  embrasures  and 
struck  the  crest  and  sides  of  the  merlons,  hurling  masses  of  earth  from 
the  outside  among  the  gunners,  1  am  happy  to  inform  you  that  no  cas¬ 
ualty  of  moment  occurred  to  the  troops,  nor  was  material  in  jury  done 
to  the  battery.  What  damage  or  loss  was  sustained  by  the  enemy  I 
was  not  able  to  discover,  but  his  retreat  indicated  that  our  fire  had 
become  too  warm  for  further  endurance.  As  early  as  I  received  infor¬ 
mation  of  the  second  attack  and  repulse,  1  ordered  forward  more  troops 
and  hastened  during  the  night  to  Sewell’s  Point  to  make  such  other 
dispositions  as  might  be  necessary  to  defend  the  post  against  any  fur¬ 
ther  and  more  formidable  assaults  which  the  enemy’s  large  naval  and 
military  forces  at  Old  Point  would  enable  him  to  make. 

I  can  not  close  this  brief  account  of  the  engagement  without  express¬ 
ing  my  admiration  of  the  enthusiasm  and  bravery  manifested  by  the 
troops.  Where  officers  and  men  displayed  so  much  merit  it  would  be 
invidious  to  discriminate,  and  1  therefore  refer  you  to  the  accompany¬ 
ing  report  of  Captain  Colquitt  for  further  particulars.  His  position,  as 
commanding  officer  of  the  post,  gave  him  an  opportunity  of  displaying 
the  qualities  which  adorn  the  soldier,  and  the  general  appreciation  of 
his  gallantry  and  merit  by  those  under  his  command  enable  me  to  com¬ 
mend  him  most  warmly  to  your  consideration. 

In  conclusion,  I  would  state  that,  in  consequence  of  the  want  of  a 
Virginia  or  Confederate  flag  for  the  occasion,  the  flag  of  Georgia, 
belonging  to  Captain  Colquitt’s  company,  was  planted  on  the  ramparts 
during  the  engagement,  and,  while  the  hottest  fire  was  prevailing,  two 
members  of  his  company,  whose  names  I  will  forward  you  when  reported 
to  me  as  deserving  particular  notice,  fearlessly  passed  to  the  outside  of 
the  battery  and  deliberately  removed  the  sand  and  other  obstructions  to 
the  range  of  one  of  the  guns  while  shot  and  shell  were  striking  all 
about  them. 

I  am,  general,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Walter  Gwynn. 

Major-General  Lee, 

Commanding  Forces  of  Virginia ,  Richmond ,  Va. 


Report  of  Captain  Peyton  H.  Colquitt,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  at  Sewell’s  Point. 


Sewell’s  Point,  Va.,  May  19 ,  1801. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  an  engagement  this  evening 
between  the  Confederate  troops,  consisting  of  the  City  Light  Guards, 


G48  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

Columbus,  Ga.;  Wootlis  Rides,  Captain  Lamb;  detachment  of  the 
Norfolk  Juniors,  under  Lieutenant  Holmes;  detachment  of  Light  Artil¬ 
lery  Blues,  under  Lieutenant  Nash,  all  under  my  command,  and  the 
steamer  Monticello  and  Federal  steam  tug,  which  lasted  for  one  hour 
and  a  half,  in  which  nobody  was  hurt  on  our  side.  The  enemy  fired 
with  great  accuracy,  several  balls  passing  through  the  embrasures  ot 
the  fort,  one  striking  a  32-pounder  within  the  battery,  and  one  shell 
bursting  in  the  fort.  From  three  to  five  shots  from  our  battery  took 
effect,  we  think;  others  struck  around  the  steamer.  The  troops  acted 
with  great  bravery,  and  I  had  to  restrain  them  in  their  enthusiasm. 
The  dag  of  Georgia  was  hoisted  over  the  fort  in  the  absence  of  the 
Confederate  dag.  Our  firing  was  less  frequent  than  that  of  the  enemy, 
as  our  ammunition  was  scarce;  only  two  rounds  left  after  the  engage¬ 
ment.  Your  aids,  Major  William  E.  Taylor,  R.  R.  Collier,  and  Colonel 
Thomas  Newton,  were  present  and  aided  in  the  struggle. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

Peyton  H.  Colquitt. 

Major-General  Gwynn. 

Commanding  Forces ,  Norfolk  Harbor. 

P.  S. — Two  members  of  the  City  Light  Guards  (Georgia)  dug  away 
the  sand  in  front  of  one  of  the  portholes  during  the  hottest  of  the  fire. 


Report  of  Flag-Officer  Stringham ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic 

Blockading  Squadron ,  suggesting  service  for  U.  S.  sloop  Cumberland. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads ,  May  19 ,  1861. 

Sir:  In  forwarding  Flag-Ofdcer  Pendergrast’s  communication*  of 
May  18, 1861,  to  the  Department,  I  take  the  liberty  of  making  a  single 
suggestion  in  reference  to  the  disposition  of  the  Cumberland,  growing 
out  of  the  fact  of  the  certain  presence  of  large  steamers  at  Charleston, 
as  per  communication  containing  list  of  vessels  as  furnished  by  Mr.  H. 
Loriug,  of  Boston,  to  the  Department. 

I  respectfully  suggest,  if  the  Department  sees  fit  to  comply  with  Com¬ 
modore  Pendergrast’s  suggestions  of  taking  up  his  quarters  at  Fortress 
Monroe  (to  which  I  see  no  objection),  that  the  Cumberland,  instead  of 
going  immediately  to  New  York,  be  first  sent  off  Charleston  (where 
only  the  small  steamer  Harriet  Lane  now  is)  to  cruise  until  she  can  be 
relieved  by  one  of  the  large  vessels  daily  expected  to  report  here  for 
service,  after  which  the  Cumberland  might  proceed  to  New  Y^ork. 

I  inferred  from  your  communication  of  May  4,  1SG1,  that  I  might 
employ  the  Cumberland  on  blockading  duty,  but  only  at  this  port,  and 
therefore  my  suggestion. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  H.  Stringham, 

Senior  Flag-Officer  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  String  ham,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic 

Blockading  Squadron,  suggesting  immediate  occupation  of  Cape  Henry 

Virginia ,  by  troops. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  May  19,  1SG1. 

Sir  :  I  take  the  liberty  of  suggesting  to  the  Department  the  very 
great  importance  of  keeping  perfectly  free  and  clear  the  navigation  of 
the  Chesapeake,  and  of  taking  means  immediately  to  prevent  any 
occupation  of  Cape  Henry  by  the  rebels  of  Virginia. 

If  they  choose  to  occupy  the  cape  with  guns,  they  can  prevent  the 
ingress  of  vessels  of  large  size  or  at  least  do  great  damage. 

I  would  respectfully  suggest  the  immediate  occupation  of  that  point 
by  a  force  of  at  least  a  thousand  men  and  some  heavy  guns.  With 
boards  the  soldiers  could  easily  erect  qunrters  ample  and  comfortable 
for  the  present,  and  that  point  once  occupied  could  be  readily  defended, 
and  if  necessary  supported  by  the  fleet. 

Eespectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  II.  Stringham, 

Senior  Flag-Officer  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy.

Portland,  June  22, 1861. 

Dear  Sir:  On  the  21st  ultimo,  my  ship  A.  B.  Thompson,  of  Bruns¬ 
wick,  Me.,  of  980  tons,  was  taken,  alter  leaving  Savannah  on  the  day 
previous,  off  Portugal  Bay,  by  steamer  Lady  Davis,  Captain  Pelot,  and 
taken  to  Beaufort,  S.  C.,  as  Ave  learn  from  our  correspondent  at  Savan¬ 
nah,  Ga.  I  have  not  received  any  information  from  the  captain  since 
she  left  Savannah. 

She  is  rather  a  fast  sailer;  she  will  make  the  rebels  a  good  sloop  of 
war.  She  can  be  converted  into  a  steamer  and  would  make  a  formida¬ 
ble  privateer.  Please  represent  this  to  our  Government  at  Washing¬ 
ton.  She  is  worth  about  $30,000  to  me,  or  us.  They  will  confer  a  great 
favor  on  us  if  they  will  send  a  steamer,  take  her  out,  and  tow  her  to 
sea.  We  presume  her  whole  crew  are  on  board. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Daniel  Hood. 


Hon.  William  [P.j  Fessenden.

Letter  from  It.  C.  Gilchrist,  C.  S.  prize  commissioner,  to  the  judge  bf  the  C.  S.  district  court, 
transmitting  papers  in  the  case  of  prize  ship  A.  B.  Thompson. 

Confederate  States  of  America, 

South  Carolina  District: 

1  would  respectfully  report  to  your  honor  that  Lieutenant  Pelot,  of 
the  C.  S.  S.  Lady  Davis ,  appeared  before  me  on  the  22d  day  of  May, 
18G1,  and  delivered  to  me  all  the  papers  of  the  ship  A.  B.  Thompson , 
taken  as  prize  by  the  said  steamer  Lady  Davis. 

The  said  papers  and  an  inventory  of  the  same  are  herewith  filed.  On 
the  24th  of  May  I  went  to  Beaufort,  where  the  said  ship  was  moored,  to 
take  possession  of  her  as  prize  commissioner.  I  found  her  safely 
anchored  under  the  guns  of  the  Lady  Davis  and  guarded  every  night 
by  a  detachment  of  nine  soldiers  from  the  fort.  I  immediately  pro¬ 
ceeded  to  examine  the  officers  and  crew  on  the  standing  interrogatories 
propounded  by  the  court,  aud  I  herewith  tile  the  full  and  explicit  replies 
given  by  the  captain,  the  first  and  second  mates,  and  two  of  the  most 
intelligent  of  the  crew,  the  largest  proportion  of  whom  were  foreigners, 
unable  to  speak  our  language. 

I  made  a  thorough  examination  of  the  whole  vessel.  There  was  no 
cargo  on  board.  Hereto  annexed  is  an  inventory  of  all  I  could  tiud. 
I  placed  a  seal  on  Marryat’s  signal  flags,  but  told  the  captain  of  the 
prize  ship  that  he  and  his  crew  could  use  the  ship’s  stores  so  long  as 
they  remained  by  the  vessel. 

For  the  purpose  of  securing  the  ship  I  had  all  the  sails  unbent  and 
stowed  away  in  the  hold ;  the  running  tackle  was  likewise  taken  down,  so 
that  the  vessel  is  completely  dismantled.  The  officers  of  the  Lady  Davis 
still  remain  in  charge  of  the  ship  and  should  the  steamer  be  ordered 
off  before  the  ship  is  more  completely  in  the  custody  of  the  court,  a 
guard  will  be  detailed  from  the  fort. 

The  officers  and  crew  of  the  prize  ship  still  remain  on  board. 

All  of  which  is  respectfully  reported. 

R.  O.  Gilchrist, 

C.  S.  Prize  Commissioner. 

Hon.  A.  G.  Magrath, 

Judge ,  Confederate  States  Court.

Examination  of  Captain  Hussey  : 

To  the  first  interrogatory:  I  was  born  in  the  town  of  Greene,  in  the 
State  of  Maine.  I  live  at  West  Woodstock,  Conn.;  have  lived  there 
five  years.  I  am  a  citizen  of  the  State  of  Connecticut. 

Second  interrogatory:  I  was  present  at  the  time  of  the  taking  of  the 
ship  A.  B.  Thompson ,  and  was  in  command  of  her.

Third  interrogatory:  The  ship  was  about  10  miles  east  of  Savannah 
bar,  as  nearly  as  I  can  judge,  at  the  time  she  was  taken.  She  was 
taken  last  Sunday,  the  19tli  of  May,  1861,  about  11  o’clock  a.  m.  She 
Avas  carried  into  Beaufort  Harbor.  The  reason  given  me,  was  that  1 
did  not  have  a  proper  clearance  from  Savannah,  and  on  that  account  she 
was  seized.  The  ship  sailed  under  the  American  or  United  States  col¬ 
ors.  1  had  no  other  national  colors  on  board,  but  had  some  Marryat’s 
signal  colors  and  a  flag  with  the  ship’s  name  on  it.  I  had  those  signal 
flags  to  communicate  with  other  vessels  or  with  the  shore  in  case  any¬ 
thing  Avas  wanted.  No  resistance  was  made  to  the  seizure.  We  Avere 
taken  by  the  steamer  Lady  Davis. 

Fourth  interrogatory:  F.  A.  Hussey  is  the  name  of  the  commander 
of  this  ship.  1  am  the  commander.  The  owners  appointed  me.  Cap¬ 
tain  James  M.  Small,  my  predecessor,  delivered  to  me  the  possession  of 
the  ship.  I  took  possession  of  her  at  Antwerp,  Belgium,  on  the  18th 
day  of  March,  1801.  I  live,  as  I  have  before  stated,  at  W  est  Woodstock, 
Conn.;  was  born  in  the  town  of  Greene,  Me.,  and  am  a  citizen  of  the 
United  States. 

Fifth  interrogatory:  The  tonnage  of  my  ship  is  9S0  tons,  or  there¬ 
abouts.  There  were  twenty-three,  counting  mariners  and  officers,  on 
board.  The  mariners  were  principally  foreigners — some  Irish,  some 
English,  and  some  Dutch.  There  was  one  American.  I  can’t  say  pos¬ 
itively  whether  there  were  any  more.  'They  Avere  shipped  in  Antwerp, 
by  two  shipping  masters  Avhom  I  employed  for  that  purpose,  someAvliere 
betAveeu  the  20th  and  25th  of  March,  1801. 

Sixth  interrogatory :  Neither  I  nor  any  of  the  officers  or  mariners  had 
or  have  any  part,  share,  or  interest  in  either  the  vessel  or  cargo.  She 
had  no  cargo,  only  ballast.  I  belonged  to  the  vessel  at  the  time  of  her 
seizure,  was  master  of  her;  I  have  only  known  this  ship  from  the  18tli 
of  March  last;  I  never  saw  her  before  I  took  command  of  her. 

Seventh  interrogatory:  The  ship’s  name  is  A.  B.  Thompson;  she  has 
been  called  by  this  name  since  she  Avas  first  registered,  some  eight  years 
ago.  She  has  never  had  any  other  name,  so  far  as  I  know.  I  left  Ant- 
Averp  on  the  27th  day  of  March  and  sailed  directly  for  Savannah,  Ga.  I 
arrived  in  SaArannali  last  Friday,  the  17th  of  May.  My  Aroyage  Avas  to 
commence  at  AntAverp  and  then  sail  to  Savannah,  where  I  Avas  to  receGe 
further  orders.  I  expected  to  receive  my  orders  from  the  pilot.  The 
pilot  told  me  that  lie  Avas  not  allowed  to  deliver  letters  to  ships  outside. 
1  therefore  left  my  ship  off  Tybee  light  and  went  up  to  Savannah,  where 
I  received  orders  from  the  owners  of  the  ship  to  take  her  to  Hampton 
lfoads;  but  hearing  that  harbor  was  blockaded,  I  concluded  to  take  the 
ship  to  New  York.  I  left  Savannah  with  the  ship  about  9  o’clock  Sun¬ 
day  morning,  and  had  just  got  sail  on  my  ship  when  Iayus  taken.  The 
ship  was  in  ballast  about  400  tons,  sand  and  stone;  she  had  no  cargo, 
and  had  none  from  the  time  of  leaving  Antwerp. 

Eighth  interrogatory:  The  owners  are  Daniel  Hood,  of  Portland; 
A.  D.  Thompson  and  George  Mustard  and  others,  of  Brunswick  [Me.]. 
The  names  of  the  owners  are  found  on  the  register.  I  know  it  from  the 
fact  of  their  engaging  me  to  take  charge  of  the  ship  and  from  seeing 
their  names  on  the  register.  They  are  citizens  of  the  State  of  Maine. 

Ninth  and  tenth  interrogatories:  There  was  no  lading  on  board  the 
vessel;  nothing  but  ballast,  Avliich  belongs  to  the  ship.

voyage.

tured  ship  A.  B.  Thompson ,  as  joint  captors  thereof,  nnder  the  follow¬ 
ing  circumstances,  to  wit:  That  on  the  morning  of  the  18th  of  May, 
A.  D.  1861,  Lieutenant  Pelot,  commanding  the  Lady  Davis ,  called  upon 
the  said  Captain  Elliott  and  requested  him  to  bring  on  board  of  the 
Lady  Davis  a  detachment  of  his  men  and  accompany  him  outside  of  the 
bar,  to  which  request  Captain  Elliott  assented,  but  that  the  weather 
proving  unfavorable  the  expedition  was  abandoned  and  Captain  Elliott 
and  his  detachment  landed  at  the  fort  with  the  understanding  that 
their  services  would  be  required  the  following  day.  That  on  the  fol 
lowing  day,  the  19th  of  May,  A.  D.  1801,  Lieutenant  Pelot  called  upon 
Captain  Elliott  and  took  him,  two  sergeants,  and  sixteen  privates,  being 
your  petitioners,  completely  armed,  and  also  took  Captain  Elliott’s  boat 
in  tow  and  proceeded  across  Port  Royal  bar.  About  8  miles  beyond 
the  bar,  the  Lady  Davis  hailed  the  ship  A.  B.  Thompson ,  and  at  the 
suggestion,  of  Captain  Elliott,  Lieutenant  Pelot  ordered  her  to  be 
boarded.  Lieutenant  Stockton,  of  the  Lady  Davis ,  then  boarded  the 
ship  from  Captain  Elliott’s  boat,  accompanied  by  Captain  Elliott  aud 
one  of  the  detachment  from  Fort  Littleton,  who  was  stationed  at  the 
signal  halyards  to  cut  them  in  case  of  foul  play.  After  some  conversa¬ 
tion  with  the  captain  the  boarding  party  returned  to  the  Lady  Davis 
and  Lieutenant  Stockton  went  on  board,  soon  after  which  Lieutenant 
Pelot,  coming  to  the  side  of  his  vessel,  asked  Captain  Elliott  whether 
he  would  take  the  Thompson  to  Charleston,  to  which  Captain  Elliott 
replied  that  he  deemed  such  an  attempt  injudicious  in  view  of  the 
blockade  then  existing  at  that  port.  Lieutenant  Pelot  then  asked 
whether  Captain  Elliott  would  take  the  Thompson  to  Port  Royal, 
to  which  he  consented.  Lieutenant  Stockton  and  Captain  Elliott 
then  returned  to  the  ship  A.  B.  Thompson ,  taking  with  them  Pri¬ 
vates  R.  M.  Fuller,  J.  E.  Chaplin,  and  M.  W.  Fripp,  who  guarded 
the  hatchway,  while  the  master  of  the  ship  was  sent  to  the  Lady  Davis 
and  the  boat  then  returned  bringing  Sergeant  B.  W.  Slowman,  Privates 
II.  E.  [C.M.  ?]  Bold,  J.  W.  Bold,  H.  C.  Morgan,  H.M.  Fuller,  H.  [M.]  Zealy, 
C.  [II.]  Willcox,  and  three  or  four  of  the  crew  of  the  Lady  Davis. 
Lieutenant  Stockton  then  placed  the  vessel  under  the  command  of 
Captain  Elliott,  who  gave  the  courses  to  the  helmsman  and  the  neces¬ 
sary  orders.  After  passing  the  shoals  at  the  mouth  of  the  harbor,  the 
Lady  Davis  hailed  the  ship  and  directed  it  to  follow  in  her  wake, 
but  finding  that  this  direction  brought  the  ship  into  shallow  water, 
where  she  struck  and  ran  great  danger  of  finally  stranding,  Captain 
Elliott  changed  her  course  and  brought  her  to  Beaufort.

Testimony  of  Lieutenant  Edward  C.  Stockton. 

Confederate  States  of  America, 

South  Carolina  District ,  in  admiralty : 

Confederate  States  of  America  ^ 

Ship  A.  B.  Thompson.  \ 

Lieutenant  Edward  C.  Stockton,  a  witness  produced  and  examined 
in  behalf  of  the  claimants,  Stephen  Elliott,  jr.,  and  others,  being  duly 
sworn  deposes: 

That  he  is  now  a  lieutenant  in  the  Marine  Corps  of  the  Confederate 
States,  but  that  he  held  a  commission  as  lieutenant  in  the  Navy  only 
from  the  State  of  South  Carolina  at  the  time  of  the  capture  of  the 
Thompson ;  that  deponent  was  in  command  of  the  steamer  Lady  Davis 
while  she  was  owned  by  the  State  of  South  Carolina,  and  under  the 
orders  of  the  governor  of  South  Carolina  as  part  of  the  coast  police  of 
the  State,  until  about  a  week  before  the  capture,  when  Lieutenant 
Thomas  P.  Pelot,  of  the  C.  S.  Navy,  took  command  of  her,  by  the  direc¬ 
tion  of  the  governor.  Deponent  came  to  Charleston  on  Friday,  the  1 7 tli 
of  May,  and  had  an  interview  with  Commodore  Tattnall,  C.  S.  Navy, 
in  which  he  learned  that  the  Lady  Davis  was  under  the  orders  of  Com¬ 
modore  Tattnall  as  a  part  of  the  C.  S.  Navy,  and  that  Lieutenant  Pelot 
had  been  ordered  by  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  Lady  Davis,  and 
that  he,  deponent,  then  had  an  interview  with  the  governor,  who 
informed  deponent  that  he  had  nothing  to  do  with  the  Lady  Davis ,  as 
she  had  been  turned  over  to  the  Confederate  States,  but  that,  as  orders 
had  been  sent  to  Lieutenant  Pelot  to  come  to  Charleston,  lie  desired 
deponent  to  keep  command  of  the  Lady  Davis  until  Pelot  could  return 
to  her.  Deponent  returned  to  Beaufort  on  Saturday  night  and  found 
Lieutenant  Pelot  in  command  of  the  Lady  Davis.  The  next  day,  Sun¬ 
day,  19tli  May,  the  Lady  Davis  went  out  in  search  of  the  U.  S.  brig 
Perry,  and  while  cruising  about  fell  in  with  and  captured  the  A.  B. 
Thompson.  Deponent  has  read  carefully  the  petition  and  claim  of  Cap¬ 
tain  Stephen  Elliott,  jr.,  and  admits  that  the  facts  stated  by  him  which 
are  within  deponent’s  knowledge  are  truly  and  accurately  set  forth, 
except  that  when  they  went  on  board  the  Thompson,  Captain  Elliott 
did  not  take  command  of  her.  Deponent  was  in  command,  and  gave 
the  necessary  orders  for  sailing  the  ship,  but  Captain  Elliott  acted  as 
pilot  and  directed  the  courses  of  the  vessel,  and  by  his  familiarity  with 
the  bar  was  of  most  essential  service  in  bringing  the  ship  in  safely; 
in  fact,  but  for  Captain  Elliott’s  knowledge  the  ship  would  probably 
have  gone  ashore,  as  there  was  no  one  else  on  board  who  knew  the  bar. 
The  names  stated  in  the  petition  are  not  known  to  deponent,  but 
deponent  requested  Captain  Elliott  to  furnish  him  with  a  list  of  his 
men,  as  deponent  considered  that  they  would  be  entitled  to  share  in 
the  prize  money,  and  deponent  has  no  doubt  that  the  list  is  correct.

Deponent  also  tliinks  that  the  statement  in  the  petition  with  regard  to 
the  conversation  between  Lieutenant  Pelot  and  Captain  Elliott  on  the 
Saturday  preceding  the  capture  is  correct,  from  what  he  has  heard 
from  Lieutenant  Pelot. 

Deponent  further  states  that  there  were  on  board  of  the  Lady  Davis 
at  the  time  of  the  capture  of  the  Thompson,  the  following  officers: 
Lieutenant  Thomas  P.  Pelot,  C.  S.  Navy,  commanding;  deponent,  lieu 
tenant  in  South  Carolina  Navy,  second  in  command;  James  Pelot, 
assistant  surgeon,  of  State  of  South  Carolina;  Midshipmen  Thomas 
and  Walker,  also  of  the  State  service;  also  two  engineers,  Geddes  and 
Yates,  appointed  by  the  State;  one  ship’s  steward,  three  quartermas¬ 
ters,  and  no  extra  petty  officers,  and,  as  well  as  deponent  remembers, 
twenty  seamen,  firemen,  and  coal  heavers;  but  this  will  appear  by  the 
log  book  of  the  Lady  Davis. 

Deponent  further  says  that  the  Lady  Davis  is  about  250  tons  burden, 
and  the  Thompson  is  about  980  tons,  and  the  number  of  the  crew  on  the 
Thompson  was  about  twenty-three. 

Deponent  further  states  that  in  his  opinion  the  soldiers  under  the 
command  of  Captain  Elliott  did  duty  on  this  occasion  as  marines. 

E.  C.  Stockton, 
Lieutenant,  C.  S.  Marines. 

Sworn  to  before  me  this  29th  June,  1801.

Testimony  of  Lieutenant  Thomas  P.  Pelot. 

Lieutenant  Thomas  P.  Pelot,  C.  [S.|  Navy,  being  duly  sworn,  says: 

Examined  by  Mr.  Trescot: 

I  was  in  command  of  the  steamer  Lady  Davis  at  the  time  of  the  cap¬ 
ture  of  the  ship  A.  B.  Thompson.  The  crew  consisted  of  twenty- three 
n  en,  myself,  and  the  officers  who  were  with  me.  Lieutenant  Stockton, 
Surgeon  Pelot,  Midshipmen  Walker  andThomas,  Chief  Engineer  Geddes, 
Assistant  Engineer  Yates,  Pilot  Murray,  were  the  officers.  We  like¬ 
wise  had  Captain  Elliott,  of  the  Beaufort  Volunteer  Artillery,  and  about 
fifteen  or  twenty  of  his  men.  On  Saturday,  the  18th  of  May,  I  went  to 
see  Captain  Elliott  at  his  residence,  and  asked  him  to  go  on  board  the 
Lady  Davis  as  a  pilot,  to  which  he  agreed.  On  our  way  to  the  boat  to 
embark  he  asked  if  1  would  allow  some  of  his  company  to  go  on  board, 
to  which  I  consented,  limiting  the  number  to  a  dozen,  and  promised  to 
call  at  the  fort  for  them.  On  the  same  day,  with  these  persons  on  board, 
we  proceeded  to  the  bar,  but,  in  consequence  of  the  threatening  appear¬ 
ance  of  the  weather,  we  returned  and  landed  the  members  of  the  Beau¬ 
fort  Volunteers.  Captain  Elliott  asked  me  to  call  on  the  following- 
day,  as  I  told  him  I  was  going  out,  and  receive  him  and  a  part  of  his 
company  on  board,  which  in  courtesy  I  accepted.  On  the  following- 
day  (Sunday,  the  I9tli)  we  proceeded  over  the  bar.  We  saw  the  A.  B. 
Thompson  making  sail  in  the  offing,  standing  to  the  northward.  We 
approached  her,  ordered  her  to  show  her  colors  and  heave  to.  Ordered 


656  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

* 

Lieutenant  Stockton  to  board  her  and  examine  lier.v  Lieutenant  Stock- 
ton  returned  and  reported  that  the  ship  was  the  American  ship  A.  B. 
Thompson ,  of  Maine,  cleared  at  the  port  of  Savannah  by  the  deputy 
collector.  Ordered  Lieutenant  Stockton  to  take  a  prize  crew  from  the 
men  of  the  Lady  Davis  and  take  charge  of  her.  Requested  Captain 
Elliott  to  pilot  the  ship  into  Port  Royal,  which  request  he  acceded  to. 
Captain  Elliott  went  on  board  the  ship  in  the  capacity  of  pilot  at  my 
request.  When  we  took  Captain  Elliott  and  his  men  on  board  we  took 
their  boat  in  tow  at  the  same  time.  When  Lieutenant  Stockton  boarded 
the  ship,  I  think  he  boarded  her  in  Captain  Elliott’s  boat,  or  rather  the 
boat  in  which  they  came  on  board.  When  Lieutenant  Stockton  first 
went  on  board  he  was  accompanied  by  Captain  Elliott,  but  not  at  my 
request.  I  ordered  Lieutenant  Stockton  to  m.an  the  boat,  but  did  not 
specify  what  men  were  to  go  on  board.  There  were  some  of  Captain 
Elliott’s  men  in  the  boat.  After  Lieutenant  Stockton  returned  to  the 
Lady  Davis  and  reported,  I  requested  Captain  Elliott  to  pilot  the  ship 
into  Beaufort,  but  do  not  remember  the  details  of  the  conversation,  I 
had  a  pilot  of  my  own  on  board,  whom  I  retained  to  pilot  the  Lady  Davis. 
Lieutenant  Stockton  then  returned  to  the  ship,  taking  Captain  Elliott 
and  some  of  his  men  with  him.  When  Lieutenant  Stockton  returned, 
he  sent  the  captain  and  officers  of  the  Thompson  and  her  papers  back 
to  the  Lady  Davis  by  my  orders.  The  prize  crew  was  then  sent  back  to 
the  ship.  I  detailed  that  crew  (I  think  there  were  six),  consisting  of 
the  men  of  the  Lady  Davis.  Some  of  the  men  of  Captain  Elliott’s  com¬ 
pany  accompanied  the  prize  crew;  they  asked  my  permission  to  do  so, 
and  I  granted  it,  having  no  right  to  detain  them.  I  think  they  were 
all  armed.  1  know  nothing  of  what  took  place  on  board  of  the  ship 
after  Lieutenant  Stockton  took  charge  of  her.  While  we  were  going 
into  port  I  ordered  Lieutenant  Stockton  to  give  me  a  hawser  to  tow  the 
ship,  which  I  afterwards  countermanded.  I  ordered  Lieutenant  Stock- 
ton  to  follow  in  our  wake.  I  ordered  Lieutenant  Stockton  to  cross  the 
bar  under  topsails.  A  portion  of  the  way  she  followed  in  our  wake. 
Lieutenant  Stockton  asked  permission  to  bring  the  ship  in  without 
regard  to  my  previous  orders,  as  he  had  been  advised  to  do  so.  The 
Lady  Davis  and  prize  went  in  company  to  the  town  of  Beaufort.  The 
prize  crew  remained  on  board  the  ship  until  sunset.  Lieutenant  Stock- 
ton  came  on  shore  about  that  time  and  said  that  he  had  left  a  party  of 
Captain  Elliott’s  men  in  charge  of  the  ship.  I  requested  Captain  Elliott 
to  retain  a  guard  on  board  the  vessel.  They  have  been  in  charge  of 
the  ship  until  a  few  days  ago.  The  twenty-three  men  on  board  the 
Lady  Davis  allowed  me  only  six  men  to  send  on  board  the  ship  as  a  prize 
crew.  When  I  invited  Captain  Elliott  to  go  with  me  on  the  18th,  it 
was  with  the  intention  of  attacking  the  Derry ,  an  armed  vessel  of  the 
U.  S.  Navy.  The  object  of  the  expedition  on  the  19tli  was  the  same. 
1  never  had  any  conversation  with  Captain  Elliott  about  a  list  of  the 
men  who  accompanied  him. 

Cross-examined  by  Mr.  Miles  : 

I  took  command  of  the  Lady  Davis  on  the  10th  or  11th  of  May,  by 
order  of  Governor  Pickens.  I  then  had  my  commission  from  the  Con 
federate  States.  I  had  orders  from  Governor  Pickens  to  report  to  Com¬ 
modore  Tattnall,  ivho  was  in  command  of  this  division.  I  considered 
that  the  Lady  Davis  was  then  in  the  Confederate  service.  The  engineer 
may  have  been  in  the  Confederate  service;  none  of  the  others  were. 
The  crew  was  reenlisted  into  the  Confederate  service  the  day  after  the 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


657 


capture.  The  officers  of  the  State  were  then  dismissed  between  that 
and  the  1st.  The  Lady  Davis  had  a  24-pound  howitzer  and  a  rifle  can¬ 
non;  they  both  belonged  to  the  State.  The  howitzer  was  turned  over 
to  the  Confederate  service;  the  ride  cannon  still  belongs  to  the  State. 
The  Lady  Davis  is  now  at  Beaufort,  under  the  command  of  Lieutenant 
Itutledge. 

^  I  considered  the  men  of  Captain  Elliott’s  company  as  my  guests. 
Captain  Elliott  was  absolutely  necessary  to  me,  because  I  did  not  have 
my  pilot,  but  the  men  were  not  necessary  to  me.  I  intended  to  light 
the  Perry  at  a  long  range  with  my  ride  cannon.  I  had  no  idea  of 
coming  within  range  of  her  guns.  I  had  no  intention  of  boarding  her, 
and  marines  would  have  been  of  no  use  to  me.  My  pilot  had  returned 
the  following  day;  I  therefore  did  not  ask  Captain  Elliott  to  go  with 
me,  but  he  asked  me  to  call  for  him,  which  I  agreed  to  do,  and  also  to 
take  some  ot  his  men.  I  did  not  need  or  desire  their  assistance;  I 
gave  no  command  to  Captain  Elliott  or  any  of  his  men.  Before  the 
capture,  Captain  Elliott  was  on  my  boat  as  guest;  after  the  capture 
he  was  on  the  prize  as  pilot.  The  men  were  the  whole  time  as  guests. 

All  my  orders  were  given  to  Lieutenant  Stockton  and  Midshipman 
Walker.  Captain  Elliott  did  not  claim  to  me  to  participate  in  the  prize 
money  resulting  from  the  capture  either  at  the  time  or  after  the  capture. 
I  considered  that  he  was  entitled  to  remuneration  for  his  services  as 
pilot,  but  his  men  were  entitled  to  nothing,  unless  Lieutenant  Stockton 
had  used  any  of  them  in  the  same  capacity.  The  Lady  Davis  was  250 
tons;  the  prize  ship  about  998  tons.  After  taking  out  the  prize  crew, 
I  had  men  enough  on  board  the  Davis  to  perform  all  the  necessary 
duties,  and  the  men  I  put  on  board  were  sufficient,  under  the  circum¬ 
stances,  to  man  the  prize.  The  crew  of  the  ship  assisted  in  working 
her  in ;  there  was  no  resistance  offered.  I  first  knew  of  the  claim  of 
Captain  Elliott  through  the  publication  in  the  Courier  a  few  days  ago. 
1  received  my  orders  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  go  on  board 
the  Lady  Davis  on  the  18th  of  May. 

Thos.  P.  Pelot, 
Lieutenant ,  G.  8.  JLavy.

Testimony  of  Robert  M.  Fuller.  s  * 

Robert  M.  Fuller,  being  duly  sworn,  says : 

Examined  by  Mr.  Trescot: 

I  am  a  member  of  tlio  Beaufort  Volunteer  Artillery,  now  in  the  serv¬ 
ice  of  tbe  Confederate  States.  In  May  last  1  was  in  the  service  of  the 
State,  and  employed  in  garrison  duty  in  Fort  Littleton.  I  was  one  of  the 
detachment  of  the  company  on  board  of  the  Lady  Davis.  The  list  of  the 
company  as  read  to  me  is  a  true  list  of  the  company  composing  such 
detachment,  as  far  as  I  can  remember.  I  went  on  board  of  the  Lady 
Davis  on  Saturday;  we  all  went  on  armed  and  took  our  own  rations 
with  us.  We  returned  that  same  afternoon,  and  the  next  day  the 
steamer  returned  for  us  and  took  us  on  board.  I  was  not  one  of  those 
who  boarded  the  Thompson  for  the  examination  of  her  papers.  I  went 
the  second  trip  of  the  boat  when  a  transfer  of  her  officers  was  made. 
The  party  on  board  the  boat  was  composed  of  sailors  who  rowed  the 
boat,  but  did  not  go  on  board  the  ship.  Lieutenant  Stockton,  Captain 
Elliott,  Mr.  Fripp,  Mr.  Chaplin,  and  myself,  and  perhaps  Midshipman 
Walker,  went  on  board  the  ship.  Regular  posts  were  assigned  to  us; 
we  were  all  stationed  by  the  hatchway,  armed  with  cutlasses  and  pis¬ 
tols;  we  were  the  only  armed  persons  on  board.  The  officers  were  then 
transferred  to  the  Lady  Davis.  Midshipman  Walker,  I  believe,  went 
in  the  boat  with  the  officers  and  steered  the  boat.  When  the  boat 
returned  it  brought  back  some  three  or  four  of  the  crew  of  the  Lady 
Davis  and  a  further  detachment  of  our  company.  The  sailors  of  the 
Lady  Davis  were  armed  with  cutlasses  and  pistols ;  our  muskets  were 
brought  to  us  from  the  Lady  Davis ,  and  we  were  regularly  stationed  in 
various  points  about  the  ship.  When  we  went  on  board  our  detach¬ 
ment  understood  that  we  were  to  take  part  in  whatever  service  might 
be  on  hand,  and  on  this  account  we  took  our  arms  along  with  us.  I 
know  nothing  of  the  conversation  which  took  place  between  Captain 
Elliott  and  Lieutenant  Pelot.  Lieutenant  Pelot  extended  an  invitation 
to  the  detachment  while  they  were  on  the  steamer  on  Saturday,  to 
accompany  the  steamer  the  next  day.  We  were  stationed  over  the 
ship  at  various  points  by  Captain  Elliott. 

Cross-examined  by  Mr.  Miles  : 

I  am  a  private  in  the  Beaufort  Volunteers.  I  acted  under  Captain 
Elliott’s  orders.  Lieutenant  Pelot  did  give  some  orders.  When  we 
were  going  to  the  ship  Lieutenant  Pelot  objected  to  some  one  or  two, 
myself  particularly,  that  were  going  in  the  boat,  thinking,  I  supposed, 
that  the  boat  was  overloaded.  He  gave  other  orders  with  regard  to  the 
part  of  the  Lady  Davis  we  were  to  occupy.  The  Thompson  was  really 
under  the  command  of  Captain  Elliott;  Lieutenant  Stockton  was  only 
his  mouthpiece,  to  issue  the  orders  to  the  crew,  as  I  understood  it. 
The  ship  was  worked  entirely  by  her  own  crew,  and  the  detachment  of 
the  company  and  the  Lady  Davis's  crew  did  the  same  service,  viz,  keep¬ 
ing  guard  over  the  vessel  and  crew  generally.  The  crew  of  the  ship 
seemed  to  work  very  cheerfully ;  there  was  no  resistance.  The  mem¬ 
bers  of  our  company  were  all  gentlemen  of  Beaufort. 

In  reply  by  Mr.  Trescot  : 

When  we  came  in  sight  of  the  Thompson  we  were  assigned  positions 
on  board  the  Lady  Davis  by  Captain  Elliott. 

R.  M.  Fuller. 

Sworn  to  before  me  this  8th  July,  1801. 

R.  C.  Gilchrist, 

C.  8.  Commissioner,

Report  of  Flap -Officer  Stringham ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Atlantic 
Blockading  Squadron,  regarding  transportation  to  the  North  of  families 
of  refugees. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  May  21,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that,  in  compliance 
with  your  instructions  of  May  11,  1861,  containing  a  copy  of  petition 
to  the  President  of  the  United  States  from  certain  persons,  former  resi¬ 
dents  of  Norfolk  and  Portsmouth,  Va.,  that  I  immediately.sent  Com¬ 
mander  A.  Ludlow  Case  with  a  flag  of  truce  to  Norfolk,  who  had  an 
interview  with  the  military  authorities,  who  promised  to  forward  the 
objects  of  the  flag.  In  compliance  with  which  promise,  the  enclosed 
advertisement  was  made,  and  yesterday  a  steamer  from  Norfolk,  in 
charge  of  the  late  Commander  Thomas  T.  Hunter,  of  the  Navy,  deliv¬ 
ered  on  board  the  steamer  Keystone  State  between  75  and  100  women 
and  children.  The  steamer  would  have  proceeded  immediately  to  sea, 
except  for  a  heavy  gale  then  blowing,  and  which  yet  continues  from 
the  northeast. 

She  will  proceed  to  New  York  as  soon  as  the  wind  subsides.  The 
steamer  Star  [ Monticello ]  has  again  been  fired  on  from  the  rebel  bat¬ 
teries  this  morning.  I  think  1  will  send  up  the  Cumberland  and  prevent 
the  completion  of  this  battery. 

Eespectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  LI.  Stringham, 

Senior  Flag-Officer  Blockading  Squadron.

[Enclosure.] 

Special  notice. 

To-day  a  steamer  will  leave  the  railroad  wharf,  Portsmouth,  under  a 
flag  of  truce,  to  visit  the  Federal  fleet  off  Old  Point  Comfort,  for  the 
purpose  ot  taking  to  that  place  all  women  and  children  who  may  wish 
to  join  their  Northern  friends. 

the  boat  will  start  at  12  m.,  and  all  desirous  of  leaving  will  please 
report  themselves  on  board  before  that  time. 

The  families  of  the  following  persons  have  already  permission  to  leave 
in  the  steamer:  James  Hepenstall,  L.  T.  Barnard,  J.  Lucas,  George

Navy  Department,  May  21,  1861. 
Sir:  Your  dispatches  numbered  from  1  to  10,  inclusive,  have  been 
received. 

ilie  Department  would  impress  upon  you  the  necessitv  of  a  rigid 
blockade  ot  the  port  ot  Charleston,  and  "trusts  that  no  effort  will  be 
spared  to  make  it  effective. 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  661 

llie  Niagara  was  ordered  to  that  duty,  but  important  information  as 
o  ciige  shipments  of  arms  to  New  Orleans  and  Mobile  imposed  upon 
the  Department  the  necessity  of  changing  her  destination  to  the  Gulf. 
To  supply  her  place  until  further  disposition  could  be  made,  the  Depart¬ 
ment  on  the  8th  instant  ordered  that  the  Harriet  Lane  should  perform 
that  service,  unless  you  made  other  efficient  arrangements. 

It  is  rumored  that  the  Niagara  has  left  her  station  off  the  port  of 
Charleston,  and  that  the  blockade  is  not  effective.  Trusting  that  such 
is  not  the  case,  but  informing  you  ot  the  report,  the  Department  would 
impress  upon  you  the  necessity  of  dispatching,  if  you  have  not  already 
done  so,  a  sufficient  force  to  close  the  harbor  of  Charleston,  and  there 
should  be  no  letting  up  of  the  blockade  at  that,  nor  indeed  at  any 
other  point. 

It  is  desirable  that  Savannah  should  also  be  blockaded,  and  the  force 
at  your  disposal  already  is  believed  to  be  sufficient  for  that  purpose. 
As  soon  as  possible  an  interdiction  of  all  intercourse  with  the  States 
in  insurrection  should  be  instituted  and  established  and  every  port 
effectually  closed.  This  is  a  primary  object,  and  our  naval  force  should 
not  be  delayed  from  its  execution  or  diverted  to  any  other  purpose.  I 
take  it  for  granted  that  the  Minnesota  will  not  have  left  Hampton  Iioads 
before  the  receipt  of  this  dispatch,  but  as  early  thereafter  as  in  your 
judgment  the  circumstances  will  warrant  it  is  desirable  that  the  force 
which  can  be  spared  from  the  Chesapeake  should  be  set  before  the 
other  ports  on  the  coast,  and  especially  before  the  two  important  ones 
indicated. 

In  a  few  days  the  Wabash  will  join  your  command  and  perform  duty 
wherever  you  shall  direct.  A  list  of  sixteen  vessels  to  constitute  a  part 
of  the  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron  has  already  been  transmitted  to 
you.  Others  of  our  public  vessels,  as  soon  as  they  can  be  got  in  readi¬ 
ness,  will  join  you,  not  only  those  repairing  at  the  yards,  but  others 
returning  from  foreign  stations. 

Commodore  Pendergrast  will  for  the  present  remain  at  his  station 
with  the  Cumberland  while  you  are  absent  with  the  Minnesota ,  and  will 
have,  in  addition  to  such  other  vessel  or  vessels  as  you  may  order, 
Ward’s  flotilla  to  carry  out  his  command.  The  arrival  of  the  Freeborn 
of  this  flotilla  will  enable  you  to  send  the  Dawn  on  more  effective  serv¬ 
ice.  Under  no  circumstances  should  the  blockade  once  established  be 
raised. 

To  your  judgment  and  discretion  the  Department  confides  the  duty 
of  establishing  the  blockade. 

Before  your  arrival  on  your  station  special  instructions  were,  from 
the  necessity  of  the  case,  given  to  such  vessels  as  were  dispatched  to 
check  the  insurgents  and  carry  out  the  purposes  of  the  Government  in 
closing  the  ports.  These  commanders  had  general  instructions  to  cap¬ 
ture  privateers,  vessels  having  arms,  munitions,  or  articles  contraband 
of  war,  or  which  were  sailing  under  any  authority  or  pretended  authority 
not  known  or  recognized  by  the  United  States. 

Each  aud  all  of  these  vessels  from  the  Chesapeake  to  Key  West, 
whatever  may  have  been  their  previous  general  orders,  are  subject  to 
your  command. 

The  importance  of  your  movements  and  the  great  interests  involved 
to  the  Government  and  country  will  render  frequent  and  detailed 
reports  from  you  necessary. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Elag-Officer  S.  H.  Stringham, 

Comdg.  Atlantic  Blockading  /Squadron,  Hampton  Roads,  Virginia.

Report,  of  Flag-Officer  String  ham,  V.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic 

Blockading  Squadron ,  regarding  disposition  of  vessels  of  his  command. 

TJ.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads ,  May  33,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  receipt  of  your  letter  of  May 
17,  with  list  of  vessels  to  compose  the  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

As  soon  as  the  Wabash  arrives  I  shall  send  her  off  Charleston. 

Not  being  acquainted  with  the  force  or  character  of  the  other  vessels, 
except  as  follows,  I  can  not  now  say  the  exact  disposition  I  shall  make 
of  them. 

Brig  Ferry  will  leave  immediately  for  the  coast  of  Florida. 

Harriet  Lane  [isj  very  serviceable  for  the  Chesapeake.  She  can  not 
carry  coal  except  for  a  few  days. 

Dawn  [is]  very  good  for  blockading  York  River. 

Monticello  [is]  now  engaged  in  blockading  James  and  Elizabeth  rivers, 
under  command  of  Captain  Henry  Eagle.  A  most  efficient  vessel. 

Union  [has]  not  arrived;  can  not  speak  of  her. 

Reliance  is  about  the  size  of  a  frigate  launch.  She  could  not  go  into 
the  Chesapeake  Bay  with  the  wind  we  have  had  last  day  or  two. 

Resolute ,  a  sister  vessel,  I  am  informed,  to  the  Reliance. 

Daylight ,  Mount  Vernon,  Penguin,  and  Albatross  have  not  arrived. 
I  can  not,  therefore,  speak  of  them,  and  can  only  repeat  that  nothing 
shall  be  wanting  on  my  part  with  the  vessels.  The  Department  has 
assigned  me  to  keep  as  strict  a  blockade  as  possible  on  the  Atlantic 
coast. 

1  am  glad  to  hear  the  Department  has  purchased  the  Yankee.  She 
is  serviceable  here,  only  requiring  to  have  metal  on  her  to  protect  from 
worms. 

I  again  call  the  attention  of  the  Department  to  the  Quaker  City.  She 
is  a  most  efficient  steamer  and  is  doing  excellent  service  in  boarding 
everything  at  Cape  Henry.  I  hope  she  will  be  retained  here,  though  I 
think  $500  or  $G00  per  diem  will  be  fair  allowance. 

I  also  acknowledge  receipt  of  your  favor  of  May  18.  I  have  and 
shall  continue  to  give  full  protection  to  all  claiming  shelter  of  the 
American  flag. 

I  shall  exercise  my  best  judgment  in  reference  to  disposition  of  prizes 
which  I  may  take.  This  had  led  me  to  send  the  vessels  thus  far  to 
Philadelphia  and  New  York,  which  1  shall  continue,  unless  otherwise 
advised,  except  in  case  of  small  vessels,  which  I  may  send  to  Washing¬ 
ton,  not  being  willing  to  trust  them  to  sea. 

I  shall  be  most  happy  to  communicate  and  cooperate  with  Major- 
General  Butler  on  his  arrival  here.  Since  commencement  of  the  above 
letter  the  Union  has  arrived. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  H.  Strin gii am, 

Flag-Officer,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy.

Office  of  Johnson  &  Higgins, 

Average  Adjusters  and  Insurance  Brokers, 

No.  89  Wall  Street,  New  York,  April  25,  1S61. 

Dear  Sir:  Our  steam  tug,  the  Uncle  Ben,  was  chartered  by  the 
Government  in  connection  with  the  Yankee,  in  which  boat  we  are  also 
interested,  through  Mr.  Russell  Sturgis,  of  this  city,  to  accompany  the 
expedition  to  reenforce  Fort  Sumter. 

Through  the  constant  succession  of  adverse  gales  which  prevailed  at 
the  time,  we  now  learn  that  she  was  compelled  to  put  into  Wilmington, 
N.  0.,  for  coal;  and  by  Mr.  Whitlock,  of  the  firm  of  Jones,  Neilson  & 
Whitlock,  of  this  city,  who  has  just  arrived  from  that  place,  we  are 
informed  that  the  vessel  was  seized  there  by  a  mob,  and  that  after 
temporarily  confining  them  in  the  cabin,  the  officers  and  crew  have 
been  since  thrown  into  prison,  and  from  the  increasing  venom  on  the 
part  of  those  people  against  Northerners,  and  their  knowledge  that  the 
boat  was  employed  in  the  service  named,  we  entertain  serious  appre¬ 
hensions  of  the  safety  of  the  lives  of  the  men.  We  beg  that  you  will 
take  the  subject  into  serious  and  immediate  consideration  and  devise 
some  plan  for  their  relief. 

Yery  respectfully, 

Johnson  &  Higgins. 


Hon.  Simon  Cameron, 

Secretary  of  War,  Washington.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Stringham ,  IT.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic 

Blockading.  Squadron,  regarding  disposition  of  vessels  and  requirements 

for  an  efficient  blockade. 

U.  S..S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads ,  May  24,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  tlie  honor  to  acknowledge  receipt  of  your  letter  of 
instructions  of  May  21,  1861. 

From  the  tenor  of  this  dispatch  I  infer  you  expected  the  Minnesota 
was  or  ought  to  be  at  sea.  Under  this  impression  I  shall  sail  to-morrow 
morning  for  Charleston,  leaving  directions  for  those  vessels  on  the  list 
which  you  furnished  me,  and  which  have  not  yet  arrived,  to  follow  in 
the  same  direction  as  soon  as  they  shall  report  here. 

The  Wabash  is  a  vessel  well  qualified.  The  Albatross,  Penguin ,  Day¬ 
light,  and  Mount  Vernon  I  have  not  seen  and  can  not  therefore  say 
what  qualities  they  possess  for  blockading  at  sea,  but  I  must  in  all 
candor  say  to  the  Department  that  the  Thomas  Freeborn,  Reliance,  and 
Resolute  are  unfit  in  any  respect  to  go  and  be  employed  on  the  Atlantic 
coast,  and  hardly  fit  for  the  Chesapeake.  I  have  sent  Captain  Ward 
with  these  three  vessels  to  the  Potomac  and  down  the  Chesapeake  as 
far  as  the  Eappahannock  to  prevent  any  and  all  communication  from 
Virginia  to  Maryland. 

The  Dawn  being  quite  a  small  vessel,  I  do  not  think  she  can  be 
better  employed  than  at  York  Eiver  and  thereabouts. 

The  Union  has  been  ordered  and  is  now  on  her  way  to  Savannah; 
also  the  Perry  is  on  her  way  to  Florida,  off  St.  Mary’s  Eiver. 

The  Monticello  is  well  employed  in  preventing  all  communication 
from  James  Eiver  to  the  Elizabeth,  and  ready  here  for  other  service 
when  needed. 

The  Harriet  Lane  is  off  Charleston.  The  Cumberland  I  leave  here. 
This  disposes  of  all  the  vessels  of  which  I  have  any  information.  A 
day  or  two  after  my  arrival  the  Pocahontas  came  here  and  informed  me 
she  was  blockading  off  the  mouth  of  the  Eappahannock.  I  have 
learned  from  Captain  Ward,  who  is  direct  from  Washington,  that  this 
last-named  steamer  is  now  at  Washington,  whither  she  has  gone 
without  orders  or  even  my  knowledge  until  now. 

With  this  report  the  Department  will  see  there  is  but  one  vessel  for 
Florida,  and  none  on  the  coast  of  North  Carolina. 

1  would  respectfully  state  to  the  Department  that  in  my  judgment 
to  make  the  blockade  of  the  Atlantic  coast  perfect  and  strict,  I  require 
at  least  from  twelve  to  fifteen  more  efficient  and  seagoing  vessels. 
Steamers  are  preferable,  or  steamers  in  connection  with  sailing  vessels, 
frigates,  or  sloops  of  war. 

1  would  respectfully  state  that  in  my  judgment  there  is  required  at 
least  from  four  to  five  vessels  for  the  coast  of  Florida,  four  or  five  on 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  665 

tlie  coast  of  Georgia,  four  or  five  on  the  coast  of  South  Carolina,  and 
the  same  number  on  the  coast  of  North  Carolina,  and  the  Chesapeake 
will  require  at  least  four  or  five  more.  The  cruising  ground  which  you 
have  assigned  me  is  very  extensive,  from  900  to  1,000  miles.  I  shall 
nevertheless,  do  with  the  means  I  now  have  all  that  1  possiblv  can  to 
carry  into  effect  the  blockade. 

In  your  letter  of  May  18,  you  wish  me  to  communicate  and  cooperate 
v  ith  Major-General  B.  F.  Butler.  I  have  met  with  him  since  his  arrival 
and  we  have  communicated  together  about  affairs  in  this  neighborhood. 
I  have  just  called  upon  him  to  say  that  I  leave  to-morrow,  which  he 
regrets  very  much,  as  he  wishes  the  services  of  the  vessels  in  the 
movement  which  he  contemplates  making. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  H.  Stringjiam, 

Flag-Officer ,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy. 


Letter  from  Flag-Officer  Stringham,  U.  S.  Nary,  commanding  Atlantic 
Blockading  Squadron ,  to  Commodore  Baubling ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding 
existing  conditions  of  his  command. 


U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Hoads,  May  24,  1861. 

Dear  Commodore:  I  have  received  your  esteemed  [favor]  of  21st 
May.  In  answer,  I  shall  tirst  inlorrn  you  that  I  sail  to  morrow  for 
Charleston  to  comply  with  the  generardesire  which  seems  to  prevail 
that  I  should  be  there,  although  ordered  to  the  Chesapeake  by  the 
Department,  as  I  supposed  to  arrange  and  station  the  blockading 
squadron.  When  I  left  Boston,  I  did  not  know  a  single  vessel  that 
would  compose  the  fleet,  except  the  Minnesota. 

On  my  arrival  here,  I  found  the  Cumberland  and  Harriet  Lane.  The 
Monticello  was  at  ^  ork  River,  blockading'  there.  The  Hawn  first 
arrived.  After  I  put  her  in  proper  condition,  she  appearing  from  the 
requests  and  requisitions  made  by  her  commander  to  be  in  want  of 
most  everything,  I  ordered  her  to  relieve  the  Monticello ,  and  ordered 
the  Monticello  to  take  the  station  of  the  Harriet  Lane,  I  having  received 
orders  to  send  the  latter  to  Charleston,  where  she  is  at  present. 

Then  came  the  Perry,  short  of  officers.  I  had  to  detain  her  a  few 
days  for  her  purser,  occupied  in  the  interval  with  supplying  her  many 
wants.  She  is  now  on  her  way  to  Florida. 

Next  came  the  flotilla  of  Captain  Ward.  I  should  like  to  have  you 
see  them,  that  I  might  have  your  opinion  of  their  qualities  for  block¬ 
ading;  two  of  them  certainly  not  equaling  in  safety  or  capacity  a  line- 
of-battle  ship’s  launch,  and  the  Thomas  Freeborn,  the  commander’s 
vessel,  with  guards  I  observed  to  day  about  1  foot  from  the  water’s 
edge.  I  have  sent  them  to-day  to  guard  the  Potomac  and  prevent  all 
intercourse  between  Virginia  and  Maryland. 

Next  comes  the  Union,  a  long,  low  steamer,  and  quite  a  nice  looking 
vessel,  rather  in  distress  from  defective  magazine.  1  hurried  her  off'  to 
Savannah,  and  after  1  leave  in  the  morning,  I  leave  behind  the  Cum¬ 
berland  and  the  Monticello  to  do  duty  at  this  point.  When  I  shall  see 
the  other  vessels  mentioned  I  can  not  now  say,  but  will  give  you  my 


666 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

> 

V 

opinion  that,  with  the  addition  of  twelve  or  fifteen  more  good  vessels, 
of  these  three  or  four  frigates,  for  offshore  cruising,  and  steamers  inshore, 
I  might  make  a  strict  blockade. 

As  you  will  no  doubt  remember,  the  coast  from  Key  West  to  the 
Chesapeake  is  from  900  to  1,000  miles. 

If  you  can  have  the  vessels  sent  me  I  shall  be  much  gratified.  At 
the  same  time  I  will  suggest  that  the  better  arrangement  for  the  com¬ 
mander  of  such  a  squadron  would  be  at  some  point  where  the  vessels 
can  communicate  to  him  and  receive  instructions  for  cruising,  etc., 
from  time  to  time,  until  he  gets  them  fairly  located  according  to  their 
adaptation  for  the  services  required  of  them,  when  he  could  cruise  him¬ 
self  with  more  propriety  and  keep  a  general  supervision  of  the  block¬ 
ade. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  IT.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer ,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Blockading  Squadron,  to  Captain  Eagle,  U.'  S.  Navy,  commanding 

U.  S.  S.  Monticello,  regarding  blockade  duty. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  May  25,  1861. 

Sir  :  Herewith  find  enclosed  the  proclamation  of  the  President  of 
the  United  States  in  reference  to  blockading. 

On  the  arrival  of  the  Harriet  Lane,  which  vessel  will  be  sent  to  relieve 
you  at  your  present  post,  you  will  take  in  a  full  supply  of  coal  and  proceed 
oft  the  harbor  of  Y  ilmington,  JST.  C.  I  wish  to  impress  upon  you  the 
importance  of  maintaining  a  strict  blockade,  preventing  the  ingress 
and  egress  ot  all  vessels,  excepting  under  the  following  exceptions: 

Navy  Department,  May  4,  1861. 

The  Department  would  in  every  instance  allow  at  least  fifteen  days  for  neutral 
vessels  to  depart  with  or  without  cargo  after  the  blockade  is  set  with  sufficient 


force. 


You  will  not  capture  or  detain  any  foreign  vessel  proceeding  toward 
the  entrance  of  a  blockaded  port  if  she  shall  not  previously  have 
received  from  one  of  the  blockading  squadron  a  special  notification  of 
the  existence  of  the  blockade,  provided  she  has  not  contraband  goods 
on  board. 

This  notification  must  be  inserted  in  writing  on  the  muster  roll  of  the 
neutral  vessel  by  the  cruiser  which  meets  her,  and  it  should  contain  the 
announcement,  together  with  statements  of  the  day  and  the  latitude 
and  longitude  in  which  it  was  made. 

You  will  communicate  with  me  as  often  as  convenient.  Wishing  you 
a  pleasant  cruise, 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  II.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Captain  Henry  Eagle, 


U.  S.  Navy. 


[Endorsement.] 


Handed  to  Lieutenant  Braine  this  day,  May  31,  1861. 

Henry  Eagle, 

Captain.

Order  of  Flag-Officer  Pendergrast,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  West  India 
Squadron,  to  Captain  Fagle,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Monti¬ 
cello,  to  cooperate  with  Major-General  Butler,  TJ.  S.  Army. 


U.  S.  Ship  Cumberland, 

Off  Fortress  Monroe,  May  27,  1861. 

Sir  :  General  Butler  having  requested  that  the  steamers  Quaker  City, 
Harriet  Lane,  and  Monticello  be  placed  at  his  disposal,  I  have  granted 
his  request. 

You  will  therefore  be  governed  by  any  orders  you  may  receive  from 
him,  and  on  your  return  report  yourself  to  the  flagship. 

I  have  sent  Lieutenant  Selfridge  on  board  the  Quaker  City  with  an

U.  S.  S.  Monticello  (late  Star), 

Hampton  Roads,  May  27,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  am  in  receipt  of  your  letter  of  yesterday’s  date. 

Herewith  I  enclose  the  report  of  the  engineer  of  this  ship  in  which 
you  will  perceive  the  necessity  of  this  vessel  going  to  a  workshop  to 
have  the  repairs  made.  Should  she  continue  steaming  a  few  days 
more  she  will  require  more  extensive  repairs,  in  addition  to  repairs 
mentioned  in  said  letter.  She  has  cracked  the  starting  bar  and  broken 
the  turnover  center  bar.  The  vessel’s  bottom  is  not  coppered;  she 
should  go  into  fresh  water  to  destroy  the  worms.  The  pivot-gun  car¬ 
riage  requires  considerable  repairs.  It  was  used  on  board  the  frigate 
Mississippi  many  years  ago. 

This  vessel  was  sent  off  from  the  navy  yard  requiring  many  articles 
in  consequence  of  the  great  desire  to  send  her  on  service. 

I  respectfully  state  that  I  consider  that  it  would  not  be  safe  to  send 
this  shiji  to  sea  without  first  completing  the  repairs  required. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Henry  Eagle,

Instructions  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Flag-Officer  Stringham,  U.  S. 
A  ary,  commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  regarding  matters 
pertaining  to  his  command. 


Navy  Department,  May  28, 1861. 

Sir  :  From  the  tenor  of  your  letter  of  the  24th  instant  I  suppose  that 
you  are  at  this  time  oft  Charleston  with  the  Minnesota.  The  importance 
of  a  rigid  and  effectual  blockade  of  that  port  is  a  necessity,  and  it  was 
the  desire  of  the  Department  that  the  blockading  squadron  should 
keep  this  in  view  which  prompted  the  remarks  on  the  21st  instant.  As 
soon  as  the  Wabash  arrives  out  she  can  relieve  you  of  that  duty  and 
enable  you  to  return  with  the  Minnesota  to  Hamilton  Roads,  where  you 
can  probably  best  exercise  your  command  and  direct  the  movements  of 
the  squadron. 

It  is  essential  that  the  intercourse  between  Virginia  and  Maryland 
and  the  opposite  shore  of  Virginia,  which  is  represented  as  carried  on 
to  some  extent,  should  be  prohibited,  and  for  this  duty,  as  well  as  clos¬ 
ing  the  inlets,  it  is  believed  that  the  flotilla  under  Commander  Ward 
will  be  found  serviceable. 


678 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  number  of  vessels  sent  you  is  not  so  large  as  tbe  Department 
would  wish  nor  of  the  description  that  would  be  preferred,  but  we  have 
to  conform  to  existing  circumstances.  We  shall  add  to  the  number  as 
rapidly  as  circumstances  will  admit,  and  if  you  can  not  line  the  whole 
coast  with  vessels  you  will  use  such  as  you  have  to  the  best  advantage 
by  closiug  the  most  important  points  to  the  extent  of  your  ability. 

Had  the  Department  received  your  dispatch  suggesting  that  the 
Cumberland  should  be  assigned  to  the  blockading  duty  off'  Charleston, 
it  would  have  assented  most  cheerfully  to  the  proposition,  for  the  object 
was  and  is  a  strict  blockade  of  that  harbor.  The  late  arrival  of  the 
Minnesota  on  tbe  blockading  ground  rendered  it  necessary  that  the 
Department  should  assign  such  of  the  vessels  to  duty  which  were  there 
in  advance  of  her.  It  will  be  happy  to  be  relieved  of  this  necessity 
and  to  commit  the  entire  charge  of  the  squadron  to  you,  unless  other¬ 
wise  specifically  ordered. 

The  Pawnee ,  Pocahontas ,  and  some  small  steamers  on  the  upper  waters 
of  the  Potomac  will  be  more  immediately  under  the  supervision  of  the 
commandant  of  the  Washington  navy  yard  and  this  Department. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Flag-Officer  S.  H.  Stringham, 

Commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  off  Charleston.

Report  of  Flap- Officer  Stringham ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Atlantic  Block¬ 
ading  Squadron,  regarding  vessels  required  for  an  efficient  blockade. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 

Off  Charleston  Harbor,  May  30,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  tlie  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  I  arrived  off 
this  harbor  the  evening  of  May  28,  and  the  experience  of  a  day  con¬ 
firms  the  propriety  and  correctness  of  my  suggestions  heretofore  made 
to  the  Department  as  to  the  number  and  class  of  vessels  requisite  to 
establish  and  carry  out  a  strict  blockade  of  the  Atlantic  coast — not 
less  than  five  or  six  for  the  coast  of  each  State,  and  they  fast  and  of 
sufficient  capacity  to  carry  coal  for  some  time,  like  the  Pensacola,  Hart¬ 
ford,  Iroquois ,  and  that  class,  or  the  Atlantic  and  Baltic,  with  two 
heavy  guns,  not  less  than  10-inch. 

Such  as  the  Dawn  and  her  class  are  of  little  use  for  Atlantic  block¬ 
ading. 

Yesterday,  29th,  while  we  lay  close  in  near  the  bar,  a  steamer  came 
down  toward  us  from  Charleston  under  great  head  of  steam.  I  stood 
off  a  little  in  hopes  she  would  follow  us  into  deep  water.  I  intended 
to  try  and  cut  her  off,  but  she  only  came  a  little  way  outside  of  the  bar 
and  then  returned.  She  was  very  fast,  going  2  miles  to  our  1 ;  others 
were  visible  up  in  the  harbor. 

I  was  in  hopes  of  finding  the  Harriet  Lane  off  here,  but  did  not,  she 
no  doubt  having  returned  to  Hampton  Eoads  for  coal. 

This  morning  I  discovered  a  steamer,  which  proved  to  be  the  Union. 
She  is  out  of  coal.  I  shall  send  her  to  Hampton  Eoads  for  supply,  with 
orders  to  return  immediately. 

I  trust  the  Department  will  give  me  vessels  of  the  class  I  have  men¬ 
tioned  above,  and  sufficient  in  numbers  to  make  an  efficient  blockade. 
I  can  not  make  it  strict  with  less  than  20  or  25  vessels  on  the  Atlantic, 
besides  those  small  ones  which  are  only  fit  for  the  Chesapeake. 

I  boarded  last  night  a  small  schooner  from  North  Carolina,  bound  to 
Florida.  I  ordered  her  to  return  to  North  Carolina. 

With  the  number  of  vessels  I  have  stated  above,  most  no  doubt 
being  steamers,  they  would  keep  a  strict  coast  guard  in  passing  and 
repassing  for  their  coal  at  Hampton  Eoads  from  their  various  stations. 

I  shall  remain  off  here  as  long  as  my  coal  will  permit  and  then 
return  to  Hampton  Eoads  for  supply. 

Eespectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  H.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy.

Report  of  Lieutenant  Trenchard,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Key¬ 
stone  State,  of  the  movements  of  that  vessel  on  transport  duty. 

U.  S.  S.  Keystone  State, 

Washington,  May  31,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  arrival  of  this  vessel,  which  sailed 
from  here  under  instruction  from  the  Department  of  the  16th  instant. 

The  Keystone  State  left  Washington  on  the  17th,  reaching  the  squad¬ 
ron  in  Hampton  Roads  the  following  morning.  I  communicated  at  once 
with  Flag-Officer  Stringham  in  reference  to  the  refugees  from  Norfolk, 
and  he  directed  me  to  await  their  arrival. 

At  2  p.  m.  on  the  20th,  116  women  and  children  were  brought  down 
from  Norfolk  under  a  flag  of  truce  and  placed  on  board  this  steamer. 

The  sailing  of  the  vessel,  in  consequence  of  a  northeast  gale,  was ' 
delayed  until  the  morning  of  the  22d,  when  she  left  for  New  York, 
with  the  English  bark  Hiawatha  in  tow,  by  direction  of  Flag-Officer 
Stringham.  The  bark  was  seized  for  violating  blockade.  During  the 
delay  attending  the  sailing  of  the  Keystone  State  35  of  the  refugees 
were  transferred  by  their  own  request  to  the  Baltimore  and  Philadel¬ 
phia  steamer  for  passage.  Accompanying  this  will  be  found  a  list  of 
the  names  of  the  refugees.  The  steamer  arrived  at  New  York  at  6  p.  m., 
the  22d,  and  the  passengers  soon  after  landed  in  safety.  The  Hiawatha 
was  anchored  near  the  navy  yard,  in  charge  of  her  prize  master,  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Russell,  XT.  S.  Navy.  The  munitions,  etc.,  were  landed  at  the 
navy  yard,  and  after  receiving  on  board  the  provisions  and  stores  for 
Washington,  together  with  articles  shipped  for  the  use  of  the  squadron 
off  Fortress  Monroe,  by  order  of  Commodore  Breese,  we  left  the  navy 
yard  at  New  York  at  noon  of  the  29th  and  in  twenty-four  hours  after 
reached  Hampton  Roads,  communicated  with  Flag-Officer  Pendergrast, 
and  left  for  Washington,  arriving  at  4  oYlock  p.  in.  this  day. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Stephen  D.  Trenohard, 

Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Letter  from  Lieutenant  Lowry ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  U.  S.  8.' Pawnee,  to  the  Sec¬ 
retary  of  the  Navy ,  suggesting  means  for  making  effectual  the  blockade 
of  Norfolk  and  Richmond ,  Va. 

U.  S.  S.  Pawnee, 
Potomac  River ,  June  f  1861. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  submit  to  the  consideration  of  the  Government  of 
the  United  States  the  following  information  and  suggestions : 

By  the  enclosed  pamphlet*  and  maps*  it  will  be  perceived  that  Norfolk 
and  Richmond  are  not  yet  blockaded  or  completely  cut  off  from  the  sea. 
They  have  a  back  outlet  by  way  of  the  Chesapeake  and  Albemarle 
Canal.  By  that  water  route  vessels  of  any  draft,  by  lightening,  buoy¬ 
ing,  or  floating,  can  be  passed  from  Richmond  or  Norfolk  through  said 
work,  which  is  GO  feet  wide  and  has  an  average  depth  of  8  feet,  into 
North  Landing  River;  thence,  through  Coanjock  Bay,  by  the  North 
Carolina  cut  of  the  canal,  into  North  River,  through  Albemarle,  Cro- 
atan,  and  Pamlico  sounds,  to  the  entrance  of  Ocracoke  Inlet,  when,  with 
little  nautical  skill,  vessels  of  heavy  drafts  can  be  easily  passed  into 
the  ocean.  A  simple  inspection  of  the  maps  will  convince  the  naval 
officer  of  the  great  advantages  and  facilities  the  enemy  will  have  in 
possessing  this  vast  internal  water  navigation  unmolested,  thereby 
having  an  egress  and  retreat  to  and  from  the  sea  for  vessels  loaded 
with  provisions  and  munitions,  and  an  easy  harbor  for  prizes  or  cap¬ 
tured  goods  taken  out  of  prizes  of  too  heavy  a  draft  to  cross  the  inlet, 
or  a  safe  refuge  for  privateers  from  our  heavy  ships  of  war.  Already 
are  their  privateers  preying  upon  our  commerce,  and  from  these  very 
waters  issue  with  impunity. 

Our  statistics  inform  us  that  a  great  portion  of  our  coasting  trade 
frequents  the  waters  of  North  Carolina.  We  are  also  informed  that  the 
waters  of  these  inland  sounds  wash  the  shores  of  a  vast  soil,  abounding 
in  rich  productions,  as  cotton,  corn,  grain,  lumber,  tuiqientine,  and  pro¬ 
visions  of  all  kinds.  The  fisheries  are  of  great  value  and  extensively 
worked.  The  shores  of  Currituck  are  lined  with  large  and  expensive 
hotels  and  cottages,  where  in  summer  crowds  of  wealthy  resort  for  sum¬ 
mer  bathing.  Nag’s  Head  is  a  place  of  great  importance  in  this  respect. 
The  waters  are  covered  with  vessels  carrying  on  inland  trade,  while 
many  steamers  ply  to  and  from  the  many  towns  and  villages.  All  this 
being  the  case,  and  having  an  uninterrupted  communication  with  Nor¬ 
folk  and  Richmond  by  water,  the  effect  of  a  blockade  from  the  Rip 
Raps  will  to  a  great  extent  be  evaded,  except  as  against  our  own  North¬ 
ern  commerce  and  of  foreign  nations.  I  believe  it  to  be  my  duty  to 
bring  to  the  notice  of  the  Government  facts  which  may  have  been  over¬ 
looked,  and  to  suggest  that  an  effective  blockade  of  Ocracoke  Inlet 
and  Beaufort  is  absolutely  [necessary]  to  cut  Norfolk  and  Richmond 
from  communication  with  the  sea,  and  to  prevent  the  rebel  privateers 
from  putting  to  sea  from  the  waters  of  North  Carolina,  and  effectually 
blockade  her  ports.  In  my  opinion,  this  can  be  accomplished  by  the 
stationing  of  two  vessels  of  war  outside— of  the  Paionee  class— and  by 
the  equipment  of  several  steam  canal  boats  of  the  type  of  the  J.  Jerome 
and  Diamond  State ,  now  plying  to  this  port.  These  vessels  draw  little 
water,  are  strong,  can  carry  a  rifle  gun,  and  sufficient  stores  and  men  to 
make  them  efficient  enough  to  meet  anything  in  the  waters  of  North 
Carolina.  In  case  of  meeting  overpowering  numbers,  intending  to  board, 
they  are  sufficiently  high  out  of  water  to  make  that  hazardous,  and  with 
the  larger  vessel  in  the  offing  they  can  always  have  a  base  to  fall  back 


Not  found.

upou.  A  number  of  these  vessels  are  accessible  on  the  Cheasapeake 
and  Delaware,  and  Delaware  and  Earitan  Canal  Company.  The  under¬ 
signed  confidently  asserts  that  there  is  no  part  of  the  country  in  armed 
rebellion  against  the  Government  which  can  be  so  easily  and  so  terribly 
made  to  feel  the  power  of  the  United  States  by  its  occupation  by  the 
Federal  forces  as  the  inland  coast  of  North  Carolina.  So  long  as  the 
canal  is  open  and  in  the  hands  of  tile  rebels  Norfolk  and  Richmond,  in

in  North  Carolina,  have  a  ready  access  to  the  sea  or  an  easy  and  safe 
communication  with  each  other. 

The  undersigned’s  knowledge  of  this  matter  arises  from  a  large  pecu¬ 
niary  interest  which  he  and  his  family  hold  in  shares,  the  work  having 
been  entirely  done  by  Northern  men  and  capital.  Any  information 
desired  by  the  Department  will  be  cheerfully  given.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Pender grast,  U.  S.  Nary ,  commanding  West  India 
Squadron ,  regarding  the  blockading  force  off  Fortress  Monroe. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Cumberland, 

Off  Fortress  Monroe,  Va.,  June  2 ,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  would  respectfully  inform  the  Department  that  it  will  be  nec¬ 
essary  for  me  to  send  the  U.  S.  S.  Quaker  City  to  New  York  for  repairs 
and  that  she  may  receive  a  proper  crew  under  her  new  charter.  She 
will  not  be  absent  longer  than  four  or  live  days.  I  would  also  state 
that  the  blockading  force  here  is  small  at  present,  being  composed 
entirely  of  this  ship,  Harriet  Lane ,  Quaker  City ,  and  the  U.  S.  S.  Baum, 
now  at  the  mouth  of  York  River.  The  captured  steam  tug  Young 
America ,  which  has  been  very  serviceable  to  us  here,  has  at  last  broken 
down  and  it  is  absolutely  necessary  that  she  should  go  to  some  place 
for  repairs,  and  I  would  feel  obliged  if  the  Department  would  order 
another  small  tug  in  her  place,  to  act  as  a  tender  to  this  ship. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  J.  Pendergrast, 

Flag-Officer,  Commanding  West  India  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.
