Report  of  Flag-Officer  Stringham,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Atlantic 
Blockading  Squadron,  regarding  the  movements  of  the  flagship,  and  the 
capture,  June  3,  1861,  by  U.  S.  brig  Perry ,  of  the  Confederate  privateer 
schooner  Savannah. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 

Off  Charleston  Harbor,  June  6,  1861. 
Sir  :  Since  my  arrival  on  this  station,  of  which  I  apprised  you,  I  have 
been  engaged  in  carrying  into  effect  the  blockade. 

The  first  vessel  spoken  was  May  29,  a  small  schooner,  the  Mary,  from 
Washington,  N.  C.,  bound  to  Jacksonville,  Fla.  I  ordered  her  back  to 
North  Carolina. 

The  Norwegian  consul  came  out  on  the  30th  of  May,  to  endeavor  to 
get  permission  for  the  Norwegian  bark  Admiral  Peter  Tordenskjold  to 


692  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

% 

V 

take  in  cargo  and  go  to  sea.  This  I  could  not  allow.  I  finally  per¬ 
mitted  the  vessel  to  go  to  sea  in  ballast. 

The  next  vessel  stopped  was  May  31,  the  English  schooner  Eliza  and 
Catherine ,  with  rice  and  lumber,  from  Charleston,  bound  to  Harbor 
Island.  I  ordered  her  back,  with  permission  to  discharge  cargo  and  go 
in  ballast,  but  reversed  this  decision  and  finally  permitted  her  to  go  with 
cargo,  on  the  personal  representation  to  me  by  the  British  consul,  ltobert 
Bunch,  esq.,  on  his  word  of  honor,  and  in  writing,  that  Captain  McKean, 
of  the  Niagara ,  had  told  him  “  twenty  days  would  be  permitted  for  ves¬ 
sels  to  depart,”  with  the  addition  that  “his  senior  (myself)  might  change 
the  terms.”  I  did  not  feel  disposed  to  alter  the  understanding  and 
arrangement,  as  I  have  endeavored  from  the  commencement,  as  I  shall 
continue  in  the  future,  to  inconvenience  as  little  as  possible  neutrals. 

On  the  2d  June  I  warned  off  a  Bremen  bark,  the  Copernicus ,  from 
Bremen  for  Charleston,  in  ballast. 

On  the  3d  of  June,  warned  off  the  Spanish  bark  Teresa  Cubana ,  from 
Barcelona  for  Charleston,  in  ballast. 

Nothing  thus  far  has  gone  in  or  out  without  my  permission,  except 
small  vessels,  which  our  depth  of  water  will  not  allow  us  to  overtake. 

June  5,  about  10  o’clock  a.  m.,  our  masthead  lookout  made  a  sail, 
which  proved  to  be  the  U.  S.  brig  Perry,  Lieutenant  Commanding  Par¬ 
rott,  with  a  prize  in  company,  it  being  a  piratical  schooner  of  about  50 
tons,  called  the  Savannah,  hailing  from  Charleston,  S.  C.,  with  a  com¬ 
mission  from  Jefferson  Davis,  dated  Montgomery,  May  18,  1861,  com¬ 
manded  by  T.  Harrison  Baker,  and  a  crew  of  nineteen  men.  She  had 
placed  some  of  her  crew  on  board  a  prize,  the  brig  Joseph ,  of  Dockland, 
Me.,  from  Cardenas,  with  sugar,  which  she  had  captured  on  the  3d 
instant,  and  ordered  to  Beaufort,  S.  C.  The  captain  of  the  Joseph , 
retained  on  board  the  schooner,  now  goes  to  New  York  in  company  with 
the  prize  master. 

I  herewith  enclose  a  copy  of  Lieutenant  Commanding  Parrott’s  report.* 

I  shall  order  the  schooner  to  New  York  in  charge  of  Prize  Master 
B.  S.  McCook,  midshipman. 

I  beg  leave  most  respectfully  to  remind  the  Department  that  I  am 
very  much  in  want  of  vessels. 

The  prisoners  of  the  schooner  Savannah,  captain,  lieutenant,  sailing 
master,  purser,  and  10  men,  G  having  been  sent  away  in  their  prize,  the 
Joseph,  are  on  board  the  Minnesota ,  and  will  be  sent  on  the  first  oppor¬ 
tunity  to  a  Northern  port. 

The  Perry  has  proceeded  to  her  station  off  Pernandina. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  H.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gjdeon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy.

Report  of  Midshipman  McCook ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  of  arrival  at  New  York  in 
command  of  prize  schooner  Savannah. 

New  York,  June  17 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  my  arrival  at  this  place  in  charge  of 
the  “armed  and  piratical  schooner  Savannah,”  captured  by  the  U.  S. 
brig  Perry ,  on  the  3d  of  June.  I  have  in  my  possession  a  letter  of 
marque  under  which  the  schooner  sailed,  signed  by  Jefferson  Davis, 
and  the  Savannah’s  log  book,  all  of  which  I  have  delivered  to  the 
proper  authorities  at  this  place.  I  bring  with  me  as  passengers  the 
captain  of  the  American  brig  Joseph ,  captured  by  the  Savannah ,  and 
Joseph  Leeds,  a  native  of  New  Jersey.  I  have  also  one  of  the  Savan¬ 
nah’s  crew,  who  will  be  delivered  to  the  U.  S.  marshal.  In  compliance 
with  my  orders,  I  will  at  once  return  to  my  ship. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedieut  servant, 

It.  Sheldon  McCook, 
Midshipman ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

cello,  regarding  the  condition  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Monticello, 

June  3,  1861. 

Sir:  I  find,  upon  enquiry,  that  this  vessel  has  not  been  docked  for 
over  twenty  months.  This,  in  connection  with  the  fact  that  her  bot¬ 
tom,  now  in  sight,  already  shows  signs  of  the  attack  of  the  worms,  I 
would  suggest  the  importance  of  her  being  sent  to  the  nearest  point  to 
be  docked,  cleaned,  and  to  receive  a  coat  of  patent  verdigris,  or  cop¬ 
pered.  She  is  not  coppered,  save  a  few  feet  below  the  water  line  from 
amidships  forward,  and  iii  southern  waters  she  would  soon  be  rendered 
unfit  for  service. 

I  am,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I).  L.  Braine,  IJ.  S.  Navy, 

Lieutenant.

U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane, 

Hampton  Roads ,  June  4 ,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  communi¬ 
cation  of  the  3d  instant,  with  its  enclosures.  In  reply  I  have  to  say 
that  I  am  confident  that  no  steamboat  or  tug  has  passed  down  James 
River  since  I  have  been  placed  at  Newport  News  to  assist  in  its  protec¬ 
tion.  There  is  a  tug  [that]  comes  down  from  Norfolk  every  night  as  far 
as  the  batteries  at  Sewell’s  Point  and  returns  in  the  morning,  always 
under  cover  of  the  guns  of  the  above-named  place.  Craney  Island 
Flats  prevent  my  getting.said  steamer  within  range  of  the  guns  of  this 
vessel.  I  would  respectfully  state  that  I  have  again  made  a  careful 
reconnoissance  of  the  shore  opposite  Newport  News,  and  have  fio  report 
that  there  is  a  sand  battery  on  the  south  side  of  Nausemond  River  at 
Pig  Point,  prepared  to  mount  seven  guns,  but  it  is  not  yet  finished,  and 
1  am  inclined  to  think  that  no  guns  are  yet  mounted,  although  there 
appears  to  be  about  fifty  men  employed  in  completing  the  work.  There 
is  also  a  battery  on  the  south  side  of  Chuckatuck  Creek  preparing  for 
four  guns.  To  the  eastward  of  Nansemond  River,  at  the  mouth  of  Hog 
Creek,  there  is  a  field  battery  of  three  guns.  From  that  point  to  Cra¬ 
ney  Island,  a  distance  of  about  3.1  miles,  I  see  nothing  indicating  guns 
or  batteries.  I  have  examined  James  River  as  high  as  Day’s  Point  (10 
or  12  miles  above  its  mouth)  and  no  signs  of  fortifications  can  be  seen. 
I  have  tried  during  the  morning  to  draw  the  fire  of  the  batteries  by

The  above  is  respectfully  submitted  by  your  obedient  servant,

IT.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane, 

Hampton  Iioads ,  June  5,  1861. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  orders  from  General  Butler  to  make  a  recon- 
noissance  of  Pig  Point  and  vicinity,  etc.,  I  this  morning  at  4:50  got 
underway  with  my  ship  from  off  Newport  News  and  stood  toward  Craney 
Island,  steaming  close  in  and  along  the  shore.  When  off  Pig  Point  I 
observed  near  the  beach  a  number  of  men  apparently  engaged  in 
transporting  guns  by  means  of  ox  teams  and  wheel  carriages,  while 
others  were  seen  near  the  embrasures  of  the  battery  with  the  secession 
flag  flying  over  them.  At  8:30  a.  m.  I  approached  as  close  to  the  bat¬ 
tery  as  the  flats  would  allow,  a  distance  of  about  1,800  yards,  and 
opened  fire,  which  was  promptly  returned  by  the  rebels,  from,  I  )udge, 
seven  guns,  four  of  which  were  either  42  or  32  pounders  and  the  others 
appeared  to  be  24-pounder  howitzers.  Two  of  the  shot  took  effect  on  the 
vessel,  one  passing  through  the  plank-sheer  forward  of  the. fore  rigging 
on  the  port  side  and  out  through  the  starboard  bulwarks;  the  other 
through  the  fore  rigging,  grazing  the  foremast.  Several  of.their  heavy 
shot  passed  over  the  vessel  and  struck  some  distance  beyond..  The  shell 
from  their  howitzers  all  fell  short.  Thirty  rounds  of  shot  and  shell  were 
thrown  by  us,  nearly  all  of  which  fell  short;  some  few,  however,  were 
observed  to  strike  within  the  embrasures.  The  rebels  fired  about  fifty 
shotand  shell.  Having  accomplished  my  object  o.f  drawing  the  fire  of  the 
enemy,  and  thereby  discovering  the  strength  of  their  battery,  and  find¬ 
ing  the  range  of  my  guns  less  than  theirs,  after  an  engagement  of 
forty-five  minutes  I  drew  off  out  of  range.  From  the  enclosed  report 
of  the  surgeon  yoa  w.ill  perceive  that  five  of  our  men  were  wounded. 
It  affords  me  much  pleasure  to  bear  testimony  to  the  gallant  conduct 
of  the  officers  and  men  under  my  command. 

Respectfully  submitted. 

John  Faitjstce,  Captain. 

Flag-Officer  G.  J.  Pendergrast, 

Commanding  West  India  Squadron ,  off  Fortress  Monroe ,  Va.

Report  of  Brigadier-General  Huger,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  at  Norfolk,  Va.,  regarding 

attack  on  Pig  Point  battery. 

Headquarters  Forces  of  Virginia, 

Norfolk,  Va.,  June  6  [5],  1861. 

Sir  :  The  steamer  Harriet  Lane  was  occupied  yesterday  in  reconnoiter- 
ing  our  battery  at  Pig  Point,  mouth  of  the  Xansemond  Eiver,  and  this 
morning  took  up  a  position  and  opened  fire  upon  the  battery,  doing  but 
little  damage  and  injuring  no  one.  The  battery  replied,  and  after  firing 
some  twenty  shots  the  steamer  hauled  off  suddenly  and  proceeded  to 
Old  Point. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Benj.  Huger, 

Brigadier-  General ,  Commanding . 

Major-General  E.  E.  Lee, 

Commanding  Forces  of  Virginia. 

P.  S. — One  gun,  a  32-pounder,  burst,  without  injuring  any  one.  I 
have  sent  two  to  replace  it.

ing  attack  on  Pig  Point  battery. 

Headquarters  Forces  Norfolk  Harbor, 

Norfolk ,  Va.,  June  7,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  received  information  that  on  the  5th  instant  the  Harriet 
Lane  was  hit  twice  by  the  battery  at  Pig  Point.  One  shot  struck  the 
waterways,  passed  through  a  tub  of  musket  balls,  damaged  the  fore¬ 
mast,  and  weut  out  through  the  top  of  the  rail.  Six  men  were  wounded 
by  the  scattering  of  the  musket  balls. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Ben.t.  Huger,

Report  of  Commander  Pegram,  Virginia  navy,  of  the  attack  by  U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane  on  Pig 

Point  battery. 

Pig  Point  Battery,  June  5,  1861. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  the  Federal  steamer  Harriet 
Lane  stood  within  range  of  this  battery  at  9  a.  m.  to-day,  and,  taking 
a  position  at  the  distance  of  1J  miles,  commenced  firing  upon  us  with 


700 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


shot  and  shell  from  11  inch  shell  gun  and  32  pounders.  v  She  fired  about 
thirty- three  shot  and  shell,  many  of  them  well  directed,  but  no  one  of 
our  party  was  hurt,  nor  did  the  fortifications  sustain  any  injury.  A  32- 
pounder  shot  struck  the  muzzle  of  one  of  our  8-iuch  shell  guns  and 
cracked  it  from  the  face  to  the  chase  ring.  The  gun  at  the  same  time 
was  run  in  for  loading,  and  although  the  shot  was  broken  into  three 
fragments  in  the  midst  of  our  men,  no  one  sustained  the  slightest  injury. 
A  number  of  shells  exploded  near  and  around  us,  but  all  fell  harmless 
to  the  ground.  In  return,  we  fired  twenty-three  shot  and  shell.  Four 
or  five  were  seen  to  take  effect  in  the  hull  of  the  steamer,  and  I  am 
inclined  to  believe  did  her  some  injury,  from  the  manner  in  which  she 
moved. 

For  men  who  had  never  before  been  in  action,  the  Portsmouth  Rifles 
were  remarkably  cool  and  self-possessed,  and  after  a  few  rounds  got  the 
range  of  the  enemy  and  fired  admirably  well.  Every  officer  and  man 
behaved  in  the  most  spirited  and  creditable  manner,  and  were  so  regard¬ 
less  of  danger  that  I  had  often  to  interpose  my  authority  to  prevent 
their  exposing  themselves  unnecessarily  to  the  enemy’s  fire.  The  action 
lasted  about  fifteen  or  twenty  minutes. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  B.  Pegram, 
Commander ,  Virginia  Navy. 

Commodore  French  Forrest, 

Virginia  Navy ,  Commanding  Naval  Station ,  Norfolk,  Va.

the  insurgent  States,  with  your  remarks  as  to  the  number  and  class  of 
vessels  requisite  for  that  service,  have  been  duly  considered,  and  so  far 
as  circumstances  will  admit  it  will  be  the  policy  of  the  Department  to 
carry  them  into  effect. 

We  have  not  vessels  of  the  exact  description  wanted  for  this  service 
at  the  present  moment,  and  must  therefore  avail  ourselves  of  such  as 
we  have.  It  will  be  a  primary  object  to  close  the  principal  ports,  and 
with  the  remaining  vessels  (together  with  such  as  are  passing  to  and 
from  the  depots  or  on  orders)  to  perform  coast-guard  service.  In  this 
way  an  interdiction  of  commercial  intercourse  with  the  insurgents  will 
be  substantially  effected. 

It  is  the  intention  of  the  Government  to  prohibit  foreigners  from  hav¬ 
ing  traffic  and  making  exchanges  with  those  who  are  in  insurrection. 
There  is  no  place,  except  at  Alexandria,  where  there  is  a  collection 
district,  with  the  proper  collecting  officers,  to  collect  revenue  duties  or 
grant  clearances,  in  any  of  the  insurrectionary  States. 

Foreigners,  consequently,  should  not  enter  and  leave  these  harbors 
and  traffic  with  the  insurgents,  nor  must  there  be  intercommunication 
by  sea  with  them  on  the  part  of  our  own  citizens  in  any  of  the  States 
while  they  are  resisting  the  Government  and  disregarding  its  laws. 

It  is  possible  that  some  of  the  lighter  craft  may  in  thick  weather  and 
at  night  run  the  blockade,  but  your  great  effort  will  be  to  prevent  it. 
For  this  purpose  the  suggestion  is  a  good  one,  that  there  should  be 
before  each  of  the  principal  ports  one  large  vessel  attended  by  two 
others  of  lighter  draft. 

The  great  hazard  that  must  be  run  will  soon  cause  a  general  cessa¬ 
tion  of  commercial  intercourse,  and  unremitting  vigilance  will  effec¬ 
tually  extinguish  it.  The  Wabash ,  unless  you  otherwise  direct,  will  be 
ordered  to  relieve  you,  and  thus  enable  you  to  renew  your  position  at 
Hampton  Roads. 

It  has  been  deemed  advisable  to  continue  Flag-Officer  Pendergrast 
and  the  vessels  of  his  squadron,  with  the  exception  of  the  Macedonian 
and  Bainbridge ,  on  the  coast  to  aid  and  assist  in  the  blockade,  until  we 
can  add  to  your  command  from  other  sources. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Flag-Officer  S.  H.  Stringham, 

Commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

by  a  gentleman  of  character  and  respectable  position  in  society,  whose 
statements  1  think  may  be  relied  on  as  correct.  Whether  you  can 
ascertain  further  particulars,  or  would  be  able  to  afford  relief  to  the 
parties  thus  detained  for  discharging  their  duty  with  fidelity,  I  am  una¬ 
ble  to  advise,  but  communicate  to  you  the  facts  in  the  case. 

The  difficulty  of  supplying  your  squadron  with  water  on  this  exten¬ 
sive  line  of  coast  has  suggested  itself  to  the  Department  as  well  as

yourself.  Could  the  Government  possess  itself  of  an  accessible  posi¬

where  it  could  obtain  a  supply  of  water  and  perhaps  have  a  coal  depot,

[Enclosure.] 


Confidential.]  Guilford,  Conn.,  June  2 ,  1861. 

Dear  Sir  :  I  am  in  possession  of  facts  respecting  the  port  of  George¬ 
town,  S.  C.,  which  I  feel  it  my  duty  to  communicate  to  your  Depart¬ 
ment,  and  I  write  at  the  request  of  Hon.  John  Woodruff,  ex-Memberof 
Congress  from  this  district.  Perhaps  you  may  recollect,  sir,  that  I  have 
spent  a  number  of  years  in  Georgetown,  S.  C.,  and  a  friend  of  mine  has 
just  returned  from  there. 

They  have  in  the  jail  of  that  place  the  collector  and  his  deputy. 

John  Merriman,  the  collector,  has  been  confined  since  last  December 
for  merely  writing  to  the  Department  his  intention  of  clearing  vessels 
from  that  port  as  before,  under  the  United  States,  and  they  are  now 
threatening  to  hang  them. 

There  is  a  man  in  that  place  who  has  a  commission  from  Jeff.  Davis 
for  privateering,  and  is  about  fitting  out  a  craft  for  that  purpose. 

A  great  proportion  of  the  rice  grown  in  South  Carolina  is  raised  in 
that  vicinity,  and  is  carried  by  steamers  to  Charleston.  The  steamers 
which  carry  the  rice  run  the  blockade  in  foggy  weather  by  keeping- 
close  inshore. 

We  have  a  number  of  Northern  merchants  there,  whose  goods  have 
just  been  confiscated  and  they  ordered  to  leave.  They  are  now  ready 
to  volunteer  their  services  to  our  Government  to  go  back  and  open  the 
jail  doors  and  liberate  those  true-hearted  patriots,  provided  the  Gov¬ 
ernment  will  send  a  steamer.  The  bar  affords  11  feet  of  water  at  high 
tide.  It  would  require  but  a  small  force  to  accomplish  it. 

If,  sir,  you  should  consider  these  matters  of  sufficient  importance  for 
your  attention,  I  can  give  you  every  particular  respecting  the  place,  the 
entrance,  and  a  good  pilot  over  the  bar. 

Ybrnrs,  very  respectfully, 


F.  A.  Drake. 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy.

oidy  this  ship  and  the  Harriet  Lane  in  Hampton  Boads,  and  the  Damn

[Enclosure.] 

IT.  S.  S.  Quaker  City, 

Hampton  Roads ,  June  7 ,  1861, 

Sir:  Pursuant  to  your  letter  of  instructions,  I  have  made  an  exami¬ 
nation  of  the  boilers  and  engine  of  the  U.  S.  steam  tug  Yankee  and  find 
the  engine  entirely  out  of  order  and  unlit  for  service. 

I  find  that  the  steam  and  exhaust  valves  leak  so  badly  as  to  necessi¬ 
tate  their  being  faced  or  newly  ground  in;  that  the  cam  is  so  much 
worn  as  to  require  entire  renewal.  The  air  pump  is  also  not  in  good 
order,  the  floating  top  requiring  a  new  face.  The  force  pumps  of  the 
engine  require  overhauling.  All  the  connections  of  the  engine  require 
to  be  fitted  with  new  brasses.  The  steam  or  donkey  pump  requires  thor¬ 
ough  overhauling,  as  it  will  not  work  either  on  the  sea  or  bilge.  I  find 
that  the  boiler  is  so  much  exposed  as  to  require  covering  with  felt  and 
canvas  to  prevent  condensation,  and  also  that  the  safety  valve  leaks  so 
badly  as  to  render  it  impossible  to  keep  any  pressure  of  steam  on  the 
boiler.  The  base  of  the  smoke  pipe  requires  an  apron  fitted  to  it  so  as 
to  prevent  rain  or  other  water  from  running  over  the  steam  drum  or 
boiler. 

Most  respectfully,  yours,  obediently, 

S.  Farrer, 

Chief  Engineer  U.  S.  S.  Quaker  City. 

Flag-Officer  Pendergrast,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  U.  S.  Naval  Forces ,  Hampton  Roads.

TJ.  S.  Flagship  Cumberland, 

Off  Fortress  Monroe,  Va.,  June  8,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  of  the  capture  of 
a  small  sloop  of  about  15  or  20  tons  on  the  5th  instant  by  the  U.  S.  S. 
Harriet  Lane.  The  said  sloop  was  loaded  with  provisions,  and  for  some 
time  past  has  been  engaged  in  carrying  marketing  from  Smithfield  to 
Norfolk.  1  have  directed  that  she  be  used  by  the  Harriet  Lane  at  the 
mouth  of  James  River.  She  is  of  small  size  and  value  and  is  not  worth 
sending  to  a  court.  1  would  be  pleased  to  have  the  instructions  of  the 
Department  in  regard  to  her.  An  inventory  of  the  articles  on  board 
has  been  taken.  The  captain  of  the  sloop,  having  been  engaged  in  a 
business  that  I  am  not  altogether  satisfied  with,  I  have  detained  him  a 
prisoner  on  board  of  this  ship;  the  other  two  men  remain  on  board  of 
the  sloop. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  J.  Pendergrast,

U.  S.  S.  Quaker  City, 
Hampton  Roads ,  June  7 ,  1861. 

Sir:  Commander  Carr,  U.  S.  Navy,  the  commanding  officer  of  this 
vessel,  has  handed  me  an  extract  of  a  communication  to  you  from  the 
honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  to  the  effect  that  the  owners  of  the 
Quaker  City  keep  that  vessel  in  repair,  and  the  Government  is  not 
called  upon  for  any  of  her  expenses. 

1  have  most  respectfully  to  remark,  as  the  agent  for  the  owners  ot 
the  Quaker  City ,  that  the  question  is  not  one  of  expenses,  it  is  simply 
to  find  a  place,  materials,  and  mechanics  wherewith  to  keep  her  in  run¬ 
ning  order. 

It  is  unnecessary  to  detail  now,  after  the  repeated  representations  to 
you,  the  condition  of  the  vessel  and  the  necessity  of  repairs. 

Be  assured,  sir,  that  she  will  run  as  long  as  possible,  and  I  only  ask 
that  reasonable  opportunities  may  be  afforded  to  keep  her  machinery 
in  an  efficient  state. 

Most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thomas  W.  Wilson. 

Flag-Officer  Pendergrast,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  U.  8.  Naval  Forces,  Hampton  Roads. 


U.  S.  S.  Quaker  City, 
Chesapeake  Bay ,  June  5,  1861. 

Sir:  Having  been  informed  that  the  charter  of  the  above-named 
steamer  has  been  renewed  by  the  Government  for  a  period  of  ninety 
days,  I  beg  respectfully  to  inform  you  that  having  been  originally 
ordered  to  prepare  the  ship  for  thirty  days  only,  my  stock  of  engine 
stores  and  material  will  soon  require  replenishing,  and  although  the 
engine  and  boilers  are  still  comparatively  in  order,  yet  the  ordinary 
wear  of  over  forty  days’  steaming  will  shortly  necessitate  a  return  to 
some  port  where  the  advantage  of  a  machine  shop  can  be  obtained. 

Respectfully  submitting  the  foregoing  to  your  consideration,  I  am, 
yours,  very  respectfully, 

Solon  Farrer, 

Chief  Engineer.

Commanding.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Stringham,  U.  S.  Navy,  comihanding  Atlantic 

Blockading  Squadron,  regarding  operations  of  his  command  and  capture 

of  brig  Hattie  Jackson. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 

Off  Savannah,  June  11,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  liad  the  honor  of  addressing  you,  under  date  of  June  G,  advis¬ 
ing  the  Department  of  the  occurences  off  Charleston  up  to  and  includ¬ 
ing  that  date,  which  I  forwarded  by  the  prize  to  the  IT.  S.  brig  Ferry, 
the  schooner  Savannah,  in  charge  of  Midshipman  It.  S.  McCook. 

On  the  Gth  instant,  about  8  p.  m.,  I  was  much  gratified  by  the  arrival 
of  the  steamer  Union,  Lieutenant  Commanding  J.  E.  Goldsborough,  and 
Flag,  Lieutenant  Commanding  Lewis  C.  Sartori,  and  on  the  7tli,  about 
8  a.  in.,  by  the  arrival  of  the  frigate  Wabash ,  Captain  Samuel  Mercer. 

The  same  day  I  ordered  the  Union  to  proceed  to  her  station  off 
Savannah. 

On  tlie«8th  instant  we  discovered  a  vessel  to  the  south  and  west  of 
our  station.  I  ordered  the  Flag  to  see  what  vessel  it  was ;  she  reported 
the  Union,  which  vessel  had  chased  a  steamer  with  a  vessel  in  tow. 
The  commander  of  the  Union  supposed  one  Avas  a  privateer,  from  the 
fact  of  being  fired  on  by  the  vessel  in  tow.  They  escaped,  going  into 
Stono. 

The  Union  returned  to  Savannah.  I  ordered  the  Flag  to  look  care¬ 
fully  after  these  vessels.  Up  to  the  time  of  my  departure  nothing  was 
seen  of  them. 

Leaving  the  Wabash  and  Flag  off  Charleston,  I  came  down  to  Savan¬ 
nah  yesterday.  When  off  St.  Helena  [S.  C.j  we  boarded  a  bark  stand¬ 
ing  off  the  land  under  easy  sail.  She  proved  to  be  the  English  bark 
Edward,  from  Liverpool  for  Savannah,  Avith  salt  and  coal.  The  chief 
mate  came  on  board  of  us  and  reported  that  the  captain  had  been  on 
shore  since  Wednesday  last,  going  in  a  boat  from  shore;  that  the  bark 
had  been  twice  boarded,  June  6  by  U.  S.  brig  Perry,  and  8th  June  by 
U.  S.  S.  Union,  each  time  Avarned  off  and  notified  of  the  blockade. 
Under  these  circumstances  and  other  statements  of  suspicious  character, 
I  ordered  the  bark  to  follow  in  charge  of  Lieutenant  Bryant. 

She  followed  us  to  our  present  anchorage,  when  I  ordered  Acting 
Master  Josiah  Snow  to  visit  and  examine  the  bark,  Avho  reported  the 
cargo  of  salt  as  having  been  evidently  moved,  Avliich,  in  connection 
with  the  statement  of  the  mate,  that  a  shore  steamer,  the  Robert 
Clinch ,  having  been  twice  alongside,  the  absence  for  so  long  a  time  of 
the  captain,  etc.,  raised  a  strong  suspicion  in  my  mind  of  her  having 
been  engaged  in  an  unlawful  proceeding.  Yet  under  the  circumstances 
of  the  absence  of  the  master,  and  all  the  ship’s  papers  being  out  of  the 
possession  or  control  of  the  mate  and  he  unable  to  produce  any  for 
my  examination,  I  have  finally  concluded  to  order  this  \Tessel  to  pro¬ 
ceed  at  once  to  sea,  going  to  any  foreign  port  or  to  a  port  in  the  United 
States  north  of  the  capes  of  Virginia. 

We  also  boarded  the  English  schooner  Victoria,  from  Ha\Tana,  bound 
to  New  York,  and  after  noting  the  circumstances  on  her  papers  she 
proceeded  on  her  voyage;  and  at  same  time  yesterday  witnessed  the 
capture  by  the  steamer  Union  of  the  brig  Hattie  Jackson,  owned  in 
Savannah,  bound  from  Matanzas  to  Savannah  with  molasses.  I  have 
ordered  her  to  New  York,  under  charge  of  Lieutenant  N.  C.  Bryant. 

We  are  engaged  this  morning  in  supplying  with  coal  the  Union. 
She  uses  coal  very  fast,  and  carries  but  little"  She  is  not  fit  for  an 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  715 

Atlantic  blockading  vessel,  will  only  do  near  a  coal  depot.  I  herewith 
forward  the  oaths  of  the  crew  of  the  Minnesota. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  H.  Stringiiam, 

Flag-Officer,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 
Hon.  Gideon  Welles.

Worcester,  June  9,  1861. 

Honored  Sir  :  I  take  the  liberty  of  suggesting  that  there  may  be 
some  piratical  work  going  on,  or  landing  of  contraband  articles  sup¬ 
plying  Maryland  and  Virginia,  etc.,  at  Smith’s  Island,  situate  north 
and  adjoining  the  entrance  of  Capes  Charles  and  Henry,  the  mouth  of 
the  Chesapeake. 

The  island  may  be  some  8  or  so  miles  long.  I  am  not  posted  on  this, 
but  there  are  several  places  of  inlet  to  it  between  the  continent  and  it, 
and  very  few  houses  on  the  island.  It  used  to  belong  to  G.  W.  Parke 
Custis,  and  now,  I  suppose,  to  Colonel  Lee  (that  was);  formerly  belonged 
to  General  Washington. 

Please  excuse  the  liberty  I  have  taken  in  thus  addressing  you.  A 
vessel  may  easily  look  around  occasionally.  I  only  feel  desirous  to 
serve  the  Union,  and  thus  discharge  an  impression  on  my  mind.  I  am 
a  resident  of  Washington  and  do  not  sign  my  name,  as  I  may  be  much 
injured  if  known  in  this  at  present,  but,  if  desirable,  after  a  while  will 
make  myself  known. 

With  great  respect,  your  humble  servant,  '  Union. 

His  Excellency  W.  Scott, 

Lieutenant-General ,  U.  S.  Army.

U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane, 

Off  Newport  News ,  June  11,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  state  that  repairs  are  absolutely  necessary 
to  this  vessel  and  her  engines;  her  boilers  also  require  a  thorough  over¬ 
hauling;  the  shill’s  provisions  will  be  exhausted  by  the  30th  of  this 
month;  that  the  terms  of  service  of  many  of  my  crew  and  engineer 
department  will  expire  within  ten  days,  and  that  the  armament  of  this 
ship  is  by  no  means  such  as  should  be  provided  to  render  her  efficient 
in  the  present  state  of  affairs. 

In  view  of  these  facts,  and  of  the  important  events  that  may  soon  be 
expected  to  transpire  in  this  vicinity,  I  have  to  request  that  this  ship 
be  ordered  to  Few  York  for  the  necessary  repairs,  alterations,  and  sup¬ 
plies  at  as  early  a  day  as  possible,  in  order  that  when  called  upon  for 
active  service  in  the  face  of  the  enemy  we  may  not  be  so  liable  to  defeat 
and  disgrace,  as  would  be  the  case  in  our  present  condition  if  again 
called  upon  to  encounter  a  determined  and  well-armed  enemy. 

I  would  also  respectfully  call  your  attention  to  the  enclosed  report 
of  my  chief  engineer. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Faunce, 

Commander. 

Flag-Officer  G.  J.  Pendergrast, 

Flagship  Cumberland,  off  Fortress  Monroe. 

[Subenclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane, 

Off  Newport  News,  Va.,  June  5,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  again  the  honor  to  call  your  attention  to  the  condition 
of  the  boilers  and  engines  of  this  vessel.  Steam  having  been  kept  up 
on  the  ship  ever  since  she  left  the  Brooklyn  navy  yard,  in  February 
last,  with  the  exception  of  three  days  only,  the  engines  require  repack¬ 
ing  throughout.  Not  only  do  the  boilers  require  some  repairs  necessary 
to  their  strength  under  pressure  of  steam,  but  the  valve  motion  con¬ 
tinues  much  deranged,  and  the  engine  frames  work  badly  on  account  of 
the  corroding  away  of  the  holding-down  bolts,  which  has  already  caused 
the  breaking  of  the  exhaust-pipe  connection,  thereby  destroying  the 
vacuum,  and  so  greatly  reducing  the  power  of  the  engines  as  to  destroy 
their  capacity  for  quick  action.  This  was  unpleasantly  the  case  to-day 
during  the  action  with  the  battery  on  Pig  Point,  ivlien,  for  some  time, 
I  was  under  the  greatest  anxiety  lest  the  engines  should  lose  their 
action.  Situated  as  we  then  were,  this  might  have  resulted  in  the  loss 
of  the  ship  and  serious  calamity  to  all  on  board, 


718 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Under  these  peculiar  circumstances,  and  in  order  tlilrt  tlie  vessel  may 
retain  her  reputation  for  efficiency,  1  beg  leave  to  submit  the  necessity 
of  lier  soon  undergoing  the  necessary  repairs. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  R.  Dezburgh, 

Chief  Engineer. 

Captain  Jno.  Faunce, 

U.  S.  S.  Harriet  Lane.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Flag-Officer  Stringham,  U.  S. 
Navy,  commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  regarding  the  clos¬ 
ing  of  the  ports  of  North  Carolina  by  means  of  sunken  vessels,  and 
transmitting  correspondence  suggesting  the  importance  of  closing  the 
port  of  Fernandina. 

Confidential.]  Navy  Department,  June  14,  1861. 

Sir:  I  send  you  herewith  copies  of  letters  received  at  this  Depart¬ 
ment  from  the  Assistant  Secretary  of  the  Treasury  and  the  collector  at 
Wilmington,  Del.  The  suggestions  in  regard  to  Fernandina  and  the 
importance  of  having  an  armed  vessel  at  that  point  have  been  hereto¬ 
fore  made  by  other  parties.  This  is  probably  the  most  important  port 
to  close  up  on  the  eastern  coast  of  Florida.  It  is  also  deemed  advis¬ 
able  that  an  armed  vessel  should,  at  all  events  for  a  period,  be  stationed 


720 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


off  Cape  Fear,  provided  it  can  be  done  without  weakening  other  more 
important  points  that  should  be  guarded  with  unremitting  vigilance. 
It  is  represented  that  no  inconsiderable  amount  of  commerce  is  carried 
on  at  this  time  from  various  places  in  North  Carolina,  but  especially 
from  Cape  Fear.  In  regard  to  many  of  the  smaller  inlets,  it  has 
already  been  intimated  that  by  sinking  hulks  or  captured  prizes  of 
little  value,  communication  may  be  suppressed.  Hulks  can  probably 
be  obtained  at  Baltimore  to  enable  you  to  close  some  of  the  Southern 
ports.  You  will  please  give  this  subject  consideration,  and  communi¬ 
cate  your  views  to  the  Department. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy. 

Flag-Officer  S.  H.  Stringham, 

Commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


[Enclosure.] 


Treasury  Department,  June  G ,  1861. 

Sir:  The  enclosed  communication  from  Mr.  Rodney,  collector  at 
Wilmington,  Del.,  1  deem  to  be  of  sufficient  importance  to  demand  of 
me  a  statement  in  regard  to  it. 

Fernandina  is  the  Atlantic  terminus  of  the  Florida  Railroad.  Mr. 
Yulee,  formerly  of  the  Senate,  has  control  of  the  road,  and  for  the  pur¬ 
pose  of  passenger  and  mail  communication  with  Charleston  by  the  out¬ 
side  route  had  completed  last  fall  a  new  steamer,  said  to  be  fast.  It  is 
to  this  steamer,  undoubtedly,  that  the  letter  refers.  From  Savannah 
to  Key  West  there  is  no  fort  except  an  old  one  at  [St.]  Augustine.  Fer¬ 
nandina  may  be  approached  by  large  vessels  direct  from  the  sea, 
and  by  smaller  vessels  through  the  inner  passage  from  Cumberland 
Sound.  What  batteries  may  have  been  erected  this  spring  I,  of  course, 
know  not,  but  I  am  satisfied  that  the  steamer  referred  to  could  with 
ease  be  cut  out  and  at  the  same  time  the  railroad  bridge  connecting 
Fernandina  with  the  mainland  be  destroyed,  and  the  usefulness  of  that 
road  in  a  great  degree  impaired,  if  not  destroyed. 

I  am,  respectfully, 


Geo.  Harrington. 


Hon.  S.  P.  Chase. 


[Subenclosure.] 

Wilmington,  Del.,  June  4 , 1861. 

Sir:  I  have  this  moment  received  information  which  I  think  the 
Government  should  be  in  possession  of. 

Captain  Brower,  of  the  schooner  Anna  Smith ,  of  Wilmington,  Del., 
reached  here  this  day  and  reports  that  his  vessel  was  captured  by  order 
of  the  government  of  Florida  at  Cedar  Keys,  on  the  12tli  day  of  May 
last,  from  whence  he  made  liis  escape;  that  the  rebels  are  arming  with 
two  heavy  guns,  and  a  crew  to  consist  of  160  men,  a  remarkably  fast 
steamer  at  the  port  of  Fernandina,  eastern  Florida,  for  the  purpose  of 
intercepting  the  California  steamers. 

Captain  Brower  is  a  reliable  and  intelligent  man,  and  full  faith  may 
be  given  to  his  report. 

With  high  respect,  etc., 

T.  M.  Rodney. 

Hon.  S.  P.  Chase, 

Secretary  Treasury.

U.  S.  S.  Dawn, 

Hampton  Roads ,  Virginia,  June  15,  1861. 

Sir:  On  my  way  to  your  anchorage,  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you 
that  nothing  very  material  in  reference  to  the  blockade  of  York  River 
by  the  vessel  under  my  command  has  occurred  since  my  report  to  you 
of  the  29th  ultimo;  but  that,  in  consequence  of  repeated  leaks  in  the 
smaller  boiler  tines,  and  the  unreliable  condition  of  several  of  them,  I 
have  been  compelled  to  leave  my  station  in  order  to  request  a  survey  on 
them.  As,  without  the  ability  to  get  up  steam  and  anchor  instantly, 
night  or  day,  for  maneuvering,  a  vessel  of  only  two  (broadside)  guns, 
and  as  unmanageable  as  this  steamer  is  with  her  sails,  I  feel  an  unwill¬ 
ingness  to  imperil  her  safety  by  such  inefficiency,  or  to  fail  in  accom¬ 
plishing  the  object  of  the  Government  in  an  effectual  blockade  of  that 
river. 

After  patching  the  leak  referred  to  in  my  report  of  the  29tli  we 
steamed  out  of  Hampton  Roads  the  nest  morning  for  our  station,  but 
had  not  got  within  10  miles  of  it  (being  under  28  pounds  of  steam  only) 
before  we  sprang  a  leak  in  another  tine,  which,  soon  extinguishing  the 
fire,  compelled  us  in  the  face  of  our  foe  to  conceal  our  crippled  condi¬ 
tion  from  view  by  making  the  last  5  miles  from  our  usual  anchorage 
under  the  square  sail  alone,  the  wind  being  (fortunately)  abaft  at  tiie 
time. 

Having  anchored  about  6  miles  from  Yorktown  and  repaired  that 
leak  as  soon  as  possible,  we  have  kept  the  fires  banked  (with  steam 
under  28  pounds)  ever  since,  except  on  the  following  occasions,  viz: 
At  early  dawn  on  the  7th  (after  a  dense  fog  in  Chesapeake  Bay  during 
the  previous  day  and  night  had  lifted),  having  discovered  three  ships 
at  anchor  from  5  to  7  miles  to  the  eastward  and  northward  and  east¬ 
ward  of  Back  River  light  house,  and  supposed  that  they  might  have, 
in  the  fog,  eluded  the  blockade  below,  we  got  up  steam  and  anchor 
and  ran  alongside  of  each,  boarding  two  of  them  and  having  a  boat 
with  the  captain  and  his  papers  sent  to  us  from  the  other.  On  exam¬ 
ination  of  their  papers  found  that  they  had  been  properly  endorsed 
by  one  of  the  blockading  force  off  Cape  Henry  two  or  three  days 
before.  Previously  to  this  (on  the  3d  June)  we  had  pursued  a  schooner 
beating  across  the  mouth  of  York  River  from  Poquosin  Flat,  which, 
upon  coming  up  with,  and  ordering  the  skipper  with  his  papers  on 
board,  proved  to  be  the  prize  F.  W.  Johnson  (loaded  with  railroad  iron), 
and  sent  by  you  to  Baltimore  under  the  command  of  Mr.  Chisholm. 

On  another  occasion  (5th  June)  we  steamed  out  of  York  River  to 
cut  off  a  sailboat,  but  failing  in  that  we  boarded,  at  anchor  on  the  east 
side  of  York  Spit,  a  Baltimore  brigantine,  bound  to  one  of  the  West 
India  Islands  from  Baltimore. 

The  day  before  yesterday  we  got  up  steam  and  anchor  and  ran  over 
to  the  east  side  of  York  Spit  to  procure  sand  from  one  of  the  small 
islands  eastward  of  Monday’s  Marsh  Point,  returning  to  our  usual 
anchorage  in  the  middle  of  York  River  the  same  afternoon. 

Yesterday,  about  10  a.  in.,  while  at  anchor  with  fires  banked  and 
steam  at  27  pounds,  a  leak  commenced  in  one  of  the  small  Hues  on 
starboard  side.  We  immediately  got  underway,  not  wishing  to  be 


724 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


caught  in  a  disabled  condition,  and  steamed  down  the  river,  burning 
wood  to  keep  the  fires  in,  until  ive  could  reach  a  place  of  more  security 
from  any  attack  from  a  very  superior  force  that  a  knowledge  of  our 
crippled  state  might  provoke.  When  we  had  reached  the  buoys  about 
10  miles  from  Yorktown,  our  fires  giving  out,  we  anchored,  and  as 
soon  as  possible  patched  the  leak. 

By  7  p.  m.  we  had  about  28  pounds  of  steam  up  again  and  fires 
banked  for  the  night,  when  about  10  o’clock  a  leak  broke  out  in  another 
small  flue  about  amidships,  compelling  us  to  let  off  steam  and  blow  the 
water  out  of  the  boiler  again  preparatory  to  patching  for  the  fourth 
time.  At  daylight  this  morning  we  examined  and  repaired  the  leak, 
and  got  up  steam  and  anchor  this  afternoon  with  the  intention  of 
steaming  down  here,  lest  by  remaining  longer,  even  with  the  fires 
banked,  the  flues  might  give  out  altogether. 

Since  writing  my  report  I  have  been  handed  a  communication  by  the 
first  assistant  engineer  in  reference  to  the  condition  of  our  boiler  and 
flues,  a  copy  of  which  is  herewith  submitted. 

Also,  accompanying  this,  a  duplicate  requisition  from  the  different 
departments  as  to  our  wants,  the  gunner’s  being  more  particularly  in 
answer  to  your  order  of  the  7th  June. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

William  Chandler, 
Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Flag-Officer  G.  J.  Pendergrast, 

Commanding  Home  \  West  India ]  /Squadron.

U.  S.  (Chartered)  Steamer  Dawn, 

June  15,  1861. 

Sir  :  The  following  is  in  our  opinion  a  correct  statement  in  regard  to 
the  Dawrds  boiler: 

The  boiler  is  24  feet  8  inches  in  length,  and  10  feet  in  diameter;  has 
two  furnaces  6  feet  6  inches  long  by  4  feet  3  inches  wide;  has  one  30- 
iuch  and  one  12-inch  Hue  running  rorward  from  each;  has  thirty  8-inch 
return  flues.  The  shell  of  the  boiler  is  three-eighths  of  an  inch  thick, 
and  in  good  order.  The  30-inch  flues  have  never  leaked  any.  The 
8-iucli  flues  are  in  a  very  bad  condition;  the  iron  is  not  more  than  one 
thirty-second  of  an  inch  thick  in  many  places,  varying  from  that  to  one- 
eighth  of  an  inch.  They  can  not  be  patched  so  as  to  make  them  safe, 
and  they  are  likely  to  give  out  at  any  time,  even  with  a  pressure  of  25 
pounds  to  the  square  inch.  The  furnaces  are  worn  considerably,  but 
have  not  given  us  any  trouble  since  we  left  New  York. 

A.  W.  Reynolds, 

First  Engineer. 

L.  Burhans, 

Second,  Engineer. 

Saml.  Tomlinson, 

Third  Engineer. 

Captain  Wm.  Chandler, 

Commander.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Stringiiam,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Atlantic 

Blockading  Squadron,  of  cruise  from  June  11  to  18,  and  referring  to 

prize  vessels  Savannah  and  FLallie  Jackson. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  June  18,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  receipt  of  your  favor  of  May 
24,  instructing  me  to  furnish  duplicate  instructions  to  prize  masters,  so 
that  one  copy  may  be  deposited  with  the  clerk  of  the  district  court  to 
which  the  prize  may  be  sent. 

Also  yours  of  same  date  apprising  me  that  the  steamer  Flag ,  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Commanding  Lewis  0.  Sartori,  will  form  part  of  the  Atlantic 
Blockading  Squadron.  1  have  informed  you  of  her  arrival  off  Charles¬ 
ton,  June  G,  in  company  with  the  Union,  and  I  am  now  prepared  to  say 
that  I  find  her  a  very  useful  vessel,  having  excellent  capacity  for  coal, 
which  will  obviate  the  necessity  of  leaving  her  station  except  at  long 
intervals.  She  is  off  Charleston  in  company  with  the  Wabash. 

Also  yours  of  May  27,  apprising  me  of  the  recharter  of  the  Quaker 
City ,  and  that  she  will  form  part  of  the  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Also  of  same  date  with  reference  to  allowance  for  pilots  when  they 
mess  in  the  wardroom.  I  acknowledge  receipt  of  your  last  esteemed 
favor  under  date  of  May  28,  1861,  which  reached  me  also  off  Charles¬ 
ton,  with  the  arrival  of  the  Wabash,  Flag ,  and  Union.  I  availed  myself 
of  the  presence  of  the  two  former  at  Charleston  to  go  off  Savannah. 
With  my  proceedings  there,  1  have  already  made  the  Department 
acquainted  by  letter  June  11.  1  returned  off  Charleston  June  12,  where 

1  remained  until  15th,  when  I  left  for  Hampton  Roads,  where  I  arrived 
on  the  18th  instant. 

Nothing  of  consequence  occurred  at  Charleston  previous  to  my  leav 
iug,  except  an  official  visit  from  the  English  consul,  Robert  Bunch,  esq., 
in  company  with  Henry  Thompson,  master  of  the  British  bark  Edwards, 
feeling  relieved^to  find  his  bark  had  not  gone  to  New  York  in  charge  of 
a  prize  master.  ’  The  consul  |  was]  satisfied  when  the  circumstances  were 
explained  upon  which  I  acted.  By  consent  of  the  consul,  Mr.  Cliatard 
went  with  him  to  Charleston,  whither  he  was  proceeding,  via  Savannah, 
in  the  brig  Hattie  Jackson,  when  she  was  captured  by  the  U.  S.  S. 
Union. 

Mr.  C.  is  a  planter  of  Cuba,  having  frequent  intercourse  with  the 
United  States.  His  wife  and  one  daughter  are  now  in  Charleston,  and 
another  married  and  settled  in  Boston. 

1  could  not  refuse  to  comply  with  his  request  to  be  taken  on  board 
this  ship  instead  of  being  sent  forward  by  the  Jackson.  I  hope  this 
will  not  meet  the  disapproval  of  the  Department. 

We  arrived  off  Fortress  Monroe  and  anchored  about  noon  to-day, 
after  a  short  passage  from  Charleston,  without  any  incident  of  impor¬ 
tance. 

There  are  on  board  this  ship  thirteen  persons,  including  the  captain 
of  the  schooner  Savannah,  of  whose  capture  1  have  already  apprised

U.  S.  Steam  Frigate  Wabash, 

Off  Charleston,  June  18,  1861. 

Sir:  The  Union  arrived  at  this  anchorage  this  morning  at  9  o’clock, 
and  I  have  dispatched  the  Flag  to  take  her  place  off'  Savannah.  It 
will  be  almost  useless  to  send  the  Union  here  again.  She  will  be  an 
admirable  vessel  for  the  Chesapeake  Bay,  drawing  10  feet  when  full.  I 
hope  some  more  efficient  vessel  will  be  substituted  for  her.  I  am  sorry 
to  lose  the  services  of  the  Flag  at  this  important  point. 

The  Vandalia  arrived  here  on  the  16th  instant,  and  will  be  of  some 
service  to  us. 

I  am,  sir,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Saml.  Mercer, 

Captain.

Report  of  Captain  Mercer,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Wabash,  of 
the  capture  of  the  ship  Amelia,  June  18,  1861. 

U.  S.  Steam  Frigate  Wabash, 

Off  Charleston,  June  19,  1861. 

Sir:  Yesterday  the  Union  arrived  here  about  9  in  the  morning. 
Soon  after  her  arrival,  I  ordered  her  to  board  a  vessel  which  made  her 
appearance  to  the  northward,  wind  then  at  northeast.  She  proved  to 
be  a  vessel  belonging  to  Charleston,  from  Liverpool,  under  American 
colors.  As  she  was  bound  into  Charleston  we  captured  her,  and  I  had 
a  prize  crew  placed  on  board,  and  gave  her  in  charge  of  Acting  Master 
John  W.  Bentley,  with  orders  to  proceed  with  her  to  Philadelphia.  She 
will  take  her  departure  to-day. 

The  Flag  went  to  Savannah  yesterday,  to  relieve  the  Union  off  that 
port. 

1  have  given  Captain  Goldsborough  orders  to  report  to  the  senior 
naval  officer  at  Hampton  Roads.  I  shall  feel  the  loss  of  the  Flag  at 
this  point  very  much.  Indeed,  with  this  large  ship,  which  can  not 
approach  the  shore  nearer  with  safety  than  3  miles,  and  the  Vandalia, 
a  sailing  vessel,  I  fear  that  the  blockade  will  not  be  as  effectual  as  it 
has  been.  It  is  to  be  hoped  that  an  efficient  steamer  or  two  may  be 
sent  down  to  us  very  soon — vessels  that  will  carry  plenty  of  coal.  The 
vessel  captured  is  the  Amelia ,  of  Charleston.  She  came  very  near  get¬ 
ting  in,  and  would  have  done  so  if  the  pilots  of  Charleston  had  kept  a 
bright  lookout.  The  captain  of  the  Amelia  says  there  are  several 
American  vessels  bound  to  Charleston  under  English  colors,  so  I  beg 
of  you  to  lose  no  time  in  sending  us  down  a  steamer  or  two. 

I  am,  sir,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Saml.  Mercer, 

Captain. 

Flag-Officer  S.  II.  Stringham, 

Comdg.  U.  S.  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Flagship  Minnesota. 

P.  S. — This  ship,  the  Vandalia,  and  the  Flag  were  present  and  in 
sight  when  the  Union  captured  the  Amelia,  and  all  equally  entitled  to 
prize  money  if  she  should  be  condemned. 

S.  Mercer, 

Captain.

Report  of  Commander  Goldsborough,  U.  S.  Wavy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

Union ,  of  the  capture  of  the  ship  Amelia ,  June  18,  1861. 

U.  S.  Steamer  Union, 
Potomac  Flotilla ,  A  ugust  31,  1861. 

Sir:  In  compliance  with  your  instructions  of  the  22cl  instant  to  fur¬ 
nish  the  Department  with  a  detailed  report  of  the  capture  of  the  ship 
Amelia  by  the  Union  under  my  command,  I  have  the  honor  to  make 
the  following  statement: 

On  the  morning  of  the  IStli  of  June,  being  off  the  harbor  of  Charles¬ 
ton,  a  sail  was  discovered  in  the  offing  to  windward  about  12  miles, 
standing  in  shore,  and  apparently  under  easy  sail.  I  was  directed  by 
Captain  Mercer  to  go  in  pursuit.  Chase  was  immediately  given,  and 
as  we  approached  she  changed  her  course,  and  stood  from  us;  but 
seeing  that  we  were  gaining  upon  her,  and  while  in  the  act  of  firing  a 
gun,  she  tacked  and  stood  for  us.  Upon  coming  up,  she  proved  to  be 
the  ship  Amelia,  from  Liverpool,  belonging  and  bound  to  Charleston, 
with  an  assorted  contraband  cargo.  I  took  possession,  and  convoyed 
her  to  the  anchorage,  where  the  Wabash,  Captain  Mercer,  lay,  and  to 
whom  I  turned  her  over.  The  next  day,  Captain  Mercer  sent  her  with 
a  prize  crew  to  Philadelphia,  and  directed  me  to  convoy  her  well  into 
the  Gulf  Stream,  which  I  did. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  E.  Goldsborough, 
Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  I).  C.

I  have  received  appointments,  with  oaths  enclosed,  for  Acting  Masters

ture  to  return  the  appointment  of  Mr.  Green,  having  sent  him  to  New 
York  by  the  brig  Hallie  Jackson  with  a  letter  to  Commodore  S.  L. 
Breese.  His  conduct  was  such  on  board  this  ship  (he  having  been 
reported  to  me  by  Captain  Van  Brunt  as  intoxicated  twice  within  four 
or  five  days)  that  I  recommended  Commodore  B[reese]  to  let  him  go, 
as  being  of  little  service. 

1  have  also  received  your  letter  of  June  5,  in  which  I  am  informed 
“  it  is  the  intention  of  the  Government  to  prohibit  foreigners  from  hav¬ 
ing  traffic  and  making  exchanges  Avith  those  Avho  are  in  insurrection.” 
1  will  here  only  say  in  reference  to  my  action  since  taking  command  that 
J  have  looked  upon  the  seceding  and  blockaded  States  as  enemies  and 
have  treated  them  as  such. 

I  am  also  in  receipt  of  your  letters,  “  confidential,”  of  dates  June  5,

munications  from  T.  M.  Rodney,  June  4,  Wilmington,  Del.,  and  George 
Harrington,  Treasury  Department,  June  G. 

Respectfully,  yours,  obediently, 

S  H.  Stringham,

Order  of  Lieutenant  Sartori,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Flag ,  to 
Master  Kautz,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  proceed  to  Philadelphia  in  charge  prize 
brig  Hannah  Balch. 

U.  S.  S.  Flag, 

Off  Charleston,  June  20,  1861. 

Sir:  You  will  take  command  of  the  prize  brig  Hannah  Balch,  cap¬ 
tured  12  miles  southeast  of  the  light  house  off  Savannah  on  June  20, 
1861,  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Flag,  commanded  by  and  with  my  authority,  and 
proceed  with  her  to  the  port  of  Philadelphia. 

On  your  arrival  there  you  will  report  to  Captain  DuPont  or  the  com¬ 
manding  officer  present  at  the  navy  yard.  As  soon  after  as  practicable 
you  will  report  yourself  as  the  prize  master  of  the  Hannah  Balch  to  the 
Hon.  John  Cadwalader,  judge  of  the  U.  S.  district  court  for  the  southern 
district  of  Pennsylvania,  placing  in  his  hands  all  the  papers  connected 
with  the  capture,  and  await  his  instructions. 

The  arms  and  accouterments  for  yourself  and  men  will  be  placed  in 
your  charge,  for  which  you  will  give  receipt  to  the  gunner  of  this  ves¬ 
sel.  After  the  Hannah  Balch  is  placed  in  possession  of  the  civil 
authorities  you  will  receive  instructions  from  Captain  Du  Pont  as  to 
the  disposition  of  your  men  and  their  arms,  and  you  will  proceed  to 
Hampton  Eoads  and  report  to  the  senior  naval  officer  there. 

You  will  deliver  no  papers  to  the  custom-house  officers  or  other  per¬ 
sons  without  authority  from  the  judge  of  the  U.  S.  district  court,  and 
you  will  remain  in  charge  of  the  prize  until  relieved  by  the  said  judge. 

Let  me  impress  upon  your  mind  the  necessity  of  unceasing  watchful¬ 
ness  and  vigilance  until  the  vessel  is  placed  in  possession  of  the  proper 
authorities  in  Philadelphia. 

I  am,  sir,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  C.  Sartori. 


Master  A.  Kautz,  U.  S.  Navy.

Letter  from  Flag-Officer  Stringham ,  U.  S.  Navy,  coffihnanding  Atlantic 

Bloclcading  Squadron ,  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  enquiring  into 

Department1  s  action  regarding  discharge  of  seized  vessels. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads ,  Jtme  20,  1861. 

Sir:  On  my  arrival  at  this  point  I  had.  the  honor  of  receiving  letters 
from  the  Department,  which  I  have  acknowledged  in  my  communica¬ 
tions  of  18th  and  19th  instant. 

I  venture  to  defer  the  subjects  of  your  confidential  communications 
until  I  receive  answer  to  au  application  for  a  day’s  personal  visit  to 
Washington,  which  I  ventured  to  make  by  letter  of  June  18. 

The  remaining  important  subjects  of  consideration  are  contained  in 
your  letter  of  June  5,  in  which  you  honor  me  with  the  remark  that  the 
suggestions  in  your  (my)  dispatch  No.  23,  in  reference  to  the  interdic¬ 
tion  of  communication  in  the  insurgent  States  “meets  the  approval  of 
the  Department,  and  it  will  be  the  policy  of  the  Government  to  carry 
them  into  effect,”  and  that  “it  is  the  intention  of  the  Government  to 
prohibit  foreigners  from  having  traffic  and  making  exchanges  with 
those  who  are  in  insurrection.” 

I  confess  that,!  am  at  great  loss  to  understand  and  wholly  unable  to 
explain  how  I  can  have  made  such  a  gross  mistake  as  appears  to  have 
been  made  by  me,  if  I  am  correctly  informed  (though  I  confess  yet 
unofficially),  that  most,  if  not  all,  the  vessels  seized  by  me  and  being 
from  secession  ports  and  owned  in  rebellious  States,  yet  have  been 
permitted  to  go  free. 

I  could  not  look  upon  the  vessels  with  secession  State  clearances, 
some  with  secession  flags  in  their  possession,  which  I  know  they  have 
proudly  and  defiantly  displayed  (with  the  old  flag  of  our  country  in 
their  hands  only  to  be  used  for  deception  and  fraud),  as  deserving  of 
any  more  consideration  than  any  other  enemy  of  my  Government. 

While  I  have  uniformly  treated  neutrals  with  the  utmost  forbear¬ 
ance,  giving  them  every  aid  and  comfort  in  my  power  consistent  with 
duty,  I  have  not  hesitated  to  do  what  I  thought  was  also  my  duty 
toward  traitors  and  rebels,  and  shall  continue  to  use  the  force  granted  me 
by  the  Department  to  confound  these  last  whenever  and  wherever  I  can. 

I  should  be  pleased  to  hear,  if  not  an  inconsistent  request,  the 
grounds  upon  which  vessels  have  been  discharged,  that  I  may  avoid  in 
the  future  committing  like  errors.  I  enclose  for  the  Department  a  cor¬ 
rect  copy  of  the  document  *  taken  from  the  Savannah ,  and  under  which 
she  sailed;  the  original  went  forward  with  the  prize  master,  to  be 
delivered  to  the  district  judge  U.  S.  court. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant. 

S.  H.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer ,  Atlantic  Bloclcading  Squadron. 
Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy.

day  for  tlie  purpose  of  putting  the  boiler  and  machinery  of  this  steamer 
in  order  as  far  as  I  could,  but  for  a  subsequent  verbal  order  from  you 
on  the  17th,  directing  me  to  return  to  my  station  in  York  River  and 
remain  there  four  or  live  days,  or  until  you  could  receive  a  reply  from 
Washington  in  reference  to  this  steamer.  In  obedience  to  which  verbal 
order,  we  got  up  (about  15  pounds)  steam  and  anchor  and  steamed 
out  of  Hampton  Roads  that  alter  noon,  reaching  our  anchorage  in  York 
River  (between  the  buoys)  before  dark  the  same  evening,  where  we  have 
been  lying  ever  since,  with  the  lires  banked,  at  15  to  17  pounds  of  steam 
(and  without  any  occurrence  of  importance  save  a  very  slight  leak  in 
one  of  the  small  Hues  last  night),  until  this  afternoon  about  6  o’clock. 
We  then  got  underway  in  pursuit  of  a  large  fore-and-aft  schooner  off 
the  mouth  of  York  River  and  beating  down  the  Chesapeake,  ivliich 
proved  to  be  the  Arctic ,  Captain  Hicks,  from  Georgetown,  bound  to 
Yew  York.  She  had  already  had  her  papers  endorsed  by  the  Pawnee. 

It  was  my  intention  to  have  returned  to  York  River  this  evening  and 
to  have  anchored  within  5  or  G  miles  of  Yorktown,  and  to  morrow  after¬ 
noon  to  have  steamed  down  to  Hampton  Roads,  in  obedience  to  your 
verbal  order  of  the  17tli;  but  while  in  the  act  of  boarding  the  Arctic , 
the  Baltimore  mail  steamer,  from  Fortress  Monroe,  approached,  and  an 
officer*  on  board  of  her  informed  me  that  there  were  orders  for  me  at 
the  Roads,  whither  I  am  now  proceeding  to  report,  on  my  arrival,  in 
jierson,  on  board  your  ship. 

We  are  now  running  with  from  12  to  15  pounds  of  steam,  which  I 
think  is  about  as  much  as  it  would  be  safe  to  carry. 

Enclosed  is  a  memorandum  of  coal,  provisions,  wood,  and  water  on 
hand. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient 

WillIam  Chandler,

Memorandum. 


Pune  22,  1S61. 

From  a  source  entitled  to  credit  I  learn  that  the  commander,  Decey, 
of  the  yacht  Camilla  (formerly  America),  went  to  Montgomery,  and 
afterwards,  about  June  1,  sailed  from  Savannah  with  two  ordnance 
officers  (Lieutenant  North  and  Colonel  E.  C.  Anderson)  to  Europe,  to, 
it  is  supposed,  procure  rifled  cannon  and  bring  back  the  commissioners 
of  the  Confederate  States.  It  is  probable  the  yacht  has  gone  to  Liver¬ 
pool,  as  the  agent  in  Savannah,  is  Andrew  Low,  a  branch  of  the  house 
of  Isaac  Low  &  Co.,  of  Liverpool.  The  yacht  is  very  fast,  and  will 
probably  attempt  to  run  the  blockade,  passing  into  some  shallow 
inlet  on  the  Southern  coast  with  the  British  flag  flying.  The  Lady 
Davis,  carrying  one  rifled  gun,  is  now  in  Savannah  harbor,  trying  to 
get  to  Charleston  through  the  inland  passage,  coming  out  at  St.  Helena 
Sound. 

The  steamers  Everglade  and  St.  Mary's,  under  new  names,  are  now  in 
Savannah  harbor  trying  to  get  out.  Every  telegraph  operator  takes 
an  oath  to  the  Confederate  States,  etc.,  and  the  telegraphic  laws  and 
regulations  are  very  stringent.

Affair  on  the  Rappahannock  River ,  June  '24,  1861. 

Report  of  Lieutenant  Braine,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Monticello. 

U.  S.  S.  Monticello, 

Off  the  Rappahannock  River ,  June  24,  1861. 

Sir  :  Agreeably  to  your  order  of  yesterday  I  left  the  Roads,  and  after 
organizing  a  launch’s  crew  and  exercising  them  at  the  gun,  I  anchored 
in  Lynn  Haven  Bay. 

Early  this  morning  I  started  for  Smith’s  Island,  at  the  entrance  of 
the  Chesapeake  Bay,  supposing  that  to  be  the  island  referred  to  in  your 
instructions.  Upon  a  conversation  with  the  pilot,  1  determined  that 
the  island  you  alluded  to  was  Smith’s  Island,  near  Tangier  Island. 

Accordingly  I  steered  up  the  Chesapeake  Bay,  speaking  many  ves¬ 
sels  which  had  not  been  boarded.  I  stopped  to  endorse  their  papers, 
in  the  usual  manner. 

Receiving  information  from  the  pilot  of  a  nature  that  led  me  to  believe 
I  might  capture  the  steamer  Virginia  at  a  short  distance  from  the  mouth 
of  the  Rappahannock  River,  and  it  being  about  3  p.  m.  and  not  being 
able  to  reach  Pocomoke  Sound  before  night,  I  ran  a  short  distance  up 
the  river,  and  turning,  on  the  way  down  not  seeing  any  sign  of  a  steamer, 
the  pilot  assured  me  of  the  strong  Union  sentiments  of  a  gentleman 
named  William  Gersen  [Gresham],  residing  on  the  bank.  By  this  state¬ 
ment,  and  hoping  to  get  some  information,  I  sent  the  launch  ashore,  fully 
armed  and  equipped,  under  charge  of  Master’s  Mate  Lewis  A.  Brown 
and  Assistant  Surgeon  ILeber  Smith,  and  pilot,  Mr.  Phillips. 

They  landed,  with  gig,  from  the  launch,  and  were  cordially  received 
(as  I  could  plainly  see  the  master  of  the  house  shake  hands  with  them, 
and  the  same  thing  was  repeated  to  me  on  their  return).  Hardly  had 
this  occurred  when  they  were  tired  upon  by  a  body  of  about  eighty  men. 
They  returned  the  fire,  and  retreated  to  the  boat  and  shoved  off.  Turn¬ 
ing  the  bow  of  the  launch  toward  the  shore,  they  served  their  gun  effec¬ 
tually.  I  opened  the  ship’s  battery  on  the  rebels  with  grape  and  shell 
at  600  yards,  and  succeeded  in  demolishing  the  house  and  killing  and 
wounding  many,  completely  silencing  their  tire. 

The  men  on  board  this  ship,  short-handed  as  we  were,  served  their 
guns  with  great  courage  and  promptness,  and  much  credit  is  due  to 
the  officers  and  men  for  the  brave  manner  in  which  they  did  their  duty. 

It  is  Avitli  much  regret  that  I  have  to  announce  that  our  assistant 
surgeon,  Heber  Smith,  was  severely  wounded  in  the  mouth,  as  also  in 
the  hand,  and  I  request  that  he  may  be  removed  where  he  can  obtain 
the  best  medical  attendance.  August  Peterson,  quartermaster,  was 
shot  in  the  stomach,  and  I  fear  he  can  not  live. 

I  am  ready,  sir,  to  proceed  immediately,  in  accordance  with  your 
instructions,  if  you  can  spare  me  a  gentleman  to  act  as  surgeon.  I  for¬ 
ward  herewith  the  report  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  L.  A.  Brown,  who 
was  in  command  of  the  expedition. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

D.  L.  Braine, 

.  Lieutenant,  in  Charge  U.  S.  S.  Monticello. 

Flag-Officer  G.  J.  Pendergrast, 

Commanding  West  India  Squadron.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Monticello, 

Off  the  Rappahannock  River,  June  21,  1861 — 8  p.  m. 

Sir:  Agreeably  to  your  orders  of  this  date  I  armed  and  equipped 
the  launch  with  eighteen  men  and  took  the  gig  in  tow. 

We  pulled  toward  the  shore  until  the  water  became  too  shallow  to 
allow  the  launch  to  proceed  any  farther,  when,  leaving  the  howitzer’s 
crew  with  four  other  men  in  the  launch,  I  took  the  balance  with  Hr. 
Smith  and  Mr.  Phillips,  the  pilot,  in  the  gig  and  pulled  on  shore. 
Dr.  Smith  and  the  pilot  went  first  and  were  cordially  shaking  hands 
with  the  owner  of  the  house  as  I  and  my  men,  armed  with  revolvers 
and  Sharps  rifies,  came  up.  I  heard  a  man  on  the  stoop  say  that  there 
was  a  company  of  well  drilled  volunteers  in  the  vicinity,  and  on  my 
turning  about  I  saw  a  company  of  armed  and  uniformed  men  stealing 
along  the  shore  as  if  to  cut  oft'  our  retreat.  I  immediately  ordered  a 
retreat  to  the  boat  and  fired  off  our  carbines,  many  of  which  missed  fire 
and  then  shoved  off,  having  waded  to  the  launch.  As  the  retreating 
tide  had  left  the  gig  high  and  dry  on  the  beach,  I  had  to  leave  it  there. 
Dr.  Smith,  surgeon,  and  August  Peterson,  quartermaster,  were  wounded 
while  wading  to  tlie  launch.  I  immediately  commenced  firing  the 
howitzer  and  did  considerable  execution  and  had  fired  a  number  of 
times  when  1  was  called  back  to  the  ship  by  your  hail.  Many  of  the 
shot  struck  the  oars  and  launch,  penetrating  the  side.  The  men  acted 
nobly  while  under  this  galling  fire,  we  being  not  more  than  70  yards 
from  the  shore,  and  they  deserve  great  credit. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  A.  Brown, 

Master'' s  Mate,  U.  S.  S.  Monticello. 

D.  L.  Braine,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Lieutenant,  in  Charge  U.  S.  S.  Monticello.

Letter  from  Brigadier-General  Magruder,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  at  Yorktown,  Va.,  to  Colonel 
Deas,  C.  S.  Army,  transmitting  statement  of  Joseph  Christian. 

Headquarters,  Yorktown,  Va.,  June  27, 1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  send  a  report  made  to  Colonel  Crump,  of 
an  abortive  attempt  to  land  soldiers  from  an  armed  steamer  in  the 
Rappahannock  River,  where  the  enemy  was  driven  back  by  our  citi¬ 
zens.  This  morning  at  sunrise  I  sent  a  force  of  1,500  men  to  support 
the  cavalry  and  artillery  under  Major  Hood,  operating  near  and  on  the 
Poquosin,  to  meet  any  party  sent  from  the  enemy’s  works  and  cut  it 
off.  I  shall  join  this  force  to-day. 

The  Reverend  Mr.  Adams  will  hand  this  to  the  colonel  commanding 
the  Virginia  forces.  I  have  been  extremely  indebted  to  this  good  and 
patriotic  minister  of  the  gospel  for  much  assistance.  He  has  lost 
everything  in  the  cause,  and  1  would  like  to  see  him  appointed  as 
chaplain  to  one  of  the  regiments  in  this  department. 

1  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  B.  Magruder. 

Colonel  George  Deas, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General,  C.  S.  Army. 

[Enclosure.] 

IIrbana,  Va.,  June  26,  1861. 

My  Dear  Sir:  I  have  just  received  a  note  by  special  messenger 
from  C.  W .  Montague,  esq.,  requesting  me  to  furnish  to  you  an  accurate 
account  of  all  the  doings  of  the  enemy  on  the  Rappahannock  on  Mon¬ 
day  evening  last.  I  have  taken  much  pains  to  gather  from  persons 
who  have  visited  the  scene  of  action  and  conversed  with  those  who 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


741 


were  engaged  in  it  the  following  particulars,  which  yon  may  regard  as 
reliable : 

About  4  p.  m.  on  Monday,  the  24th,  a  war  steamer,  the  Star  [Monti- 
cello J,  of  New  York,  of  1,000  tons  burden,  came  to,  opposite  the  house 
of  Mr.  James  W.  Gresham,  of  Lancaster,  situated  immediately  on  the 
river,  about  12  miles  below  Urbana,  on  the  Lancaster  side.  She  dis¬ 
patched  to  the  shore  three  barges,  one  a  very  large  one,  with  a  swivel 
in  the  bow,  and  two  smaller  ones,  all  filled  with  armed  troops.  The 
large  barge  grounded  on  the  flats.  The  other  two  came  ashore  with  a 
number  of  armed  men,  variously  estimated  at  between  thirty  and  sixty. 
After  reaching  the  shore  some  six  or  eight  proceeded  up  to  Mr.  Gresham’s 
house.  One  of  the  party  accosted  Mr.  Gresham  and  introduced  another 
of  the  party.  The  first  named,  it  seems,  was  the  pilot,  who  was  captain 
of  a  wood  vessel,  and  acquainted  with  Gresham,  lie  enquired  if  he 
had  any  chickens  or  lambs  for  sale.  Mr.  Gresham  replied  that  he  had 
a  plenty,  but  not  a  d — done  for  that  party,  lie  then  took  the  pilot 
aside  and  told  him  they  had  better  be  getting  away,  as  there  were 
troops  in  the  neighborhood,  and  that  lie  did  not  wish  his  premises  to  be 
the  scene  of  a  battle,  as  his  mother  was  very  ill  in  the  house.  While 
they  were  talking  a  small  company  of  Lancaster  troops,  about  thirty 
in  number,  were  seen  coming  down  the  road  in  double-quick  time.  The 
alarm  was  given,  and  the  enemy  fled  precipitately  to  their  boats,  our 
men  firing  into  them  as  they  shoved  off.  In  their  flight  they  left  one 
of  the  barges.  The  men,  in  great  confusion,  crowded  into  the  other, 
and  others  wading  out  to  the  large  barge  on  the  flats.  In  their  Might 
they  left,  besides  the  barge,  two  breechdoading  rifles,  a  revolver,  and 
several  swords,  with  coats,  hats,  and  shoes,  thrown  away  in  their  hasty 
retreat.  It  is  confidently  asserted  that  four  of  the  enemy  were  killed 
in  the  boat.  Nobody  hurt  on  our  side.  As  soon  as  our  men  fired  on 
the  enemy  the  ship  opened  her  guns  on  Mr.  Gresham’s  house.  She  fired 
fifty-three  shot  and  shell,  seventeen  of  which  took  effect,  damaging  the 
house  to  the  amount  of  at  least  $1,000.  As  in  all  of  our  engagements, 
the  preservation  of  life  was  most  remarkable.  One  of  the  balls  struck 
the  bed  on  which  Mrs.  Gresham  was  lying  ill.  She  was  then  removed 
to  an  outhouse  and  a  bombshell  came  in  and  exploded  in  the  room  with¬ 
out  injury  to  anyone. 

I  have  given  you  in  a  very  hurried  manner  these  particulars,  which 
I  gather  from  most  reliable  sources  of  information.  You  will  unite  with 
us  in  contemptuous  indignation  at  the  cowardly  conduct  of  these  das¬ 
tardly  scoundrels,  avIio,  refusing  to  meet  half  their  number  face  to  face, 
at  a  safe  distance,  in  their  ship,  destroy  the  property  of  our  citizens. 

I  hope  to  be  able  to  visit  your  camp  soon  and  renew  the  acquaintance 
I  had  the  pleasure  of  having  with  you  last  winter. 

Hastily  and  truly,  yours, 

Jos.  Christian. 

Colonel  Charles  A.  Crump, 

Gloucester  Point ,  Va.

Report  of  Commander  Carr ,  U.  S.  Wavy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Quaker 

City ,  of  attack  by  Confederate  force  upon  a  boat  party  from  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Quaker  City, 
Hampton  Roads,  June  24,  1861. 

Sir:  While  on  the  cruising  ground  of  this  vessel  this  morning,  I 
picked  up  a  man  named  Peter  Lynch  in  an  open  boat,  and  who  described 
himself  as  a  refugee  from  Norfolk. 

He  informed  me  also  that  a  man  named  Hayes,  late  master  plumber 
of  the  Norfolk  navy  yard,  had  lied  with  him,  and  was  at  the  time  wait¬ 
ing  on  the  beach. 

1  immediately  dispatched  an  armed  boat  under  charge  of  Acting- 
Master  Mather  to  bring  him  off,  but  which  was  fired  upon  before  reach¬ 
ing  the  shore  by  a  large  body  of  mounted  troops,  who  rushed  from  a 
concealed  rendezvous  in  the  woods. 

I  regret  to  inform  you  that  James  Loyd,  ordinary  seaman,  was 
wounded,  I  fear  mortally. 

Acting  Master  Mather  managed  his  boat  to  my  satisfaction,  and  the 
boat’s  crew  behaved  well. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

O.  Carr, 

Commander,  U.  S.  Wavy,  Commanding  Quaker  City.

Baltimore,  June  19 , 1861. 

Scr:  I  have  reason  to  suspect  that  quite  au  amount  of  aid  and  com¬

Report  of  Lieutenant  Albert  Kautz ,  U.  S.  Navy,  of  the  recapture  of  the 
prize  brig  Hannah  Balch  by  the  C.  S.  privateer  Coffee ,  June  25,  1861. 

Washington,  I).  C.,  November  20,  1861. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  my  arrival  in  this  city,  after  having 
been  a  prisoner  for  more  than  four  months.  I  was  ordered  to  the  her¬ 
maphrodite  brig  Hannah  Balch ,  as  prize  master,  on  the  20th  of  June  last, 
by  the  commanding  officer  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Flag,  off'  Charleston,  S.  C. 

I  steered  eastward  till  I  reached  the  Gulf  Stream,  and  kept  in  it 
till  I  was  captured  on  the  25th  of  June,  about  30  miles  to  the  south¬ 
ward,  and  eastward  of  Cape  Hatteras. 

The  swell  of  the  sea  and  the  wind  were  both  from  the  eastward.  I 
had  made  a  reasonable  allowance  for  them,  and  I  attribute  my  being- 
20  miles  to  the  westward  of  my  reckoning  to  the  inaccurate  chronome¬ 
ter  belonging  to  the  vessel.  The  steamer  which  captured  me  was  the 
steamer  Coffee ,  formerly  of  Norfolk,  and  had  been  cruising  off'  Cape 
Hatteras,  running  out  in  the  morning  and  back  in  the  evening.  She 
was  commanded  by  Thomas  B.  Crossen  [Thomas  M.  Crossau  j,  formerly  of 
the  U.  S.  Navy,  and  carried  a  32-pounder  mounted  on  a  pivot  carriage ; 
she  also  had  quite  a  number  of  soldiers  on  board.  I  endeavored  to 
make  my  escape  by  setting  all  sail  and  running  free,  but  the  steamer 
being  a  fast  one  and  the  brig  a  slow  sailer  I  was  soon  overtaken  and 
compelled  to  surrender. 

I  caused  the  three  muskets  1  possessed  and  as  many  pistols  and  cut¬ 
lasses  to  be  thrown  overboard  to  prevent  them  from  falling  into  the 
hands  of  the  enemy.  The  six  men  I  had  with  me  were  sent  to  Fort 
Macon,  N.  C.  The  three  merchantmen  who  belonged  to  the  vessel  were 
released,  and  I  was  sent  to  Raleigh.  I  received  a  parole  to  live  in  War¬ 
ren  County,  N.  C.,  but  on  the  25th  of  August  it  was  taken  from  me  and 
I  was  sent  to  Richmond,  Ya.,  where  I  was  confined  in  a  cell  by  order 
of  Jefferson  Davis,  for  the  alleged  reason  that  A.  G.  Hudgins  was  con¬ 
fined  in  the  Tombs  in  New  York. 


*  See  p.  738. 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


745 


Ou  the  29tli  ultimo  I  was  granted  a  parole  of  fifty  days  for  the  pur¬ 
pose  ot  effecting  an  exchange.  I  pledged  myself  to  return  to  Rich¬ 
mond  a  prisoner,  it  1  failed  to  get  an  exchange.  I  also  pledged  myself 
to  call  upon  the  President,  and  urge  au  exchange  of  prisoners  now  held 
in  Richmond  for  those  held  by  the  U.  S.  Government. 

Patriotic  motives  and  a  sympathy  for  the  unfortunate  prisoners  in 
Richmond  induced  me  to  act  as  I  did.  I  need  scarcely  say  that  I  was 
exceedingly  anxious  to  secure  my  own  liberty. 

Trusting  that  the  Department  will  sustain  me  in  my  action,  and 
honing  soon  to  be  able  to  take  service, 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Albert  Kautz, 
Lieutenant ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Flay -Officer  Stringham ,  U.  S. 

Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  regarding  transfer 

of  cannon  from  War  Department. 

Xavy  Department, 

Washington ,  June  25,  1861. 

Sir:  In  accordance  with  your  suggestion,  instructions  will  be  issued 
by  the  War  Office,  subject  to  the  approval  of  Major-General  Butler,  to 
transfer  to  your  charge  one  of  the  large  pieces  of  ordnance  known  as 
the  Rodman  cannon,  together  with  its  equipment  and  ammunition,  for 
service  afloat  in  the  waters  adjacent  to  Old  Point  Comfort. 

As  the  rifled  cannon  now  lying  near  Fortress  Monroe  has  not  been 
yet  fully  tested,  and  as  considerable  time  would  elapse  before  a  trial 
could  be  made  and  the  projectiles  prepared,  the  Department  woidd  in 
consequence  recommend  you  to  take  the  shell  gun  of  15  inches’  bore, 
which  is  already  proved,  mounted  on  its  carriage,  and  supplied  with  a 
sufficiency  of  shells  for  present  service. 

In  the  book  of  Rodman  on  experiments  with  cannon  and  powder  (for¬ 
warded  to  you  by  this  mail),  at  page  290,  you  will  find  all  requisite  infor¬ 
mation  relative  to  the  weights  of  charge  and  shell,  elevation,  range,  and 
recoil  for  the  XV-incli  gun,  by  which  you  will  perceive  that,  with  an 
elevation  of  25  degrees,  a  charge  of  50  pounds,  and  a  shell  of  315 
pounds,  the  range  obtained  was  4,686  yards. 

It  may  be  well  to  remark  that  the  bore  is  not  chambered,  and  the 
ordinary  form  of  cartridge  bag  will  answer  for  the  charge. 

For  the  purpose  of  preparing  the  gun  for  active  operations  afloat 
you  will,  with  all  practicable  dispatch,  cause  to  be  purchased  a  suitable 
vessel  to  sustain  its  weight  of  49,099  pounds,  exclusive  of  carriage  and 
equipment,  and  fit  the  vessel  in  such  a  manner  as  your  experience  may 
dictate. 

Should,  however,  difficulties  arise  with  respect  to  the  price  of  the 
vessel,  by  notifying  this  Department  the  matter  will  be  promptly 
attended  to. 

When  the  vessel  and  gun  are  fully  prepared  for  service  you  will  be 
guided  by  such  circumstances  in  the  operations  as  the  pending  hostilities 
may  demand. 

I  am,  very  respectfully, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Senior  Flag-Officer  Silas  H.  Stringham,  U.  S.  Xavy, 

Commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads.
