Post-Office, 

Wilmington,  Bel.,  June  21,  1861. 

Sir  :  Yesterday  I  telegraphed  to  Mr.  Hoffman,  collector  at  Baltimore, 
that  Hon.  G.  P.  Fisher  had  written  to  me  from  Dover  that  a  lady  named 
Bell,  accompanied  by  her  son,  were  en  route  for  Baltimore  to  sail  for 
Virginia  in  a  small  vessel  recently  repainted  and  renamed  in  Baltimore. 
The  husband  of  the  lady  is  in  the  Confederate  (or  rebel)  Army.  The 
vessel  nominally  trades  to  eastern  shore  of  Maryland  (really  to  Virginia) 
with  stores.  The  female  has  been  up  to  Philadelphia;  from  thence  to 
Baltimore  several  times,  and  no  doubt  is  collecting  information. 

The  vessel,  it  is  believed,  slips  in  and  out  of  York  Biver  during  the 
temporary  absence  of  the  Harriet  Lane.  I  have  collected  information 
from  the  mail  agent  on  the  Delaware  road.  I  believe  that  constant 
communication  is  carried  on  through  the  navigable  waters  of  Delaware 
and  Maryland,  and  that  I  could  carry  any  material  I  choose  from  Phila¬ 
delphia  to  Virginia  at  any  time. 

Very  respectfully, 


A.  H.  Grimshaw, 

Postmaster. 


Hon.  G.  Welles.

[Enclosure.] 

When  I  lett  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  three  vessels  had  just  arrived,  one 
with  a  cargo  of  railroad  iron  from  Cardiff,  Wales;  one  with  a  cargo  of 
molasses,  from  Cardenas;  and  one  with  a  cargo  of  lime  from  Maine. 
The  latter  vessel  was  bound  to  Charleston,  but  finding  that  harbor 
blockaded,  put  into  the  port  of  Wilmington.  When  I  left,  no  blockade 
was  established  off  the  Cape  Fear  Biver,  and  I  have  not  seen  any 
account  of  any  since  my  arrival  North.  Unless  Wilmington  is  block¬ 
aded,  the  blockade  of  Charleston  Harbor  is  a  practical  nullity.  There 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


747 


is  direct  railroad  communication  between  the  two  places,  and  for  com¬ 
mercial  purposes  Wilmington  is  as  near  the  interior  of  South  Carolina 
as  her  own  port  of  Charleston.  According  to  the  published  terms  of 
the  blockade,  a  vessel  attempting  to  enter  is  warned  off;  when  warned 
off,  she  can  proceed  to  Wilmington  without  molestation  and  discharge 
her  cargo.  Vessels  drawing  12A  feet  water  can  enter  the  Cape  Fear. 
The  same  will  apply  to  Beaufort  and  Ocracoke  inlets  on  the  coast.  A 
vessel  entering  Albemarle  Sound  can  land  her  cargo  in  Norfolk,  not¬ 
withstanding  the  efficient  blockade  established  there.  The  Dismal 
Swamp  Canal  and  the  Albemarle  and  Chesapeake  Canal  offer  facilities 
of  communication.  Vast  quantities  of  corn  are  sent  from  the  eastern 
counties  of  North  Carolina  to  Norfolk  by  the  routes  indicated.  So 
long  as  the  rebel  troops  can  receive  abundance  of  corn  from  North 
Carolina,  rice  from  Wilmington  and  Charleston,  bacon  and  pork  from 
Memphis  and  New  Orleans,  they  can  scarcely  be  starved  out. 

Wm.  A.  Guyer, 

Norwalk,  Conn. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  Braine,  TJ.  S.  Navi/,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Monti- 
cello,  giving  information  received  from  refugees  from  Norfolk,  Ya. 

U.  S.  S.  Monticello, 
Hampton  Roads,  June  25,  1861. 

Sir  :  When  I  saw  you  this  morning  I  neglected  to  mention  that  at  1 
o’clock  on  Monday  morning,  while  at  anchor  in  Lynn  Haven  Bay,  we 
were  boarded  by  two  refugees  from  Norfolk  named  James  Lane  and 
Charles  Hazard.  They  came  off  in  a  man  of- war  boat  which  they  found 
and  launched  in  Lynn  Haven  Bay. 

They  both  belonged  to  New  York  City,  and  I  permitted  them  to  leave 
in  the  schooner  R.  C.  A.  Ward,  bound  to  that  place,  and  gave  them 
rations  for  six  days.  They  gave  me  the  following  information: 

Norfolk  and  its  vicinity  is  crowded  with  troops.  In  the  navy  yard  at  Gosport,  the 
machine  shop  is  in  fair  working  order.  The  Merrimack  has  been  raised  and  is  now  in 
the  dry  dock.  She  was  burned  nearly  to  her  copper  and  her  machinery  is  effectually 
destroyed. 

They  report  that  “troops  are  being  sent  from  Norfolk  to  Smithfield, 
and  from  that  point  across  the  James  River  to  Yorktown.”  I  also 
learn  that  the  steamer  Glen  Cove,  running  up  James  River,  was 
destroyed  by  tire. 

I  am,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

D.  L.  Braine, 

Lieutenant ,  U.  S.  Navy,  in  Charge  TJ.  S.  8.  Monticello. 

Flag-Officer  S.  H.  Stringham, 

Commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Stringham ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic 

Blockading  'Squadron ,  regarding  Engineer  Jordan ,  late  II.  S.  Navy, 

and  the  burning  of  steamers  Merrimack  and  Glen  Cove. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  June  26,  1861. 

Sir:  I  herewith  send  a  letter  from  Marshall  F.  Jordan,  second 
assistant  engineer,  U.  S.  Navy,  now  on  board  this  ship. 

As  I  am  informed  by  the  commander  of  the  Mount  Vernon  that  he  is 
a  strong  secessionist,  will  the  Department  please  inform  me  what  I 
shall  do  with  him? 

The  commander  of  the  Mount  Vernon  asked  Mr.  Marshall  [Jordan]  if 
he  would  take  an  oath  not  to  light  against  the  United  States,  provided 
he  was  permitted  to  leave.  He  indignantly  answered,  No!  He  would 
be  d - d  if  he  would  ever  take  that  oath. 

I  am  happy  to  inform  the  Department  that  reliable  information  was 
received  from  two  deserters  who  were  on  board  of  the  Monticello  yes¬ 
terday,  named  James  Lane  and  Charles  Hazard,  that  the  Merrimack 
was  burned  to  the  water’s  edge.  She  was  taken  into  dry  dock,  exam¬ 
ined,  and  pronounced  worthless.  Her  machinery  was  all  destroyed. 
Also  that  the  secession  steamer  Glen  Cove ,  running  up  James  ltiver, 
was  destroyed  by  fire. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  II.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer ,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy.

Report  of  Flap -Officer  Stringham,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic 

Blockading  Squadron ,  regarding  disposition  of  captured  vessels  Sally 

Magee  and  Amelia. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads ,  June  26 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  of  the  capture  this  morning  of 
the  bark  Sally  Magee,  from  Rio  de  Janeiro,  bound  to  Richmond,  Ya., 
where  she  is  owned,  and  the  cargo  also.  I  shall  send  her  to  New  York, 
in  charge  of  Lieutenant  Bryant. 

I  have  taken  from  the  Union  the  three  mates  and  twelve  men  found 
on  board  the  ship  Amelia  when  she  was  captured  off  Charleston,  June 
18,  1861.  This  ship  was  sent  to  Philadelphia.  Will  the  Department 
please  inform  me  what  I  shall  do  with  these  prisoners?  The  crew  are  a 
miserable  set  of  Chinamen,  Malays,  etc.  The  officers  are  English  and 
American. 

The  captain  and  crew  of  the  Savannah ,  also  of  the  Hallie  Jackson,  a 
list  of  whose  names  I  have  already  forwarded  to  the  Department,  were 
sent  in  the  Harriet  Lane  to  New  York  June  24. 

Yesterday,  in  Lynn  Haven  Bay,  the  Quaker  City  discovered  a  boat 
pulling  toward  them,  which  proved  to  have  a  man  in  it,  deserting  from 
the  secessionists.  He  informed  them  there  was  another  man  on  shore 
wishing  to  leave.  The  ship’s  boat  pulled  for  the  shore,  but  before  arriv¬ 
ing  it  was  tired  on  by  a  large  party,  which  suddenly  appeared  in  view 
and  which  led  them  to  suppose  the  other  man  was  captured.  Unfor¬ 
tunately  a  shot  from  the  shore  reached  the  boat,  mortally  wounding  one 
man,  who  has  since  died. 

The  Union  will  go  to  sea  to-day  to  return  to  her  station  off  Savannah. 
I  wish  very  much  1  had  a  more  competent  seagoing  vessel  to  send  in 
her  place. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  IT.  Stringiiam, 

Flag-Officer ,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Stringham ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Atlantic 

Blockading  Squadron,  regarding  proposed  transfer  of  Rodman  cannon 

for  the  use  of  the  Navy. 

IT.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads ,  June  27,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  receipt  of  your  letter,  dated 
June  25,  in  which  you  apprise  me  that  instructions  will  be  issued,  sub¬ 
ject  to  the  approval  of  Major-General  Butler,  to  transfer  to  my  charge 
one  of  the  large  pieces  of  ordnance  now  at  this  point,  known  as  the 
Rodman  cannon,  and  that  for  the  purpose  of  preparing  the  gun  for  active 
operations  afloat  “you  (I)  will  take  all  practicable  dispatch  to  cause  to 
be  purchased  a  suitable  vessel  to  sustain  its  weight,  49,099  pounds, 
exclusive  of  carriage,  etc.,  and  lit  the  vessel  in  such  manner  as  your 
(my)  experience  may  dictate.” 

I  hasten  to  inform  the  Department  that  there  is  no  vessel  here  that 
could  be  used  with  any  advantage,  and  I  doubt  whether  we  shall  be 
able  to  procure  one  this  side  of  New  York. 

If  the  Department  will  direct  one  to  be  purchased  there  and  properly 
fitted,  or  if  they  will  permit  me  to  go,  I  think  1  might  select  a  suitable 
one  and  have  her  immediately  put  in  proper  condition  to  receive  the 
gun,  and  carry  into  effect  as  soon  as  practicable  the  wishes  of  the 
Department. 

1  have  received  the  work,  Rodman  on  Experiments  with  Cannon  and 
Powder,  mentioned  in  your  letter  June  -15. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  H.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy.

I  have  just  heard  from  a  reliable  source  that  about  fifteen  days  since 
the  rebel  force  in  and  near  Norfolk,  Va.,  amounted  to  about  10,000 
men,  and  also  that  the  steamer  Yorktoicn  had  been  strengthened, 
houses  taken  off,  and  lined  inside  above  the  water  line  with  railroad 
iron,  and  carried  a  battery  of  eight  32-pounder  rifled  guns,  and  is  com¬ 
manded  by  Lieutenant  R.  B.  Pegram,  late  U.  S.  Navy.  This  may  be 
of  service  to  the  Navy  Department. 

Phelps. 


While  Charleston  and  Savannah  as  well  as  Virginia  ports  are  block¬ 
aded,  our  port  (Wilmington,  N.  C.)  is  overlooked.  Vessels  from  Eng¬ 
land  arrive  and  bring  us  what  is  wanted,  our  railroads  distributing  to 
every  point  of  the  compass  aid  and  comfort  to  the  Confederate  States. 
Six  British  vessels  have  entered  and  cleared  since  the  paper  blockade 
was  declared.  One  is  now  loading  for  England,  her  cargo  furnishing 
funds  to  bring  out  munitions  from  England.  More  vessels  are  expected 
with  railroad  iron. 

Jacob  Brewster.

[Enclosure.] 

Tire  ship  Alliance,  which  was  ordered  away  off  Charleston  some  time 
since  by  the  U.  S.  blockading  squadron,  has  been  lying  in  this  harbor 
(St.  Johns)  two  weeks.  Yesterday  (Sunday)  the  Palmetto  flag  was 
flying  at  her  mizzen  all  day.  She  now  hails  from  Liverpool,  England, 
but  was  formerly  owned,  and  perhaps  is  still  in  reality  owned,  in 
Charleston,  S.  C.  Her  captain  and  mate  both  belong  there.  She  is 
loaded  with  railroad  iron,  and  is  now  waiting  orders  from  Liverpool. 
There  are  suspicions  that  she  has  also  arms  beneath  the  iron  rails.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Stringham ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic 
Bloclading  Squadron ,  of  the  rescue  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Quaker  City  of  a 
small  boat  containing  refugees. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads ,  July  f  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  yesterday,  June 
30,  the  U.  S.  S.  Quaker  City,  while  cruising  off  Cape  Henry,  discovered 
and  picked  up  a  small  sailboat  containing  seven  men.  She  brought 
them  and  the  boat  to  the  flagship.  They  proved  to  be  five  Northern 
men,  residents  of  Pennsylvania  and  New  Jersey,  who  have  been  resid¬ 
ing  in  North  Carolina,  engaged  in  their  various  mechanical  occupations 
in  the  neighborhood  of  Washington,  N.  C. 

Fearing  ill  treatment,  and  the  alternative  of  being  compelled  to  join 
in  the  rebellion  or  suffering  personal  violence,  they  made  the  best 
arrangements  they  could,  and,  through  the  aid  of  some  Union  men 
with  whom  they  were  on  good  terms,  they  (after  a  week’s  navigation 
by  day  and  night,  the  last  part  of  it  from  near  Cape  Hatteras,  being 
out  at  sea,  and  running  great  risk  of  being  captured  at  the  various 
inlets,  where  they  represent  the  North  Carolina  rebels  to  have  a  small 
force  of  men  with  light  batteries)  have  at  last,  to  their  great  relief, 
reached  this  point,  asking  and  receiving  that  protection  which  is  due 
to  loyal  citizens. 

The  two  remaining  persons,  one  a  native  of  Wilmington,  Del.,  though 
now  resident  of  North  Carolina,  where  his  sick  wife  now  anxiously 
awaits  the  issue  of  his  effort  to  serve  these  men,  request  permission  to 
return.  The  young  man  who  accompanies  him  seems  a  well-disposed 
citizen  of  North  Carolina.  I  shall  take  the  liberty  of  permitting  them 
to  start  back  with  their  sailboat,  hoping  they  will  not  be  discovered  by 
the  secession  forces,  they  so  much  fear. 

It  was  through  the  kindness  and  aid  of  these  men  that  the  Northern 
citizens  were  able  to  get  off. 

Bespectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  H.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer ,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 
Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy.

Consulate  op  the  United  States  op  America, 

St.  Petersburg ,  May  28,  1861. 

Sir:  *  *  *  The  ship  Noemie,  from  Charleston,  Captain  John 

Johnson,  which  arrived  at  Cronstadt  last  week  with  a  cargo  of  cotton, 
I  am  informed,  displayed  the  flag  of  the  Confederate  States  at  the  main 
while  at  Copenhagen  and  Elsinore. 

The  vessel  came  into  Cronstadt  under  the  flag  of  the  Union,  but  on 
learning  what  had  occurred  before  her  arrival  here,  I  went  to  Csonstadt 
and  examined  the  ship’s  papers  deposited  with  the  agent  of  this  consu¬ 
late,  and  found  that  she  had  the  usual  United  States  register. 

The  vessel  is  owned  by  a  mercantile  firm  in  Charleston.  The  captain 
is  from  Baltimore.  Captain  Johnson  is  a  secessionist,  and  probably 
took  this  course  to  show  it  and  make  an  excitement. 

I  have  thought  proper  to  mention  these  particulars  on  account  of  the 
rumors  which  Captain  Johnson’s  desire  thus  to  exhibit  his  attachment 
to  a  bad  cause  has  produced,  some  of  which  may  find  their  way  to  the 
United  States. 

#  *  #  #  #  #  # 


I  have  the  honor  to  remain,  your  obedient  servant, 

Caleb  Croswell, 

U.  S.  Consul. 


Hon.  Wm.  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State.

Blockading  Squadron ,  regarding  purchase  of  vessel  for  Rodman  cannon. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  July  2 ,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  two  confidential  letters  from 
the  Department,  dated  June  29,  containing  copies  of  advertisements; 
also  letter  dated  June  28,  with  reference  to  boatswains.  I  think  there 
is  one  man  on  board  this  ship  competent  to  fill  this  position.  I  shall 
proceed  to  have  him  examined  professionally  and  physically,  as  directed 
and  required  by  the  Department. 

I  have  just  returned  from  examining  a  vessel  captured  here,  but  find 
her  unfit  to  carry  the  Bodman  cannon.  I  also  find  the  range  of  this 
gun  is  not  over  2f  miles,  and  this* its  extreme  range  with  the  largest 
charge  of  powder. 

I  must  say  that,  from  all  the  observation  I  can  make,  a  rifle  gun  of 
8,  9,  or  10  inch  caliber  would  be  more  effective  and  much  more  easily 
handled. 

I  think  I  have  now  at  this  point  a  vessel  which  could  carry  this  lat¬ 
ter  gun  if  she  had  a  little  additional  strengthening.  She  could  be  sent 
to  Washington  and  prepared  in  a  short  time. 

I  enclose  two  letters  from  parties  offering  vessels  to  sell  for  this  pur¬ 
pose.  I  should  prefer  the  Department  would  make  the  purchase.  I 
think  the  price  fixed  is  very  high.  The  Department  could  authorize  a 
person  to  examine  them,  however. 

I  repeat  that  I  would  prefer  a  rifle  gum.  The  vessel  I  allude  to  above 
is  a  prize. 

Bespectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  H.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer ,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Flag-Officer  Stringham,  U.  S. 
Navy,  commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  transmitting  letters 
from  the  Secretary  of  the  Treasury  regarding  transfer  of  American 
vessels  to  British  ownership. 

Navy  Department,  July  3, 1861. 

Sir:  I  herewith  transmit  for  your  information  a  copy  of  a  letter  in 
reply  to  one  from  this  Department,  addressed  to  me  on  the  27th  ultimo 
by  the  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Treasury,  respecting  the  transfer  of 
American  vessels  to  British  ownership,  and  to  the  provisional  registers 
issued  in  such  cases  by  British  consuls. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Flag-Officer  S.  H.  Stringham, 

Comdg.  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads,  Virginia. 

[Enclosure.  1 

Treasury  Department,  June  27, 1861. 
Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  letter  of 
the  25th  instant,  and  enclosure,  respecting  the  transfer  of  American 
vessels  to  British  ownership,  and  to  the  provisional  registers  issued  in 
such  cases  by  British  consuls. 

The  act  of  the  British  Parliament,  entitled  the  merchant  shipping  act, 
of  1854,  confers  on  the  consuls  of  her  Britannic  Majesty,  in  the  case  of 
the  sale  of  a  foreign  bottom  to  a  person  authorized  by  the  act  to  become 
the  owner  of  British  shipping,  the  power  of  issuing  a  provisional  or 
temporary  register,  and  to  engage  a  crew  for  a  vessel  so  transferred. 


760 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


For  con  venience  of  reference,  I  accompany  this  communication  with 
a  copy  of  the  merchant  shipping  act,  ancl  would  respectfully  refer  you 
to  sections  18  and  54,  and  to  forms  B,  C,  and  I)  in  the  appendix,  as 
having  a  special  bearing  on  the  subject  of  your  letter.  I  also  transmit 
herewith,  as  referring  to  the  same  subject,  an  extract  from  instructions 
to  British  consuls  under  the  merchant  shipping  act,  prepared  by  the 
board  of  trade,  and  approved  by  her  Britannic  Majesty’s  secretary  of 
state  for  foreign  affairs. 

As  the  British  laws  relating  to  navigation  now  stand,  a  foreign-built 
vessel,  manned  and  commanded  by  foreigners,  if  she  is  owned  by  qual¬ 
ified  persons,  is  entitled  to  carry  the  British  iiag  and  claim  British 
privileges  and  protection.  The  sole  requisite  so  to  entitle  her  is  British 
ownership. 

Bo  regulation,  it  is  believed,  can  be  prescribed,  defining  in  advance 
the  duties  of  naval  officers  in  regard  to  their  treatment  of  vessels  sail¬ 
ing  under  provisional  registers  issued  by  British  consuls.  It  must  be 
left  mainly  to  their  good  sense  and  sound  discretion  to  determine'the 
course  to  be  pursued  according  to  the  circumstances  of  each  case  as  it 
occurs.  If  they  have  satisfactory  reason  to  believe  that  the  sales  are 
in  contravention  of  the  British  laws  as  well  as  those  of  the  United 
States,  merely  collusive,  and  the  provisional  registers,  therefore,  unlaw¬ 
fully  issued,  the  vessels  should  be  sent  into  port  for  legal  proceedings. 

The  information  contained  in  the  accompanying  documents  would 
enable  officers  of  the  Navy  to  act  understanding^  in  such  cases.  They 
should  know  under  what  circumstances  and  with  what  formalities  such 
sales  can  lawfully  be  made,  and  what  papers  the  consul  is  authorized 
to  issue.  Departure  from  the  legal  requirements  in  any  material  res¬ 
pect  would  justly  occasion  suspicion  of  bad  faith,  and  the  vessel  should 
be  treated  accordingly. 

It  is  with  this  view  of  the  matter  that  the  enclosed  documents  are 
respectfully  communicated,  in  reply  to  your  letter. 

I  am,  very  respectfully, 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Ike  Navy. 


S.  P.  Chase, 
Secretary  of  the  Treasury. 


[Subenclosure.] 

Extract  from  the  instructions  to  British  consuls  under  the  merchant  shipping  act  of  1854, 
prepared  by  the  board  of  trade  and  approved  by  her  Majesty’s  secretary  of  state  for 
foreign  affairs. 

Purchases,  mortgages ,  and  sales  at  foreign  ports. 

22.  Persons  qualified  to  own  British  ships  may  purchase  foreign 
ships  at  a  foreign  port.  In  such  cases  the  ship  can  not  be  completely 
registered  until  she  arrives  at  some  port  in  the  British  dominions  where 
there  is  a  British  registrar;  but  in  order  to  prevent  the  inconveniences 
and  dangers  which  would  arise  from  the  ship’s  making  her  homeward 
voyage  without  papers  showing  the  national  character,  the  consul  is 
enabled  to  grant  a  provisional  certificate,  to  remain  in  force  until  the 
expiration  of  six  months,  or  until  the  arrival  of  the  ship  at  some  port 
having  a  British  registrar,  whichever  first  happens.  In  granting  this 
certificate  he  will  attend  to  the  following  particulars: 

He  will  require  from  the  purchaser,  or  from  the  agent  of  the  pur¬ 
chaser,  a  declaration  containing  a  statement  of  the  qualification  of  the 
purchaser,  similar  to  those  contained  in  forms  B  or  C  (as  the  case  may 
be)  in  the  schedule  to  the  act,  and  containing  also  such  of  the  other 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


761 


particulars  contained  in  tliose  forms  as  can  be  obtained  without  requir¬ 
ing  a  new  survey  or  measurement;  and  this  declaration  should,  so  far 
as  possible,  be  in  the  same  form,  and  be  made  with  the  same  formalities 
and  precautions  as  declarations  given  for  the  purpose  of  the  final 
registry  of  the  ship,  except  that  it  must  be  marked  “  Provisional.” 

He  will  then  prepare  a  certificate  of  registry,  adhering  as  nearly  as 
possible  to  the  Form  D  in  the  schedule  of  the  act,  except  that  at  the 
top  must  be  written  in  large  and  conspicuous  characters  the  word 
“Provisional,”  and  that  at  the  foot  or  in  some  conspicuous  place  must  be 
added  the  words  “This  provisional  certificate  of  registry  continues  in 
force  only  until  the - day  of - (insert  the  day  of  the  expira¬ 

tion  ot  six  months  from  the  date),  or  until  she  completes  her  voyage 

from - -  (insert  the  port  at  which  the  certificate  is  given)  to  some 

port  at  which  there  is  a  British  registrar,  whichever  first  happens.” 
The  provisional  certificate  must  be  signed  by  the  consul  instead  of  by 
the  registrar,  and  must  be  sealed  with  his  official  seal.  No  official 
number  is  to  be  inserted.  A  form  of  provisional  certificate  of  registry, 
filled  up  according  to  the  circumstances  of  the  case  as  assumed,  is 
given  in  the  appendix.  (Form  C  2.) 

He  will  keep  a  duplicate  of  the  certificate  and  send  it  with  the 
declaration  to  the  commissioners  of  customs  in  London  on  the  first 
convenient  opportunity,  and  in  so  doing  he  will  endorse  on  the  certifi¬ 
cate  a  statement  of  the  British  port  to  which  the  ship  is  bound. 

He  will  warn  the  master  and  the  purchaser,  or  his  agent,  that  the 
provisional  certificate  is  only  in  force  until  the  ship  reaches  the  first 
British  port  at  which  there  is  a  registrar,  or  at  the  expiration  of  six 
months,  whichever  first  happens,  and  that  she  must  then  be  surveyed, 
measured,  and  completely  registered.

A  pungy  boat  and  schooner  load  with  goods  in  Baltimore,  clear  for 
Deal’s  Island  or  Snow  Hill,  stop  at  Tangier  beach  inside  the  harbor, 
and  wait  for  a  suitable  night,  then  run  across  the  bay  and  enter  the 
mouth  of  York  River  and  discharge  in  Mob  jack  Bay,  and  at  other  times 
land  in  Bast  River.  The  captain  is  not  known,  but  he  has  tried  to  raise 
volunteers  in  Tangier.  The  pilot  is  known  by  the  name  of  William 
Pruitt.  Captain  John  Gibbons  gives  this  information,  and  is  ready  to 
act. 

I  have  heard  to-day  that  the  steamboat  St.  Nicholas  affair  was  a  trap 
set  to  catch  the  Pawnee.  There  may  be  other  enterprises  of  the  same 
character  on  foot,  and  it  would  be  well  to  be  on  the  lookout  for  them. 

Saml.  Hinks.

Yankee  has  just  arrived  here.  lam  sorry  to  find  by  reference  to  Mr. 
Werden’s  orders  that  he  must  proceed  direct  to  Washington. 

She  would  be  of  very  great  service  here,  as  I  have  no  small  steamer 
at  my  command. 

There  is  a  small  steamer  which  comes  down  almost  daily  from  Nor¬ 
folk,  keeping  out  of  range,  which  the  Yankee  could  prevent  and  per¬ 
haps  succeed  in  capturing,  besides  being  of  other  great  service  as  a 
towing  vessel,  for  which  ive  have  use.  I  regret  much  that  she  can  not 
stay  now. 

Yesterday  there  was  sent  to  this  place  by  the  Daylight  owe  oi  the  bay 
pungies,  about  30  tons  burden,  which  I  have  sent  this  morning  in  tow  of 
a  steamer  going  direct  to  Washington,  to  be  destroyed  or  used  there. 
She  is  one  of  those  used  in  carrying  stores  and  communications  from 
point  to  point  on  the  Chesapeake.

Report  of  Commander  Green,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  ship  James¬ 
town,  of  the  cruise  of  that  vessel  to  Savannah,  Ga. 

U.  S.  Sloop  of  War  Jamestown, 

Off  Charleston,  July  3,  1861. 

Sir:  In  compliance  with  your  instructions  of  the  18th  June  ultimo, 
directing  me  to  proceed  off'  Savannah,  Ga.,  with  this  ship  to  assist  in 
blockading  that  port,  and  to  touch  off  Charleston  on  my  way  down  to 
communicate  with  Captain  Mercer,  of  the  Wabash,  I  have  respectfully 
to  state  that  I  left  Hampton  Roads  on  the  19tli  June.  Light  airs, head 
winds,  and  squally  weather  retarded  our  passage  so  that  we  were  unable 
to  reach  Charleston  until  to-day,  3d  July.  I  have  had  an  interview 
with  Captain  Mercer  and  shall  immediately  proceed  to  Savannah,  hav¬ 
ing  a  fair  wind.  1  regret  that  I  can  not  speak  favorably  of  the  qualities 


764 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

of  tlie  ship  so  far  as  tliey  have  been  tried.  She  is  cfertain  in  “missing 
stays”  if  there  is  any  head  sea.  Always  gets  a  stern  board  and  is  very 
slow  in  paying  off.  She  is  also  very  much  wanting  in  stability.  On 
the  28th  June  1  spoke  the  Union ,  Commander  J.  It.  Goldsborough, 
bound  to  Charleston;  received  our  mail  bag,  and  transferred  to  him 
the  bags  for  the  Wabash i  and  Union.  Entire  harmony  prevails  on  board 
from  the  zealous  and  efficient  first  lieutenant,  Mr.  N.  B.  Harrison, 
down  through  all  the  grades,  and  a  strong  desire  is  manifested  to  put 
the  ship  on  a  footing  second  to  none  of  her  class.  Great  attention  has 
been  paid  to  the  exercise  of  the  battery,  especially  in  teaching  the 
details  of  using  shells. 

On  the  26th  instant  we  fired  at  a  target  sent  from  the  ship.  The  dis¬ 
tance  was  from  1,200  to  1,900  yards,  and  the  result  was  very  satisfac¬ 
tory.  The  master  is  very  attentive  to  his  duties,  but  is  young  and  has 
not  yet  passed  his  examination.  I  should  be  pleased  to  have  a  coast 
pilot  and  two  master’s  mates.  One  is  required  for  the  gun  deck  and 
spirit  room,  leaving  but  two  midshipmen  to  keep  watch,  and,  in  case  of 
sending  any  away  in  a  prize,  we  would  be  short.  The  crew  are  the  most 
ignorant  set  of  men  I  have  ever  seen  on  board  ship,  but  will,  after  being 
drilled,  be  superior  to  the  old  class  of  men-o’- war’s  men.  The  health  of 
the  ship  has  been  generally  good;  we  have  lost,  however,  one  man 
from  diarrhea,  who  has  been  unwell  for  some  months  past.  I  am  in 
want  of  a  large  general  chart  of  the  coast;  the  one  furnished  is  too 
small  to  be  run  by  with  any  satisfaction. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  etc., 

Charles  Green, 

Commander. 

Flag-Officer  Silas  H.  Stringiiam, 

Comdg.  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads ,  Virginia.

Report  of  Commander  Chandler ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Dawn , 

regarding  repairs  to  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Dawn, 

Baltimore,  Aid.,  July  4,  1861. — 9  a.  m. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  I  received,  about  3  p.  m. 
yesterday,  your  telegram  of  that  date,  directing  me  to  “hurry  the 
repairs  on  the  Dawn  and  proceed  down  the  bay  with  all  dispatch.” 

The  workmen  on  the  boiler  having  finished  about  10:30  a.  m.,  we 
immediately  commenced  cleaning  out  and  filling  the  boiler  for  a  cold- 
water  pressure,  hoisting  in  our  coal  at  the  same  time,  which  we  finished 
about  1:30  a.  m.  this  morning,  after  getting  in  about  73  tons.  We  had 
completed  our  watering  yesterday  morning  and  taken  in  all  our  stores 
except  those  required  in  the  gunner’s  department,  which  have  not  yet 
been  received.  We  found  the  boiler  and  Hues  to  stand  a  pressure  of 
45  pounds,  about  as  much  as  we  could  get  on,  our  crew  being  much 
worn  out  with  hoisting  in  and  shoveling  coal.  1  now  have  steam  up, 
and  will  proceed  down  the  bay  at  once  in  obedience  to  your  orders. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient, 

William  Chandler, 
Commander,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington. 

N.  B. — I  have  engaged  First  Assistant  Engineer  Wyatt,  but  not 
discharged  Master’s  Mate  Woodstock,  not  being  able  to  settle  his 
account.

Few  York,  June  29,  1861. 

Dear  Sir  :  As  a  good  Union  man  and  a  friend  to  the  Administra¬ 
tion,  I  take  the  liberty  of  informing  your  Excellency  about  the  port  of 
Wilmington,  F.  C.,  where  vessels  are  continually  coming  in,  changing 
their  nationality,  and  taking  cargoes  for  England  at  high  rates  to 
the  great  prejudice  of  the  port  of  Few  York.  Up  to  the  12tli  June 
none  of  the  blockading  squadron  had  been  off  Cape  Fear  Biver  to 
notify  the  fort  (Caswell)  of  the  blockade,  and  some  eight  or  ten  ves¬ 
sels  have  left  and  sailed  with  full  cargoes,  and  I  have  reason  to  believe 
vessels  have  cleared  from  here,  and  are  about  clearing  for  West  India 
ports,  and  no  doubt  will  fetch  up  there.  *  *  *  I  have  just  learned 

that  a  Carolinian  has  been  to  St.  John’s  and  chartered  a  brig  to  go  to 
Wilmington,  F.  C.,  for  a  load  of  naval  stores. 

Peter  Wilson. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,  etc.

Report  of  Commander  Livingston,  If.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pen¬ 
guin,  of  the  cruise  of  that  vessel  to  York  River ,  and  giving  information 
regarding  steamer  Wilson  C.  Small,  from  Baltimore. 

U.  S.  S.  Penguin, 
Hampton  Roads ,  July  5,  1861. 

Sir:  In  pursuance  of  your  order  of  the  29th  ultimo,  I  proceeded  off 
the  mouth  of  York  River.  I  saw  no  vessels  pass  in  or  out  of  that  river 
during  my  stay  there. 

On  the  1st  instant  your  order  of  same  date,  through  Lieutenant  Com¬ 
manding  Mygatt,  was  received  to  blockade  the  mouth  of  the  Rappahan¬ 
nock  River.  Got  underway  in  company  with  steamer  Reliance  for  the 
above  river,  and  arrived  same  evening;  saw  no  vessels  there.  On  the 
2d,  Lieutenant  Commanding  Mygatt  made  a  communication  to  me, 
which  I  herewith  enclose,  to  the  effect  that  the  engineer  had  reported 
to  him  that  it  was  necessary  for  the  Reliance  to  return  to  repair;  that 
it  was  unsafe  to  detain  her,  and  having  no  orders  in  regard  to  this  ves¬ 
sel,  I  did  not  order  a  survey,  but  suggested  the  same.  He  then  left  his 
station,  to  report  himself  to  his  commanding  officer  in  the  Potomac. 

On  the  2d  instant,  the  Mount  Vernon  arrived,  Commander  Glisson 
informing  me  that  became  to  relieve  me,  and  brought  a  pilot  for  me, 
but  no  orders  from  the  commander  in  chief;  but  from  a  conversation 
with  the  pilot,  I  inferred  that  you  wished  me  to  cruise  somewhat  at 
my  discretion  in  the  Chesapeake.  I  therefore,  at  daylight  on  the  .‘Id 
instant,  weighed  and  steamed  across  the  bay  to  Pocomoke  Sound,  board¬ 
ing  vessels  on  the  way,  as  per  list  enclosed.  On  entering  the  bay,  saw 
an  American  flag  flying  on  Tangier  Island  in  a  village  of  that  name; 
ran  into  the  harbor  and  hoisted  a  jack,  to  induce  them  to  come  off, 
which  they  soon  did.  The  three  men  who  came  off-  seemed  strong 
Union,  and  represented  to  me  that  there  was  but  one  man  on  the  island 
who  was  a  secessionist;  that  he  meant  to  hoist  a  secession  flag  to-mor¬ 
row,  and  that  a  force  would  be  over  from  Accomac  on  the  4th  to  take 


768 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


down  the  American  Hag’;  that  they  were  determined 'it  should  not  come 
down,  and  requested  me  to  remain  on  the  4th,  which  I  determined  to  do. 

July  4,  dressed  the  ship  in  honor  of  the  day.  I  was  informed  at 
Tangier  that  the  steamboat  Wilson  G.  Small,  from  Baltimore,  had 
some  days  before  been  down  with  a  load  of  goods  and  landed  at  Pun- 
goteague;  that  she  made  her  appearance  again  on  the  3d  instant,  but 
seeing  ns  in  the  harbor,  made  off.  This  boat  1  hear  is  allowed  to  trade 
only  as  far  as  Great  Annemessex  River.  In  the  evening  weighed  and  stood 
over  to  the  mouth  of  Great  Annemessex  River;  spoke  several  vessels, 
saw  nothing  suspicious,  anchored  for  the  night.  At  daylight  on  the 
5th,  weighed  and  stood  down  the  bay,  and  when  off  the  mouth  of  the 
Rappahannock,  communicated  with  the  Mount  Vernon.  Captain  Glis- 
son  had  no  news.  At  10  a.  in.  saw  steamer  Dawn  steering  down  the 
bay.  At  14  a.  m.  spoke  U.  S.  S.  Albatross ,  bound  to  Rappahannock 
River. 

Very  respectfully,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  W.  Livingston, 
Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Penguin.

cello,  of  assistance  rendered  a  shore  force  under  Colonel  Phelps ,  U.  S.

U.  S.  S.  Monticello, 

Off  Newport  News,  July  5,  1861. 

Sir  :  In  compliance  with  the  request  of  Colonel  Flielps,  we  took  a 
position  near  noon  to-day  about  5  miles  above  the  post,  for  the  purpose 
of  shelling  the  enemy  in  advance  of  a  battalion  which  moved  up  the 
left  bank  of  the  river,  and  after  our  firing  they  entered  the  woods. 
This  evening  they  returned  to  camp,  reporting  we  had  dispersed  with 
our  shell  a  body  of  cavalry  which  they  could  not  afterwards  overtake. 

Colonel  Phelps  sent  off  his  thanks  for  the  promptness  of  our  move¬ 
ment  and  the  precision  with  which  the  shell  were  thrown.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Flag-Officer  String  ham,  U.  S. 

Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  regarding  officers 

and  crew  of  chartered  steamer  Quaker  City. 

Navy  Department,  July  5,  1861. 

Sir  :  The  rates  asked  for  by  Commander  Carr,  in  your  letter  of  the 
3d  instant,  are  allowed. 

It  will  he  remembered  that  the  Quaker  City  was  chartered  by  certain 
parties  in  New  York  and  sent  to  the  Chesapeake,  and  at  the  expiration 
of  the  charter  the  Government  continued  it  for  three  months,  reserving 
to  itselt  the  right  to  place  on  board  a  naval  officer  to  command,  and 
afterwards  a  midshipman  was  added.  The  accounts  were  directed  to 
be  kept  on  board  the  North  Carolina ,  at  New  York. 

The  owners  of  the  Quaker  City  supplied  the  officers  and  crew  and  ran 
the  vessel,  and  continue  to  do  so,  unless  they  violate  the  charter. 

This  Department  can  not  make  any  acting  appointments  on  board. 

Lieutenant  Mitchell  may  be  ordered  to  the  Santee ,  so  as  to  permit 
that  vessel  to  proceed  to  sea  ivitliout  delay.  A  first  lieutenant  will  be 
sent  to  her  by  the  earliest  opportunity. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles. 

Flag-Officer  S.  II.  Stringham, 

Comdg.  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads ,  Virginia.

Navy;  and  to  report  the  Dawn  again  ready  for  service,  in  as  effective 
a  condition  perhaps  as  the  patching  of  an  old  boiler  and  very  old  flues 
could  make  her.  But  there  seemed  to  be,  soon  after  we  left  Baltimore 
yesterday  morning  (for  we  can  not  yet  get  at  the  place  in  consequence 
of  the  coal  lying  up  against  the  boiler,  and  the  coal  bunker  being  full), 
a  leakin  the  lower  part  of  the  boiler  itself  on  the  starboard  side,  about 
G  feet  from  the  after  end. 

There  are  no  passageways,  as  there  should  be,  constructed  between 
the  coal  bunkers  and  boilers  on  either  side;  and,  not  knowing  whether 
the  steamer  would  be  eventually  purchased  by  the  Government,  1  did 
not  feel  justified  in  incurring  the  expense  of  their  construction,  at  least 
(if  not  so  purchased,  and  without  benefit  to  the  Government),  before 
the  boiler  and  flues  (as  repaired)  had  been  tested,  while  the  repairs  and 
my  departure  were  so  hurried  that  the  coal  had  to  be  received  on  board 
as  soon  as  the  workmen  had  finished  and  before  the  boiler  and  flues 
could  be  tested  with  steam. 

Iu  the  cold-water  pressure  of  45  pounds  night  before  last,  however, 
there  was  no  perceptible  leak  anywhere  except  in  the  manholes,  one  iu 
each  end  of  boiler,  and  a  hand-hole  in  the  front  end,  which  was  subse¬ 
quently  repaired  as  soon  as  we  could  let  the  water  out  of  the  boilers, 
and  previously  to  filling  it  and  firing  up  again,  about  6  a.  m.,  to  come 
.down  here. 

When  the  coal  has  been  more  used  or  removed  from  the  starboard 
bunker,  we  shall  then  be  enabled  to  ascertain  more  about  this  leak,  the 
exact  location  of  which  is  now  a  matter  of  surmise;  but  the  fact  itself 
is  established  by  the  quantity  of  hot  water  in  the  bilge  and  the  diffi¬ 
culty  of  keeping  up  the  requisite  quantity  of  water  in  the  boilers, 
without  leaving  the  feed  pipe  all  the  time  open. 

We  have  been  under  a  running  pressure  of  not  exceeding  25  pounds 
of  steam,  all  the  way  down;  and  only  on  two  occasions,  while  stopping 
for  a  short  time,  did  it  rise  to  from  28  to  30  pounds. 

Last  night,  being  reluctant  to  run  past  Smith’s  Point  Shoals  without 
the  guide  of  the  light  and  light-boat  at  that  point,  Ave  came  to  anchor 
in  the  bay,  about  5  or  6  miles  to  the  southward  and  eastward  of  it,  and 
waited  for  early  daylight  to  proceed  hither. 

Accompanying  this  is  a  duplicate  requisition  from  the  engineer’s  and 
gunner’s  departments  for  articles  needed  therein  and  a  list  of  the  pro¬ 
visions  on  board. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient, 

William  Chandler, 
Commander ,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Flag-Officer  S.  H.  Stringham, 

Comdg.  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  Hampton  Roads ,  Virginia.

ReP°rt  °f  Commander  Case ,  U.  8.  Navy  (fleet  captain),  of  disrespect 
shown  to  a  flag  of  truce  by  Confederates. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  July  6,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  liave  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  your  order  I 
hoisted  a  Hag  of  truce  on  board  the  steam  tug  Adriatic  at  1  o’clock 
p.  m.  and  proceeded  toward  For  folk  to  communicate  with  General 
Huger,  as  directed. 

T\  hen  about  a  mile  below  the  Craney  Island  beacon,  and  after  hav- 
mg  passed  the  batteries  on  Sewell’s  and  Bush’s  points,  a  shot  was  tired 
at  the  tug  from  Craney  Island;  it  passed  diagonally  across  the  bow 
and  struck  within  20  feet.  Had  not  the  engine  been  stopped  at  the 
flash  ana  the  boat’s  head  turned  a  little  to  starboard,  the  shot,  must  I 
think,  have  struck  her. 

I  immediately  ordered  the  tug  anchored  and  left  in  the  barge,  with 
Midshipman  McCook,  to  communicate  with  the  boat  which  I  supposed 
would  meet  rue  from  Craney  Island,  as  it  did  when  I  was  up  with  a 
flag  ol  truce  in  May  last,  but  I  had  not  g’ot  more  than  three  or  four 
boat’s  lengths  from  the  tug  when  a  second  shot  was  tired  at  the  barge 
which  passed  directly  over  and  struck  about  30  yards  from  her. 

My  first  impulse  was  to  return  immediately  and  report  the  circum¬ 
stances  to  you,  but  my  second  led  me  to  remain  and  ascertain  if  possi¬ 
ble  if  the  flag  of  truce  had  been  fired  on  by  order  of  General  Huger 
or  the  commanding  officer  at  Craney  Island. 

Two  officers  came  off' in  a  boat  from  Craney  Island,  of  whom  I  asked 
the  name  of  the  commanding  officer  at  the  island  and  if  General 
Huger  was  still  at  Norfolk. 

The  senior  of  the  two  (1  did  not  learn  their  names)  replied,  “  Colonel 
Richardson  commands  at  Craney  Island,”  but  he  did  not  know  anything 
of  General  Huger. 

I  then  stated  that  I  was  the  bearer  of  a  flag  of  truce  to  General 
Huger,  but  before  I  could  transact  any  business  in  relation  to  it  I  must 
first  ascertain  from  them  if  General  Huger  or  the  commanding 
officer  had  ordered  the  flag  of  truce  to  be  fired  on.  If  so,  I  had  no 
further  communication  to  make,  but  should  return  and  report  the  facts 
to  you. 

I  he  senior  officer  then  stated  that  no  such  order  had  been  given* 
the  shot  striking  so  near  was  accidental;  he  knew  the  flag  of  truce  was 
coming  up;  had  reported  it  to  the  commanding  officer,  when  the  order 
was  given  to  fire  a  shot  to  stop  her. 

To  this  I  replied:  u  A.  blank  cartridge  would  have  been  all  that  was 
necessary  and  what  was  customary  to  stop  a  flag  of  truce.”  To  this 
he  said  something  about  not  knowing  what  was  customary. 

I  then  gave  him  your  letter  to  General  Huger,  saying  I  would  wait 
for  an  answer,  at  the  same  time  asking  him  to  give  my  compliments  to 
the  commanding  officer,  and  say  his  men  fired  well;  it  was  good  target 
practice. 

He  replied:  ‘‘The  circumstances  shall  be  reported  to  the  command¬ 
ing  officer.” 

I  also  stated  to  him  the  difference  in  the  reception  of  officers  coining 
with  flags  of  truce  to  us. 

The  officers  left  me  at  about  2:45  p.  m.  I  remained  until  6:45  p.  m., 
and  then  left  on  my  return  without  an  answer  from  General  Huger.

Report  of  Captain  Chauncey,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Susque¬ 
hanna,  regarding  the  temporary  disabling  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Susquehanna, 

At  Anchor  off  Lynn  Haven  Bay ,  July  6,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  in  obedience  to  instructions  from 
the  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy  of  12th  June  to  communicate  on 
my  way  down  the  coast  with  the  vessels  of  the  blockading  squadron, 
and  being  obliged  to  lie  by  for  six  hours  in  accordance  with  a  request 
from  the  chief  engineer  of  this  ship  to  effect  some  necessary  repairs  to 
the  engines,  and  while  on  my  way  up  to  the  anchorage  for  the  above 
purpose  the  starboard  water-wheel  shaft  suddenly  broke,  thus  disabling 
the  ship  for  active  and  efficient  service.  I  enclose  a  report  of  the  occur¬ 
rence  to  the  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  and  shall  await  further 
orders. 

I  am  informed  by  the  chief  engineer  of  this  ship  that  she  will  be  in 
readiness  by  8  a.  m.  to-morrow  to  proceed  to  New  York  with  one  wheel, 
if  deemed  expedient,  and  I  beg  leave  to  suggest  the  propriety  of  pro¬ 
ceeding  to  that  port  without  delay,  as  the  necessary  repairs  can  be 
effected  with  more  dispatch  at  that  place  than  elsewhere. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  S.  Chauncey, 

Captain. 

Flag-Officer  S.  H.  Stringiiam, 

Commanding  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads. 


[Enclosure.] 

N.  S.  S.  Susquehanna, 
jLt  Anchor  off  Lynn  Haven  Bay ,  July  6,  1861. 

Sir  :  After  closing  my  dispatch  of  this  morning,  and  while  proceed¬ 
ing  up  to  the  anchorage  to  communicate  with  the  flag-officer  and  with 
the  intention  of  proceeding  to  sea  this  evening,  in  accordance  with  your 
orders,  after  the  necessary  repairs  to  the  engine,  the  starboard  water¬ 
wheel  shaft  of  the  engine  broke  without  any  previous  warning,  thus 
entirely  disabling  the  ship  for  active  service.  The  result  of  a  critical 
examination  of  the  fracture  shows  an  imperfection  in  the  forging  of 
the  shaft  and  a  bad  flaw.  The  shaft  has  been  running  for  eleven  years, 
or  since  the  construction  of  the  ship,  and  has  been,  to  all  external 
appearance,  sound. 

Although  this  accident  is  a  severe  disappointment  to  me,  yet  I  con¬ 
sider  it  providential  that  it  has  occurred  at  this  particular  time  and 
place.  Had  it  taken  place  in  a  gale  of  wind  or  rough  weather,  it  might 
have  been  attended  with  more  serious  results  to  machinery,  etc. 

I  have  reported  the  facts  to  Flag-Officer  Stringiiam,  my  senior  officer, 
and  shall  await  further  orders.  I  am  informed  by  the  chief  engineer 
that  the  skip  will  be  in  readiness  by  8  a.  in.  to-morrow  to  proceed  to 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.

retary  of  the  Navy.  I  shall  suggest  to  Flag-Officer  Stringliam  the  pro¬ 
priety  of  proceeding  to  that  port  without  delay,  as  I  am  of  opinion  the 
necessary  repairs  can  be  effected  with  more  dispatch  at  that  place  than

A  drawing  of  the  engines  of  the  Susquehanna  is  in  the  Department

Report  of  Flap -Officer  Stringham,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Atlantic 

Blockading  Squadron,  regarding  disposition  of  vessels  of  his  command 

and  disrespect  shown  to  a  fag  of  truce. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  July  8,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  receipt  of  yonr  letter  of  July 
5,  with  reference  to  rates  asked  for  by  Commander  Carr,  and  the  affairs 
of  the  Quaker  City. 

Also  your  letter  of  July  apprising  me  of  the  dismissal  of  Assistant 
Engineer  Levy. 

I  have  ordered  Lieutenant  Mitchell  to  the  Santee,  and  have  ordered 
the  Santee  to  proceed  to  her  destination ;  also  the  Roanoke,  Flag-Officer 
Penclergrast,  to  proceed  off  the  coast  of  North  Carolina,  and  the  Cum¬ 
berland  to  go  to  Boston  to  be  docked,  making  just  a  short  cruise  down 
off  Hatteras. 

I  have  also  ordered  the  Daylight  off  Cape  Fear  and  the  Albatross 
off  Cape  Hatteras,  to  assist  in  blockading  the  North  Carolina  coast. 

In  compliance  with  your  instructions  contained  in  your  letter  of 
instructions  of  July  3,  with  reference  to  Miss  Segar,  I  wrote  to  Brig¬ 
adier-General  Benjamin  Huger,  on  the  5th  July,  enclosing  him  a  copy 
of  your  letter  in  regard  to  Miss  S.  This  I  had  an  opportunity  of  send¬ 
ing  direct  to  him  through  the  English  vice-consul,  Mr.  Myer  Myers, 
who  on  that  day  came  to  this  ship  under  protection  of  the  English  flag. 

On  the  Gth  I  ordered  Commander  A.  Ludlow  Case  to  proceed  with  a 
flag  of  truce  on  this  particular  business. 

By  the  kindness  of  Major-General  Butler  I  was  provided  with  a 
small  steamer,  and  Commander  Case  proceeded  on  his  mission  at 
1  p.  m. 

I  make  short  extracts  from  Commander  Case’s  report  to  me: 

After  having  passed  the  batteries  on  Sewell’s  Point  and  Bush’s  Point,  a  shot  was 
fired  at  the  tug  from  Craney  Island.  It  passed  diagonally  across  the  how  and  struck 
within  20  feet.  Had  not  the  engine  been  stopped  at  the  flash,  and  the  boat’s  head 
turned  a  little  to  starboard  the  shot  must,  I  think,  have  struck  her. 

Commander  Case  then  took  to  his  barge  and  was  proceeding  in  that 
toward  Craney  Island,  the  usual  place  where  flags  have  usually  com¬ 
municated,  but  u  had  not  got  more  than  three  or  four  boat’s  leugths 
from  the  tug  when  a  second  shot  was  fired  at  the  barge,  which  passed 
directly  over,  and  struck  about  30  yards  from  her.” 

Two  officers  came  off  in  a  boat,  and  to  the  question  of  Commander 
Case,  Who  commanded  at  Craney  Island,  received  answer,  “  Colonel 
Richardson,”  and  Whether  they  intended  to  fire  upon  a  flag  of  truce? 
the  senior  answered,  It  was  the  result  of  ignorance,  the  proximity  of 
the  firing  to  the  tug  and  barge.” 

The  commanding  officer  had  given  the  order  to  fire  the  shot  and 
stop  her. 

After  this  explanation  Commander  Case  forwarded  my  letter  to 
Brigadier-General  B.  Huger  through  this  officer,  which  stated  that  Com¬ 
mander  C.  would  receive  Miss  Segar. 

After  waiting  from  2:45  p.  m.  until  0:45,  and  receiving  no  answer  to 
his  communication,  Commander  Case  returned  and  reported  the  facts 
to  me. 

I  can  but  express  my  great  surprise  at  such  treatment,  considering 
the  courtesy  with  which  flags  of  truce  from  Norfolk  have  been  received 
by  me. 

I  feel  unwilling  to  hold  further  communication  (except  you  instruct

[Subenclosure. — Extract.] 

U.  S.  Consulate,  Liverpool,  June  7,  1861. 

Sir:  My  last  dispatch  w  as  31st  May,  by  the  Arabia. 

A  statement  was  made  to  me  on  Wednesday  by  a  shipmaster  belong¬ 
ing  to  Portsmouth,  N.  H.,  which  I  consider  of  consequence  enough  to 
report  to  you. 

He  stated  that  on  Monday  last  one  of  the  partners  of  a  large  ship¬ 
ping  house  here  remarked  during  a  conversation  on  the  reported  rais¬ 
ing  of  the  blockade  at  Charleston,  that  there  was  a  steamer  loading  in 
this  country  with  a  valuable  cargo  for  Charleston.  He  could  not  get 
from  him  where  she  was  loading,  or  her  name,  as  he  seemed  to  recollect 
himself  and  grew  uncommunicative,  and  the  captain  did  not  like  to 
appear  too  inquisitive.  The  captain  would  not  tell  me  the  name  of  the 
house,  but  from  what  he  did  say,  I  judge  it  was  that  of  Leech,  Harri¬ 
son  &  Torwood,  a  commission  house  doing  a  large  business  with  the 
United  States  and  with  numerous  Charleston  connections,  and,  on 
investigating  the  matter,  I  find  that  the  owner  of  the  Swedish  screw 
steamer  Ernest  Mercke,  which  came  here,  and  has  just  discharged  a 
cargo  from  New  Orleans,  has  been  in  frequent  communication  during 
the  past  ten  days  with  that  house,  and  that  the  chief  mate  of  the  ves¬ 
sel  has  been  heard  to  say  he  thought  she  would  go  back  to  America. 

I  am  inclined  to  think  the  statement  referred  to  her.  She  is  a  very 
fast  vessel,  having  made  the  passage  from  New  Orleans  in  twenty-two 
days,  steaming  but  a  small  part  of  the  way.  She  is  700  tons,  bark 
rigged,  funnel  red  at  bottom,  black  at  top,  hull  dark  green,  spar  deck 
white;  female  figurehead,  no  bowsprit.  She  has  no  cargo  on  board  yet, 
but  a  few  days  would  suffice  to  load  and  dispatch  her.  I  am  having 
her  looked  after. 

There  is  no  vessel  here,  or  in  any  of  the  ports  of  the  district,  loading, 
that  would  be  likely. 

Fraser,  Trenholm  &  Co.,  the  Liverpool  branch  of  John  Fraser  &  Co., 
of  Charleston,  have  bought  a  new  screw  steamer  for  the  “direct  trade,” 
but  she  is  not  named  or  ready  yet. 

^  ^  *  #  # 

With  high  respect,  1  am,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Henry  Wilding,  Vice-Consul. 

[Hon.  W.  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State.  ]

General  Report  of  Flag-Officer  Stringham ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads ,  July  9,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  the  Roanoke, 
Flag-Officer  Pendergrast,  sailed  yesterday  for  the  coast  of  Forth 
Carolina. 

The  Cumberland  sailed  to-day  for  Boston,  first  talcing  a  short  cruise 
down  off  Cape  Hatteras  and  the  coast  of  Forth  Carolina. 

I  am  informed  her  sailmaker  is  now  doing  duty  on  board  the  steam 
tug  Young  America,  at  present  repairing  at  Washington.  I  respect¬ 
fully  suggest,  and  enquire,  whether  it  would  not  be  well  to  let  him  pro¬ 
ceed  to  Boston  and  prepare  matters  in  his  department,  thus  hastening 
the  necessary  work  upon  the  Cumberland,  when  she  arrives. 

I  would  like  to  assign  an  officer  to  the  Young  America ,  Mr.  G.  W. 
Graves,  now  applying  for  the  appointment  of  acting  master,  for  which 
situation  I  know  him  to  be  fully  qualified.  lie  is  a  very  active  and 
efficient  officer,  having  served  on  board  this  ship  since  we  sailed  as 
master’s  mate. 

I  venture  I  o  ask  of  the  Department  to  send  the  Yankee  to  this  point. 

The  Army  have  constant  communication  from  Fortress  Monroe  to 
FewportFews  in  small  tug  steamers.  There  is  a  steamer  which  comes 
down  from  Forfollc  to  the  mouth  of  Elizabeth  Kiver  frequently.  I  fear, 
emboldened  by  the  absence  of  our  small  steamers,  she  may  attack  and 
capture  the  army  steamers.  The  Yankee ,  drawing  light  draft  of  water 
and  being  fast,  might  catch  this  vessel,  besides  doing  service  here  as 
she  did  before  her  removal  for  repairs. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  II.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer ,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy.

[Subenclosure.] 

Consulate  of  the  United  States  of  America, 

London,  June  22,  1861. 

Sir  :  I  have  just  learned  from  a  source  I  regard  as  reliable,  a  mer¬ 
cantile  gentleman  of  this  city,  that  a  new  screw  steamer,  of  1,000  tons 
net  burden,  built  by  Mr.  Peirce,  of  Stockton,  on  the  river  Tees,  for 
Messrs.  Walker  and  Cunard,  has  been  recently  sold  to  Fraser,  Tren- 
holm  &  Co,  of  Liverpool  and  Charleston,  S.  C. 

She  is  now,  as  my  authority  states,  taking  in  cargo  for  the  Southern 
States,  and  is  nearly  ready  for  sea. 

The  Tees  is  near  the  Scottish  border,  about  200  miles  from  London; 
but  I  shall  try  to  ascertain  her  name,  the  flag  under  which  she  will 
sail,  for  what  port  she  clears,  who  commands  her,  her  complement  of 
men,  a  description  of  her,  and  all  other  accessible  facts  concerning  her. 
I  have  this  moment  had  a  confirmation  of  the  above  statement  from  a 
gentleman  just  arrived  from  Birmingham  [England],  who  says  he  had 
a  hint  that  such  a  vessel  was  soon  to  leave  for  some  Southern  port,  and 
that  arms  were  to  be  sent  from  Birmingham  for  the  South  by  her. 
She  is  reported  as  bound  for  Charleston  direct,  but  this  is  hardly  prob¬ 
able;  she  may  [sail]  directly  for  Mexico  or  some  port  in  one  of  the  West 
India  Islands,  or  she  may  try  to  get  into  the  Satilla  River,  or  St.  Mary’s, 
Ga.,  Fernandina,  St.  John’s  River,  or  some  port  on  the  Atlantic  side  of 
Florida.  A  railroad  runs  to  Fernandina,  Fla.,  and  there  is  water 
enough  at  most  all  of  the  places  above  named  for  a  vessel  of  1,000  tons 
to  enter  with  safety. 

The  old  guns  I  reported  as  going  by  the  Golden  Fleece  to  Quebec,  and 
thence  south,  were  withdrawn  from  her  before  she  sailed  and  have  not 
yet  been  shipped.

IT.  S.  Brig  Perry, 

At  Sea,  July  9 ,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  Oth  of  June,  1861,  we 
boarded  and  warned  oft'  the  coast  the  English  bark  Sea  Queen ,  from 
Ascension,  bound  to  Charleston,  S.  C. 

On  the  9th  of  June  we  boarded  the  John  Barrow,  of  London,  from

Fernandina  and  set  the  blockade.  On  the  15th  of  June  we  boarded 
and  warned  oft'  the  coast  the  Spanish  brig  Juana  Teresa ,  from  Havana, 
in  ballast,  and  bound  for  St.  Mary’s  for  lumber.  On  the  18th  of  June 
boarded  and  warned  off  the  coast  the  English  brig  Polka,  from  Ber¬ 
muda,  bound  to  Doboy  for  lumber.  On  the  23d  of  June  boarded  the 
Russian  bark  Salmi ,  from  Fernandina,  bound  to  London  with  a  cargo 
of  steam  pitch  pine.  We  had  observed  her  at  anchor  inside  the  bar 
for  several  days.  She  reported  that  she  left  no  foreign  vessels  at  Fer¬ 
nandina  or  St.  Mary’s. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  G.  Parrott,

Report  of  Lieutenant  Parrott,  U.  8.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  8.  brig  Perry , 

regarding  the  condition  of  the  battery  of  that  vessel  and  of  the  rumored 

fitting  out  of  two  vessels  at  Savannah. 

U.  S.  Brig  Perry, 

At  Sea,  July  9, 1861. 

Sir  :  It  is  my  duty  to  report  that  on  the  occasion  of  the  firing  at  the 
Savannah ,  two  of  the  guns  of  this  vessel,  out  of  the  three  used,  had 
the  loops  of  their  pivot  bolts  broken.  These  loops  have  been  replaced 
by  others  from  the  ports  without  guns,  but  they  all  have  the  same 
defect — a  deep  gutter  for  oiling — and  it  was  at  this  place  they  were 
broken.  1  do  not  think  they  would  stand  continued  firing.  It  appears 
to  be  very  important  that  they  should  be  replaced  by  stronger  ones, 
and  it  would  be  a  short  job. 

The  guns  of  this  vessel  have  only  a  range  of  about  1  mile,  and  the 
lee  guns  can  generally  only  be  given  elevation  sufficient  to  make  their 
shot  reach  from  two-thirds  to  three-quarters  of  a  mile.  Any  vessel  she 
might  encounter  would,  I  suppose,  certainly  have  guns  of  much  greater 
range.  Even  the  Savannah ,  with  her  rifled  shot,  could  have  fired  at  us 
for  a  long  time  without  our  having  been  able  to  make  any  return.  One 
or  two  rifled  guns  would  improve  very  much  her  battery. 

The  condition  of  her  battery  as  described  above,  and  the  fact  of  her 
being  a  small  sailing  vessel,  makes  her,  I  think,  very  inefficient  for  the 
blockade,  without  the  assistance  of  a  steamer,  of  a  port  like  Fenian- 
dina,  which  is  within  six  hours  of  Savannah,  with  which  it  has  an 
inland  communication  of  12  feet  water.  Savannah  can  also  command 
the  military  resources  of  Charleston ;  she  has  a  large  number  of  steamers 
and  could  send  a  force  of  them  sufficient  for  the  purpose  against  this 
vessel  and  attack  her,  either  in  a  calm,  which  occurs  daily  and  gener¬ 
ally  lasts  a  great  part  of  the  day,  taking  positions  where  she  could  not 
bring  her  guns  to  bear  on  them,  or  by  keeping  out  of  the  short  range 
of  her  shot,  in  any  weather. 

The  captain  of  the  Russian  bark  Salmi ,  bound  out  from  Fernandina, 
informed  me  that  he  had  heard  at  that  place  that  two  steamers,  with 
100  men  each,  were  being  fitted  out  at  Savannah  for  the  purpose  of 
attacking  the  Perry.  This  report,  whether  true  or  not,  shows  the 
enemy  were  aware  of  their  opportunity  of  attacking  our  flag,  with  the 
chances  very  much  in  their  favor. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  G.  Parrott, 

Li eutenant ,  Comm anding. 

Senior  Flag-Officer  S.  H.  Stringham, 

Commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Captain  Mercer ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  8.  8.  Wabash- 
regarding  the  services  of  the  chartered  steamer  Union  off  Charles 
ton ,  8.  C. 

U.  S.  Steam  Frigate  Wabash, 

Off  Charleston ,  July  10,  1861. 

Sir  :  The  Union  is  still  here,  and  has  been  very  serviceable  to  me. 
Indeed,  I  do  not  know  how  I  should  get  along  without  her  or  some  other 
vessel  of  her  speed  and  class.  One  vessel  at  least,  a  Spaniard,  would 
have  gotten  into  this  place  in  spite  of  Lee  and  myself,  if  the  Union  had 
not  been  with  us.  In  your  communication  to  me  by  the  Union,  you  say 
nothing  to  me  about  her  return  to  Hampton  Roads  before  the  expira¬ 
tion  of  her  charter,  whereas  Goldsborougli  tells  me  you  informed  him 
that  she  would  not  be  rechartered.  Notwithstanding  this,  however,  I 
shall  detain  her  here  as  long  as  I  can  supply  her  with  coal  without  get¬ 
ting  too  low  myself,  or  until  some  other  small  steamer  shall  come  here 
to  relieve  her.  Under  the  guns  of  this  ship  she  does  not  consume  more 
than  a  ton  a  day,  and  does  not  use  more  than  Sartori  did  in  the  Flag 
when  steaming.  On  the  arrival  of  the  Union  here  she  had  on  board 
about  GO  tons.  I  have  supplied  her  with  15  tons  of  coal  since,  and  she 
now  has  about  GO  tons  on  board. 

I  have  Master’s  Mate  Cushing  on  board  here,  who  is  ordered  to  the 
Minnesota,  whom  I  would  send  to  you  by  the  Perry,  but  I  know  these 
small  vessels  have  no  room  to  spare,  and  I  shall  hold  on  to  him  for  a 
better  opportunity.  This  ship  can  remain  here  two  weeks  longer,  when 
her  coal  will  be  getting  rather  low. 

I  hope  the  Government  will  send  us  a  couple  of  small  steamers  to 
this  point. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  respectfully,  yours, 

8am l.  Mercer,  Captain. 

Flag-Officer  Silas  H.  Stringham, 

Commanding  U.  8.  Blockading  Squadron,  Atlantic  Coast.

[Enclosure.] 

St.  John,  New  Brunswick,  July  3 , 1861 

My  Bear  Sir:  There  is  in  this  port  a  vessel  of  some  700  tons,  the  Alli¬ 
ance^  which  is,  I  have  every  reason  to  suspect,  a  Southern  pirate. 

The  stern  has  the  arms  of  South  Carolina  blacked  over;  her  hull  is 
rather  old,  but  her  sjpars,  running  and  standing  rigging,  new  and  taut. 
Her  master  is  a  red-hot  secessionist,  and  on  Sunday  week  last  hoisted 
the  Palmetto  flag,  which  created  no  little  excitement  among  the  Ameri¬ 
can  ships,  they  all  hauling  down  their  national  flags. 

She  cleared  from  Liverpool  for  Charleston,  loaded  (so  said)  with  rail¬ 
road  iron.  She  was  overhauled  while  endeavoring  to  run  the  blockade 
and  ordered  off. 

She  then  went  into  New  York,  where  suspicion  was  excited  as  to  the 
contents  of  her  hold,  and  she  at  once  left  for  this  port  and  arrived  here 
some  two  weeks  since. 

She  has  a  British  register  and  is  reported  to  be  owned  in  Liverpool, 
New  York,  and  Charleston. 

Her  agents  here  are  very  much  opposed  to  the  North. 

I  have  endeavored  to  board  her,  but  was  not  permitted  to  do  so ;  no 
one  has  permission  to  see  her  hold,  and  there  are  other  circumstances 
[which]  warrant  me  in  my  conclusions. 

I  thought  it  proper  to  write  to  you  on  the  subject,  as  being  the  only 
person  in  Washington  with  whom  I  have  any  acquaintance.  If  you 
think  it  worth  the  while,  you  may  hand  this  note  to  the  proper  officers. 
Any  further  information  as  to  her  movements  which  I  can  transmit, 
either  by  letter  or  telegraph,  I  will  be  happy  to  give,  if  desired,  as  I 
love  my  country,  and  would  like  to  know  that  this  vessel,  which  I 
believe  is  loaded  with  cannon  and  munitions  of  war,  was  captured. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  C.  Peterson. 

Hon.  H.  Hamlin, 

Washington.

U.  S.  Consulate, 
Liverpool ,  June  21,  1861. 

Sir  :  *  *  *  Shipments  of  arms  by  the  screw  steamers  for  New 
lork  continue,  hut  I  do  not  hear  of  any  to  other  ports  of  the  United 
States  or  ports  adjacent,  except  Vera  Cruz,  in  Mexico;  Ceara,  in  Brazil, 
and  Halifax,  Nova  Scotia. 

The  English  ship  John  Parkinson  sailed  a  few  days  since  for  Vera 
Cruz  with  several  packages  containing  arms,  but  entered  as  hardware; 
and  another  vessel,  loading  for  the  same  place,  is  taking  several  simi¬ 
lar  packages.  The  English  bark  Ariel ,  which  cleared  17th  June  for 
Ceara,  had  on  board  the  following  contraband  articles:  Ten  cases,  12 
quarter  boxes,  and  300  quarter  barrels  gunpowder;  26  hundredweight 
shot  lead;  76  cases  lead  shot;  3  casks,  12  barrels  saltpeter;  3  casks,  1 
barrel  sulphur,  besides  167  packages  entered  as  hardware  and  63  hun¬ 
dredweight  castings.  She  has  a  black  hull  and  white  ports. 

The  Thomas  Killam ,  for  Halifax  yesterday,  had  13  cases  of  firearms. 
*  *  #  &  *  * 

There  are  here  several  vessels  belonging  to  New  Orleans.  I  have 
been  told  that  the  captains  are  instructed  by  their  owners  to  return  to 
New  Orleans.  One,  the  Picayune ,  was  entered  yesterday  to  load  for 
there.  I  shall  refuse  to  certify  her  clearance,  but,  as  the  law  stands,  I 
do  not  think  I  can  refuse  to  return  her  register.  As  there  will  likely 
be  time  for  you  to  reply  before  she  clears,  I  shall  be  glad  if  you  will 
have  me  advised  on  the  subject. 

***-*### 


With  high  respect,  T  am,  your  obedient  servant, 
[Hon.  W.  H.  Seward,  Secretary  of  State.] 


H.  Wilding.

guin,  of  the  cruise  of  that  vessel  from  July  8  to  11,  1861. 

IT.  S.  S.  Penguin, 
Hampton  Roads,  July  11, 1861. 

Sir:  In  pursuance  of  your  verbal  orders  of  the  8th  instant,  I  got 
underway  at  11  o’clock,  a.  m.  of  same  date,  communicated  with  Com¬ 
mander  Chandler  in  the  mouth  of  York  River,  delivered  bis  letter  and 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


785 


your  instructions.  The  Dawn’s  position  was  so  close  as  to  effectually 
close  the  mouth  of  the  river  and  the  approach  by  MobjackBay,  proceeded 
on  to  the  Rappahannock  and  arrived  there  at  10  p.  m.,  delivered  the  pilot, 
letter,  and  your  message  to  the  commander  of  the  Mount  Vernon.  He 
had  nothing  to  communicate  of  any  importance;  had  seen  no  vessels 
nor  learned  any  news.  I  anchored  for  the  night,  and  in  the  morning 
at  3  a.  m.  got  underway;  could  then  distinctly  hear  the  drums  of  the 
enemy  on  shore;  from  our  pilot’s  representations  the  Patuxent  is  a  ren¬ 
dezvous  for  law  breakers.  I  was  induced  to  visit  it.  Iran  into  the 
mouth  of  the  river  at  4  p.  m.  of  the  9tli  instant  (having  boarded  and 
spoken  all  vessels  on  my  way).  At  5  p.  m.  a  steamer  hove  in  sight  and 
boarded  some  vessels  outside.  Her  movement  being  unusual,  I  ran  for 
her,  brought  her  to,  and  sent  a  boat  with  Lieutenant  Budd  to  make 
enquiries.  1  found  her  to  be  the  steamer  Chester ,  of  and  from  Balti¬ 
more,  with  a  detachment  of  40  Massachusetts  and  40  Pennsylvania 
armed  troops,  with  a  brass  artillery  piece  on  board,  all  under  charge  of 
a  provost-marshal,  of  Baltimore,  who  had  been  dispatched  here  by  Gen¬ 
eral  Banks  to  search  for  the  schooner  Georgiana  that  was  reported  to 
have  left  Baltimore  with  40  armed  secessionists  or  pirates,  who  were  to 
go  to  the  Patuxent,  and  there  await  the  arrival  of  the  Mary  Washington , 
which  was  to  bring  them  two  heavy  guns.  And  further,  that  General 
Banks  had  prohibited  the  sailing  of  all  vessels  from  Baltimore  on  that 
day,  until  meridian,  the  Mary  Washington  included. 

The  Georgiana  was  described  as  a  large,  high-decked  schooner,  green 
bottom,  red  stripe;  there  is  also  a  small  vessel  of  that  name  in  the 
Chesapeake. 

Discovering  a  schooner  in  the  offing,  I  chased  her  20  miles  and  found 
her  to  be  a  Staten  Island  vessel,  bound  to  New  York.  On  my  return 
to  the  river  the  Chester  had  gone  to  Baltimore. 

I  was  engaged  until  after  dark  overhauling  vessels  in  the  Chesapeake. 
I  then  anchored  in  the  mouth  of  the  Patuxent.  Before  anchoring  I 
brought  to  the  steamer  George  Weems,  from  Baltimore,  bound  up  the 
Patuxent  with  passengers.  I  boarded  him  and  questioned  him  closely, 
as  he  is  owned  by  the  same  owner  as  the  Mary  Washington.  His  report 
agreed  with  that  of  the  Chester,  adding  that  General  Banks  had  allowed 
him  to  leave  at  10  a.  m.  in  accommodation  to  his  passengers. 

At  early  dawn  I  weighed  and  stood  a  short  distance  up  the  river, 
examining  vessels,  and  sent  a  boat  ashore  for  news.  Obtained  nothing 
satisfactory,  except  that  a  pirate  was  thought  to  be  about  somewhere. 

At  0  a.  m.  discovered  two  steamers  standing  in;  weighed  and  stood 
for  them;  they  proved  to  be  the  U.  S.  steamers  Freeborn,  Lieutenant 
Commanding  Lowry,  and  the  Resolute.  The  former  came  on  board  and 
gave  me  the  following  intelligence:  He  had  been  dispatched  by  Com¬ 
mander  Rowan,  of  the  Pawnee,  to  look  after  a  suspected  piratical  party 
in  a  small  vessel  which  intended  to  capture  the  George  Weems.  This 
suspicion  was  founded  on  the  following:  Lieutenant  Commanding 
Lowry  had  visited  Point  Lookout,  and  was  informed  by  the  woman 
who  keeps  the  light  at  that  place  that  on  Sunday  last  a  small  vessel, 
called  a  pungy,  landed  there  the  crew  of  the  vessel  lately  captured  by 
the  St.  Nicholas,  and  that  one  of  the  party  she  recognized  as  Thomas 
by  a  scar  on  his  face.  This  so-called  Captain  Thomas  has  since  been 
taken  in  Baltimore  and  is  now  a  prisoner  in  Fort  McHenry.  She  also 
stated  that  from  the  conversation  she  overheard  she  inferred  that  they 
had  some  plan  to  intercept  and  capture  the  steamer  George  Weems. 
Upon  this  information  Captain  Rowan  had  dispatched  the  Freeborn  and

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Flag-Officer  Stringiiam ,  O.  S. 
Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  requesting  an  expres¬ 
sion  of  opinion  regarding  the  blocking  of  harbor  channels  with  stone. 

Navy  Department,  July  11,  1861. 
Sir  :  It  is  proposed  by  this  Department  to  sink  vessels  in  all,  or  nearly 
all,  the  channels  opening  into  the  harbors  within  the  jurisdiction  of  your 
command,  commencing  at  the  first  inlet  south  of  the  Chesapeake,  unless 
that  one  shall  be  left  open  for  light-draft  vessels  to  get  into  Albemarle 
Sound  and  cut  oft  that  very  important  line  of  communication.  A  board 
of  distinguished  persons  are  now  investigating  this  subject,  and  their 
report  will  be  forwarded  to  you.  Should  the  work  go  forward,  the 
Department  will  buy  vessels  loaded  with  stone,  to  be  delivered  to  you 
at  Hampton  Boads,  with  such  steamers  to  assist  as  may  be  necessary. 
Your  views  with  regard  to  this  subject,  particularly  the  latter  part,  are 
invited  before  the  contracts  are  completed. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles. 

Flag-Officer  S.  H.  Stringham, 

Comdg.  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads ,  Virginia.

U.  S.  S.  Mount  Vernon, 
Rappahannock,  July  13,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  all  quiet  at  this  place;  no  vessels  have 
attempted  to  pass  in  or  out  since  our  arrival  off  the  entrance  of  the 
river. 


788 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Yesterday  I  ran  up  tlie  river  20  miles,  opposite  tlxe  'town  of  Urban  a, 
to  see  if  there  were  any  vessels  lurking  around  any  of  the  bends  in  the 
river,  and  also  to  see  if  they  were  erecting  any  batteries  on  the  banks 
of  the  river.  To  all  appearances  everything  seems  to  be  deserted; 
nothing  was  to  be  seen  on  the  river,  save  now  and  then  a  fishing  canoe, 
with  one  colored  man  in  [it],  who  immediately  on  our  approach  retreated 
into  shoal  water.  There  are  no  batteries  or  men  on  either  bank  of  the 
river  as  far  up  as  Urbana. 

The  wheat  crop  is  cut  and  stacked  in  the  fields,  and,  judging  from 
the  number  of  stacks,  I  should  pronounce  the  crop  to  have  been  very 
large.  The  corn  crop  looks  well,  and  we  saw  a  large  number  of  cattle 
grazing  on  the  banks  of  the  river.  Everything  looked  so  peaceful  that 
it  was  difficult  to  imagine  that  we  are  at  war  with  the  people  of  Vir¬ 
ginia.  The  health  of  the  officers  and  crew  is  good. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

O.  S.  Glisson, 
Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Flag-Officer  Silas  H.  Stringham, 

Commanding  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  etc.

[Subenclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Monticello, 

Above  Newport  News,  July  10,  1861. 

Sir  :  As  the  charter  of  this  vessel,  I  understand,  expires  in  a  few  days, 
I  [feel  it]  my  duty  to  call  your  attention  to  the  fact  that  this  vessel  is 
not  coppered,  and  I  learn  that  she  has  not  been  docked  for  over  twenty- 
one  months.  She  has  now  been  nearly  three  months  in  the  waters  of 
Hampton  Roads,  and  I  think  will  [suffer]  serious  injury  should  she  not 
be  coppered  or  receive  a  coat  of  metallic  paint  immediately.  Owing  to 
the  active  part  this  vessel  has  taken  in  cruising,  the  almost  con¬ 
stant  use  of  her  guns  has  injured  the  pivot  carriage  to  that  extent  that 
should  it  be  required  for  rapid  firing  I  think  it  would  soon  be  useless. 
The  10-inch  gun  is  of  the  old  pattern,  defective  in  range,  and  the 
32-pounders  of  43  hundredweight  mounted  aft  are  upon  old  carriages 
that  should  be  replaced  by  new,  or  thoroughly  repaired.  The  deck 
which  was  laid  aft  is  in  a  very  leaky  condition,  and  already  a  quantity 
of  provisions  have  been  condemned  owing  to  that  fact. 

As  to  the  seagoing  qualities  of  this  vessel  with  her  present  battery, 
she  is  not  safe,  being  in  an  ordinary  sea  very  wet,  and  her  battery 
could  not  be  served  with  accuracy,  owning  to  her  rolling  badly.  In 
smooth  water  she  will  answer  as  a  cruiser. 

I  would  suggest  that  the  pivot  gun  be  replaced  by  a  rifled  cannon 
40-pounder  or  less,  which  will  materially  increase  her  efficiency  and 
reduce  the  weight  forward;  that  her  deck  aft  be  immediately  calked, 


790 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


that  slie  he  coppered  or  receive  a  coat  of  metallic  paint.  She  lias  been 
several  times  ashore  and  in  backing  so  much  has  heated  journals. 
Working  sand  through  her  injections,  has  cut  the  lining  of  the  air 
pump.  The  boiler  leaks  and  the  soft  patches  want  renewing.  She 
requires  new  metal  in  crank-pin  brasses,  a  set  of  new  valves,  and  a 
bucket  to  the  air  pump.  The  vessel  leaks  GO  inches  in  twenty-four 
hours  and  on  that  account  needs  docking.  The  sleeves  of  her  blow 
pipe  leak  badly. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

D.  L.  Braine, 

Lieutenant ,  U.  S.  Navy.
