Report  of  Flag-Officer  Stringham ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  commanding  Atlantic 

Blockading  Squadron,  of  assistance  rendered  to  the  American  hark 

Young  Greek ,  ashore  on  Wolf  Trap  Shoal. 

U.  S.  S.  Minnesota, 
Hampton  Roads,  July  13,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  on  Thursday, 
July  11,  news  reached  me  that  a  vessel  was  ashore  on  the  Wolf  Trap, 
a  very  dangerous  place  in  Chesapeake  Bay  south  of  the  Rappahannock 
River,  and  close  to  the  Virginia  shore. 

I  immediately  ordered  Acting  Master  Josiah  Snow,  our  coast  pilot, 
to  take  one  of  our  boats  and  14  men  and  proceed  to  the  Massachusetts 
steamer  Cambridge ,  Captain  S.  H.  Mathews,  and  ask  him  if  he  was 
willing  to  go  up  the  bay,  as  I  had  no  vessel  at  my  command  to  dispatch 
to  see  if  anything  could  be  done.  He  promptly  consented  to  go. 

This  morning  they  have  returned  and  report  that  they  found  the 
American  bark  Young  Greek,  from  near  Caldera,  Chile,  South  America, 
loaded  with  copper  ore,  a  very  valuable  cargo.  She  was  proceeding  to 
her  port  of  destination  (Baltimore),  in  charge  of  a  pilot,  when,  owing 
to  the  absence  of  lights,  and  especially  the  light-boat  heretofore  sta¬ 
tioned  on  the  Wolf  Trap  and  removed  by  the  traitors,  this  vessel  ran 
aground. 

After  incessant  labor  night  and  day  in  removing  cargo  (and  princi¬ 
pally  by  the  power  of  the  Cambridge  in  towing)  from  Thursday  after¬ 
noon  until  Saturday  morning  about  2  a.  m.,  the  Young  Greek  was  suc¬ 
cessfully  extricated  from  her  dangerous  position,  and  this  morning  at 
early  dawn  she  sailed  for  Baltimore. 

On  the  lltli  instant,  at  11  a.  m.,  the  U.  S.  S.  Fenguin,  J.  W.  Livingston, 
returning  from  a  cruise  up  the  bay,  saw  the  bark  above  mentioned  and 
endeavored  to  get  her  off.  After  trying  and  not  succeeding,  he  brought 
the  captain  down  to  this  place,  and  returned  again  with  the  captain  on 
the  12tli  and  again  came  down  this  morning.  I  have  ordered  the  Pen¬ 
guin  to  cruise  off  the  capes  of  the  Chesapeake  to  supply  the  temporary 
absence  for  a  day  or  so  at  this  point  of  the  Quaker  City ,  which  has 
slight  repairs  to  make  in  her  machinery.  The  frigate  Savannah  is  in 
sight,  coming  in. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  H.  Stringham, 

Flag-Officer,  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy.

Report  of  Captain  Purviance ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  ship  St. 

Lawrence ,  regarding  the  need  of  efficient  officers  for  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  Ship  St.  Lawrence, 
Hampton  Roads ,  Virginia ,  July  15,  1861. 

Sir:  Yours  of  the  10th  instant,  in  answer  to  mine  of  8th  instant,  is 
duly  to  hand. 

In  reporting  the  inefficiency  of  the  ship  St.  Lawrence  at  this  stage  of 
the  cruise,  I  did  not  intend  my  letter  to  convey  a  complaint  against  the 
Department,  for  I  am  perfectly  aware  that  the  deficiency  in  lieutenants 
is,  as  you  say,  owing  to  the  exigencies  of  the  service.  I  am  also  aware 
of  the  trouble  experienced  as  to  acting  masters,  who  “are  selected 
with  great  care  from  the  merchant  service,”  but  I  most  respectfully  beg 
to  differ;  the  Department  has  been  most  shamefully  imposed  upon  by 
applicants  from  the  merchant  service. 

The  Department  remarks,  “whether  the  ship  will  prove  efficient  or 
not  will  depend  very  much  on  her  commanding  officer.” 

The  Department  is  very  right,  but  experience  has  long  since  proven 
to  me  that  without  efficient  under-officers  it  is  simply  impossible  to 
render  the  ship  efficient.  The  Department  may  have  a  very  efficient 
head,  but  without  competent  assistants,  I  ask,  what  would  it  be? 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  Y.  Purviance,  Captain. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy ,  Washington ,  L).  C.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Pendergrast,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  West  India 
Squadron,  regarding  the  cruise  of  the  flagship  Roanoke  from  Hampton 
Roads  to  Charleston,  S.  G.,  and  exchange  of  shots  with  Confederate 
battery  at  Hatteras  Inlet ,  N.  C.,  July  10,  1861. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Roanoke, 

Off  Charleston,  S.  C.,  July  14,  1861. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report  of  the  passage 
of  the  Roanoke  from  Hampton  Roads  to  this  place,  with  such  incidents 
as  I  have  deemed  important: 


792 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Monday <,  July  8. — At  8:30  p.  m.  fired  a  sliell  ahead  df  a  bark  and  bove 
her  to;  Lieutenant  Scott  boarded  her;  she  proved  to  be  the  American 
bark  Young  Greek ,  from  Chile,  bound  to  Baltimore. 

Tuesday ,  July  9. — At  S :  45  a  .in.  made  Bodie’s  light  house  on  starboard 
bow;  discovered  an  encampment  a  few  miles  north  of  Bodie’s  Island 
light. 

In  the  afternoon,  Wednesday,  July  10,  made  Hatteras  Inlet  and  ran 
in  toward  it;  discovered  a  battery  and  a  number  of  wooden  houses  on 
the  beach,  and  several  small  vessels  (among  which  were  two  light- 
boats)  at  anchor  inside.  Upon  nearing  the  beach,  and  when  about  2^ 
miles  from  the  battery,  it  opened  fire  upon  us,  all  of  their  shots  falling 
short.  The  colors  were  hoisted  and  we  immediately  returned  the  fire 
with  three  rounds  of  shell  from  forward  pivot  gun,  and  two  from  after 
pivot  gun,  and  five  rounds  from  rifle  howitzers;  apparently  ti\o  shots 
from  rifled  cannon  took  effect. 

Friday ,  July  12. — At  9:45  came  to  anchor  in  the  mouth  of  Cape  Fear 
River  in  7  fathoms  of  water.  Found  the  rebel  flag  flying  on  Fort  Cas¬ 
well  and  in  the  town  of  Smithville;  also  a  red  flag  flying  on  Bald  Head 
liglit-house.  Discovered  a  rebel  battery  to  the  southward  of  the  tort 
and  a  number  of  men  drilling  on  the  beach;  could  count  fourteen  guns 
(barbette)  on  Fort  Caswell  and  several  fleldpieces. 

Saturday,  July  13. — Got  underway  in  the  morning.  When  abreast 
of  Lockwood’s  [Folly]  Inlet,  and  10  miles  from  Smithville,  fell  in  with  a 
schooner.  She  proved  to  be  the  schooner  Mary,  of  Washington,  N.  C. ; 
sand  ballast,  no  cargo;  destination  unknown;  she  had  evidently  been 
abandoned  by  her  crew  upon  sighting  the  Roanoke. 

We  secured  such  papers  as  could  be  found,  took  from  her  the  foresail, 
jib  and  flying  jib,  blocks,  2  compasses,  spyglass,  lead  line,  cooking 
utensils,  and  a  few  other  articles;  scuttled  her  and  set  fire  to  her. 

Sunday,  July  14. — At  10:30  came  to  anchor  under  sail  off  Charleston 
Bar,  and  found  the  Wabash,  Vandalia ,  and  Union  here. 

Very  respectfully,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  J.  Pendergrast, 

Flag-  Officer ,  Commanding  West  India  Squadron. 

Flag-Officer  Silas  H.  Stringham, 

Comdg.  U.  S.  Blockading  Squadron,  Hampton  Roads,  Virginia.

Report  of  Flag-Officer  Pender grast,  U.  8.  Navy ,  commanding  West  India 

Squadron,  urging  the  necessity  of  small  steamers  on  the  coast  of  North 

Carolina. 

IT.  S.  Flagship  Eoanoke, 

Off  Charleston,  8.  C.,  July  15,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  it  is  very  necessary  that 
two  or  three  more  small  steamers  should  be  stationed  along  the  coast 
of  North  Carolina.  It  being  necessary  to  send  the  Union  to  Hampton 
Roads  it  leaves  but  one  small  vessel  here. 

I  have  not  as  yet  learned  of  the  arrival  of  the  Daylight  and  Albatross 
on  the  coast. 

I  may  visit  Savannah,  Ga.,  before  returning  North. 

I  regret  to  inform  you  that  thus  far  the  engines  of  the  ship  have  not 
worked  satisfactorily,  and  I  feel  some  anxiety  about  it. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  J.  Pendergrast,

this  place  to-day  and  reports  having  been  captured  by  a  privateer  in

dad,  his  vessel  was  captured  on  the  6th  instant  by  the  privateer  brig 
Jefferson  Davis  (of  Charleston,  S.  C.),  formerly  the  slave  brig  Echo. 
She  was  about  ten  days  out  of  port,  and  up  to  that  time  had  made  no 
captures.  She  was  then  about  the  latitude  of  Hatteras,  but  outside  the 
Gulf  Stream.  The  next  day  the  schooner  J.  G.  Warner  f  S.  J.  Waring ?], 
Captain  Smith,  bound  to  Montevideo,  was  captured,  and  ou  the  8th  the 
schooner  Enchantress ,  of  Newburyport,  from  Boston  for  Santiago,  shared 
the  same  fate.  On  the  9th  the  ship  Mary  Goodell ,  of  New  York,  for 
Buenos  Ayres,  was  seized,  water  and  provisions  were  taken  from  her, 
and  five  of  her  crew  voluntarily  joined  the  privateer.  She  was  then 
released  and  proceeded  on  her  voyage.  Upon  the  same  day  the  brig 
Mary  E.  Thompson ,  of  Searsport,  Captain  Havener,  from  Bangor  for 
Antigua,  was  seized.  Four  prisoners,  among  them  my  informant  White, 
were  placed  on  board,  and  she  also  was  released.  I  am  further  informed 
that  the  privateer  was  armed  with  four  light  carronades  and  one  old 
long  32-pounder  on  a  pivot  amidships;  that  she  carried  about  sixty-live 
men,  of  whom  very  few  were  sailors;  that  the  captain  appeared  to  be 
a  Dutchman,  and  that  the  chief  officer  was  named  Posted,  and  said  that 
he  had  formerly  been  in  the  Navy.  My  informant,  White,  listened 
carefully  to  the  conversation  around  him,  and  is  of  opinion  that  the 
privateer’s  officers  intended  to  sail  to  the  southward  and,  after  cruising 
near  the  Bahamas,  to  go  into  port  somewhere  on  the  coast  of  Florida. 
Prize  crews  were  put  on  board  the  brig  John  Welsh  and  the  schooners 
J.  C.  Warner  [/S'.  J.  Waring f]  and  Enchantress ,  and  they  stood  to  the 
southward.  The  port  of  Beaufort  was  mentioned  in  this  connection. 

The  Jefferson  Davis  was  a  full-rigged  brig,  with  black  mastheads  and 
yards  and  a  black  hull.  She  was  very  rusty,  and  her  pivot  gun  was 
visible  above  the  rail. 

1  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  R.  P.  Rodgers, 
Commandant  of  Midshipmen. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

rienced  captain,  one  well  acquainted  with  the  channels,  should  be  dispatched  at 
once  and  lie  as  near  the  bar  as  possible  every  night,  by  which  means  these  privateers 
and  schooners  can  all  be  captured  on  their  return. 

This  information  is  direct  from  a  person  who  was  in  Charleston 
Tuesday,  thi  9th  instant.

the  arrival  of  that  vessel  in  Hampton  Roads. 

U.  S.  Ship  Savannah, 
Hampton  Roads,  July  15,  1861. 

^  Sir  :  I  liave  the  honor  to  report  the  arrival  of  this  ship  at  Hampton 
Roads,  four  days  from  Hew  York,  in  obedience  to  an  order  of  the  Navy 
Department,  a  copy  of  which  is  herewith  enclosed,  together  with  a  list

I  have  on  board,  as  passengers,  Captain  Josiah  Watson  and  17 
marines  for  the  Niagara ;  Mr.  Patterson,  acting  master,  and  8  men 
belonging  to  the  Minnesota,  and  4  men  belonging  to  the  Freeborn ;  also

stores  for  the  vessels  of  the  squadron. 

I  beg  to  state  that  this  ship  is  short  of  her  complement  28  ordinary 
seamen,  1  gunner’s  mate,  and  1  armorer. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  B.  Hull,  Captain.

CONFEDERATE  REFORTS  ART)  CORRESPONDENCE. 

Proclamation  by  the  President  of  the  Confederate  States  of  America ,, 
regarding  letters  of  marque ,  April  17,  1861. 

Whereas  Abraham  Lincoln,  the  President  of  the  United  States,  has 
by  proclamation  announced  the  intention  of  invading  this  Confederacy 
with  an  armed  force  for  the  purpose  of  capturing  its  fortresses  and 
thereby  subverting  its  independence  and  subjecting  the  free  people 
thereof  to  the  dominion  of  a  foreign  power;  and 

Whereas  it  has  thus  become  the  duty  of  this  Government  to  repel 
the  threatened  invasion  and  to  defend  the  rights  and  liberties  of  the 
people  by  all  the  means  which  the  laws  of  nations  and  the  usages  of 
civilized  warfare  place  at  its  disposal: 

Now,  therefore,  I,  Jefferson  Davis,  President  of  the  Confederate 
States  of  America,  do  issue  this  my  proclamation  inviting  all  those 
who  may  desire,  by  service  in  private  armed  vessels  on  the  high  seas, 
to  aid  this  Government  in  resisting  so  wanton  and  wicked  an  aggres¬ 
sion,  to  make  application  for  commissions  or  letters  of  marque  and 
reprisal  to  be  issued  under  the  seal  of  the  Confederate  States. 

And  I  do  further  notify  all  persons  applying  for  letters  of  marque  to 
make  a  statement  in  writing  giving  the  name  and  a  suitable  description 
of  the  character,' tonnage,  and  force  of  the  vessel,  and  the  name  and 
place  of  residence  of  each  owner  concerned  therein  and  the  intended 
number  of  the  crew,  and  to  sign  said  statement  and  deliver  the  same  to 
the  Secretary  of  State,  or  to  the  collector  of  any  port  of  entry  of  these 
Confederate  States,  to  be  by  him  transmitted  to  the  Secretary  of  State. 

And  I  do  further  notify  all  applicants  aforesaid  that  before  any 
commission  or  letter  of  marque  is  issued  to  any  vessel  the  owner  or 
owners  thereof  and  the  commander  for  the  time  being  will  be  required 
to  give  bond  to  the  Confederate  States  with  at  least  two  responsible 
sureties  not  interested  in  such  vessel  in  the  penal  sum  of  $5,000;  or  if 
such  vessel  be  provided  with  more  than  150  men,  then  in  the  penal 
sum  of  $10,000,  with  condition  that  the  owners,  officers,  and  crew  who 
shall  be  employed  on  board  such  commissioned  vessel  shall  observe  the 
laws  of  these  Confederate  States  and  the  instructions  given  to  them 
for  the  regulation  of  their  conduct;  that  they  shall  satisfy  all  damages 
done  contrary  to  the  tenor  thereof  by  such  vessel  during  her  commis¬ 
sion,  and  deliver  up  the  same  when  revoked  by  the  President  of  the 
Confederate  States. 

And  1  do  further  specially  enjoin  on  all  persons  holding  offices,  civil 
and  military,  under  the  authority  of  the  Confederate  States  that  they 
be  vigilant  and  zealous  in  discharging  the  duties  incident  thereto. 

And  I  do  moreover  solemnly  exhort  the  good  people  of  these  Confed 
erate  States,  as  they  love  their  country,  as  they  prize  the  blessings  of 
free  government,  as  they  feel  the  wrongs  of  the  past  and  those  now 
threatened  in  aggravated  form,  by  those  whose  enmity  is  the  more  impla¬ 
cable  because  unprovoked,  that  they  exert  themselves  in  preserving- 
order,  in  promoting  concord,  in  maintaining  the  authority  and  efficacy 
of  the  laws,  and  in  supporting  and  invigorating  all  the  measures  which 
may  be  adopted  for  the  common  defense,  and  by  which,  under  the 
blessing  of  Divine  Providence,  we  may  hope  for  a  speedy,  just,  and 
honorable  peace.

Instructions  of  commandant  navy  yard,  Norfolk,  to  Captain  Hunter  Vir¬ 
ginia  navy,  regarding  transportation  for  persons  desiring  to  go  North. 


Navy  Yard,  Gosport  [Norfolk],  May  20, 1861. 

Sir  :  A  request  having  been  made  by  the  commanding  naval  officer 
near  Fortress  Monroe  under  a  flag  of  truce  on  Saturday  last  for  the 
safe  conduct  to  that  fleet  of  certain  families  supposed  here  and  detained 
against  their  wishes,  you  will  proceed  this  day  at  noon  in  the  steamer 
Empire,  under  a  flag  of  truce,  to  the  flagship  of  the  fleet  of  the  late 
United  States  off  that  point,  and  deliver  to  the  commanding  naval  offi¬ 
cer  such  women  and  children  or  other  persons  as  may  have  presented 
themselves  for  a  passage  to  return  to  their  Northern  friends. 

On  your  arrival,  you  will  say  to  the  commanding  officer  that  a  notice 
was  placed  in  the  city  papers,  informing  all  who  wished  to  go  North  to 
report  on  Monday  for  a  passage;  and  further  inform  him  that  the  com¬ 
manding  general  and  myself  will  most  cheerfully  give  every  facility  to 
any  one  to  rejoin  their  friends  who  may  elect  to  leave  the  State. 

Respectfully,  etc., 


F.  Forrest. 


Captain  Thos.  T.  Hunter, 

Virginia  Navy.

Repot  t  of  Captain  Barron,  1  irginia  navy,  to  the  governor  of  Virginia, 
regarding  naval  defenses  of  the  rivers  of  Virginia. 

Office  of  Naval  Detail  and  Equipment, 

Richmond,  June  10,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  your  Excellency  that  the  important 
duty  of  the  naval  defenses  of  the  rivers  of  Virginia  was  assigned  to 
the  officers  of  the  Virginia  navy  on  the  23d  of  April  last. 

A  few  days  previous  the  magazine  at  Norfolk,  with  upward  of  300,000 
pounds  of  powder  and  a  large  number  of  shells,  was  captured  by  Lieu¬ 
tenants  Pegram,  Sinclair,  and  Jones.  This  daring  and  unauthorized 
attack  placed  at  the  disposal  of  the  State  an  amount  of  ammunition  it 
would  be  difficult  to  supply,  and,  with  the  cannon  taken  at  the  Norfolk 
yard,  afforded  all  the  material  needed  for  the  batteries. 

The  rivers  of  Virginia  being  undefended  and  exposed  to  attack,  it  is 
due  to  the  naval  officers  of  Virginia  to  say  that  they  went  to  work  to 
defend  them  with  zeal  proportionate  to  the  necessities  of  the  case. 
Heavy  cannon  were  moved  to  their  destination  with  dispatch,  ammu¬ 
nition  and  projectiles  provided,  men  instructed,  and  every  other  prepa¬ 
ration  made  to  repel  an  opposing  force. 

In  erecting  the  batteries  at  Sewell’s  Point,  at  Pig  Point,  at  Aquia 
Creek,  and  at  Gloucester  Point  they  were  attacked  by  armed  steamers. 
Ip  each  case  the  enemy  were  repulsed,  and  the  works  continued  and 
finished  in  spite  of  their  fire. 

The  works  on  the  Elizabeth,  James,  York,  and  Rappahannock  rivers 
are  so  far  completed  as  to  justify  the  belief  that  they  will  be  able  to 
drive  off  any  naval  force  that  the  IT.  S.  Government  can  bring  against 
them. 

On  the  Potomac  River  batteries  have  been  erected  at  the  terminus 
of  the  Richmond,  Fredericksburg  and  Potomac  Railroad  on  Aquia 
Creek.  In  their  incomplete  state  they  were  attacked  three  times  by  a 
superior  force,  and  in  each  case  Captain  Lynch  repulsed  the  enemy’s 
steamers  with  considerable  loss.  If  the  attack  should  be  renewed 
Captain  Lynch  is  now  prepared  to  strike  a  more  serious  blow. 

The  command  of  the  steamer  Teaser  has  been  assigned  to  Lieutenant 
Rochelle.  Two  32-pounder  guns  have  been  placed  upon  her,  and  she  is 
now  employed  on  the  defenses  of  James  River. 

Captain  J.  R.  Tucker  is  fitting  out  the  steamer  Yorktown  with  as 
heavy  a  battery  as  she  will  bear.  She  will  be  ready  by  the  1st  of  July, 
and  will  be  a  valuable  auxiliary  to  the  defenses  of  James  River. 

A  howitzer  battery  of  six  guns  has  been  organized  by  Lieutenant 
Parker.  Four  of  the  pieces  are  now  mounted.  The  drill  of  the  men 
is  perfect,  and  this  battery  will  be  valuable,  whether  employed  in  the 
field  or  in  the  defenses  of  Richmond.

The  frigate  Merrimack  lias  been  raised,  and  is  now  in  the  dry  dock  at 
Norfolk.  The  other  sunken  ships  will  be  raised  as  soon  as  the  dock  is 
ready  to  receive  them.

Letter  from  Major-General  Lee,  C.  S.  Army,  Commanding  Virginia  forces, 
to  the  governor  of  Virginia,  making  statement  regarding  military  and 
naval  preparation  for  defense  of  that  State. 

Headquarters,  Richmond ,  Va.,  June  15,  1861. 
Sir  :  Agreeably  to  your  request,  I  submit  a  statement  of  the  military 
aud  naval  preparation  for  the  defense  of  Virginia,  from  the  period  of 
her  separation  from  the  U.  S.  Government  to  the  date  of  transfer  of 
the  military  operations  of  the  State  to  the  Confederate  Government. 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


807 


Arrangements  were  first  made  for  tlie  establishment  of  batteries  to  pre¬ 
vent  t lie  ascent  of  our  enemy  by  hostile  vessels.  As  soon  as  an  exam¬ 
ination  was  made  for  the  selection  of  sites  their  construction  was  begun 
and  their  armament  and  defense  committed  to  the  Virginia  navy.  Prep¬ 
arations  were  also  begun  for  receiving  into  the  service  of  the  State  vol¬ 
unteer  companies,  and  for  organizing,  arming,  and  equipping  them. 
Mustering  officers  were  appointed,  rendezvous  established,  and  pro¬ 
vision  made  for  their  subsistence  and  shelter.  The  primary  estimate  of 
the  number  of  troops  of  all  arms  required,  based  upon  the  points  to  be 
defended,  amounted  to  51,000  men.  The  estimated  quota  of  each  por¬ 
tion  of  the  State  has  been  furnished,  except  from  the  western  section. 
Arrangements  were  made  for  calling  out  the  volunteers  from  the  west¬ 
ern  section  at  the  same  time  and  in  the  same  manner  as  from  the 
eastern  section,  but  as  yet  it  has  been  feebly  responded  to. 

Complete  returns  from  the  troops  in  the  field  have  not  and,  from  the 
nature  of  things,  can  not  for  some  time  be  received;  but  from  the  best 
source  of  information  within  our  reach,  the  number  of  Virginia  troops 
is  about  35,000.  This  amount  probably  falls  below  the  real  number,  for 
referring  to  the  report  of  the  colonel  of  ordnance,  it  will  be  seen  that 
he  has  issued  2,054  rifles  and  carbines,  and  41,004  muskets,  in  addition 
to  pistols  and  sabers  to  the  cavalry.  Thirteen  thousand  arms  have  also 
been  issued  from  Lexington,  making  a  total  of  50,058.  Seven  thousand 
of  those  from  Lexington  and  several  thousand  from  the  arsenal  at  Rich¬ 
mond  have  been  issued  to  troops  from  other  States;  but  as  many  of  the 
Virginia  companies,  supposed  to  be  about  5,000  men,  were  armed  and 
equipped  when  received  into  the  service  of  the  State,  should  the  num¬ 
ber  of  unarmed  companies  from  other  States  not  differ  materially  from 
the  number  of  armed  companies  of  the  State,  the  number  of  Virginia 
troops  in  the  field  may  be  assumed  to  be  about  40,000.  When  it  is 
remembered  that  this  body  of  men  were  called  from  a  state  of  profound 
peace  to  one  of  unexpected  Avar,  you  will  have  reason  to  commend  the 
alacrity  with  which  they  left  their  homes  and  families  and  prepared 
themselves  for  the  defense  of  the  State.  The  assembling  of  men,  how- 
eiTer,  was  not  the  most  difficult  operation.  Provision  for  their  instruc¬ 
tion,  subsistence,  equipment,  clothing,  shelter,  and  transportation  in 
the  field  required  more  time  ar'1  1  1  or.  Ammunition  of  every  kind  had 
to  be  manufactured.  The  carriages  of  the  guns  for  river,  land,  and 
field  service  had  to  be  made,  Avith  the  necessary  implements,  caissons, 
battery  wagons,  etc.  One  hundred  and  fifteen  guns  for  field  service 
have  thus  been  provided,  from  which  twenty  light  batteries  of  four  guns 
each  have  been  furnished,  with  the  requisite  horses,  harness,  etc. 

For  the  defense  of  James  River,  two  batteries  and  two  steamers  have 
been  provided,  mounting,  altogether,  forty  guns,  ranging  in  caliber 
from  32-pounders  to  8  and  9  inch  Columbiads.  Arrangements  are  also 
in  process  for  mounting  sixty  guns,  of  different  Aveights,  on  the  defenses 
around  Richmond,  and  a  naval  battery  of  6  to  12-pounder  howiters  is 
in  process  of  organization. 

On  York  River  three  batteries  have  been  constructed,  mounting 
thirty  guns,  of  caliber  similar  to  the  guns  on  James  River. 

Sites  for  batteries  on  the  Iffitomae  have  also  been  selected,  and 
arrangements  were  in  progress  for  their  construction,  but  the  entire 
command  of  that  river  being  in  the  possession  of  the  U.  S.  Govern¬ 
ment,  a  larger  force  is  required  for  their  security  than  could  be  devoted 
to  that  purpose.  The  batteries  at  Aquia  Creek  have  only  been  pre¬ 
pared.  Twelve  guns  are  in  position  there. 


808  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


On  tlie  Rappahannock  River  a  4-gun  battery  of  '32-pounders  and 
8-mcli  Columbiads  has  been  erected. 

Six  batteries  have  been  erected  on  the  Elizabeth  River,  to  guard  the 
approaches  to  Norfolk  and  the  navy  yard.  They  mount  eighty-five 
guns,  32-pounders  and  8  and  9-inch  Columbiads. 

To  prevent  the  ascent  of  the  Nansemoncl  River  and  the  occupation 
of  the  railroad  from  Norfolk  to  Richmond,  three  batteries  have  beeD 
constructed  on  that  river,  which  will  mount  nineteen  guns. 

The  frigate  United  States  has  been  prepared  for  a  school  ship,  pro¬ 
vided  with  a  deck  battery  of  nineteen  guns,  32-pounders  and  9-inch 
Columbiads,  for  harbor  defense.  The  frigate  Merrimack  has  been  raised 
and  is  in  the  dry  dock,  and  arrangements  are  made  for  raising  the  Ger- 
mantown  and  Plymouth. 

In  addition  to  the  batteries  described,  other  works  have  been  con¬ 
structed  for  their  land  defense,  exceeding  in  many  instances  the  works 
on  the  batteries  themselves.  An  extensive  line  of  field  works  has  been 
erected  for  the  security  of  Norfolk  on  the  sides  toward  the  bay. 
Redoubts  for  the  same  purpose  have  been  constructed  at  Jamestown 
Island,  Gloucester  Point,  Yorktown,  and  across  the  neck  of  land  below 
Williamsburg.  I  have  confined  myself  to  a  general  narration  of  opera¬ 
tions,  and  for  the  details  refer  you  to  the  reports  of  several  chiefs  of 
staff. 


Very  respectfully,  etc., 


His  Excellency  John  Letcher, 

Governor  of  Virginia. 


R.  E.  Lee, 

General ,  Commanding.

Letter  from  Commander  Whittle ,  C.  S.  Wavy,  commanding  naval  defenses 
on  York  River ,  to  Captain  Ingraham ,  C.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  transfer 
of  guns  and  equipment  from  Gloucester  Point  to  Yorktown,  Va. 

West  Point,  York  Eiver,  July  12,  1861. 
Captain  :  I  inclose  herewith  the  weekly  report*  of  Commander  Page, 
in  command  of  the  naval  battery  at  Gloucester  Point.  To  the  remarks 
annexed  to  that  report  1  beg  leave  to  call  your  prompt  attention,  and 
through  you,  the  particular  attention  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy.  It 
appears  from  the  report  of  Commander  Page  that  two  14-incli  shell 
guns  sent  to  this  (his)  battery  have  been  sent  to  Yorktown  by  order  of 
Brigadier- General  Magruder,  with  equipment  and  ten  live  shells,  since 
last  report.  This  is  the  first  knowledge  I  have  had  of  this  transaction, 
and  I  desire  to  be  furnished,  at  the  earliest  convenience  of  the  Depart¬ 
ment  with  clear  and  explicit  instructions  on  this  point.  If  the  com¬ 
manding  military  officer  on  the  peninsula  is  authorized  to  remove, 
without  any  consultation  whatever  with  me,  guns  from  naval  batteries 
which  have  been  placed  under  my  orders  by  both  the  highest  military 
aud  naval  authority,  my  position  here  as  commanding  the  naval  defenses 
on  York  Eiver  is  a  delusion  and  a  farce. 

I  am  sir,  respectfully  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  C.  Whittle, 

Commanding  Naval  Defenses  on  York  River. 

Captain  D.  N.  Ingraham, 

In  Charge  Office  of  Ordnance  and  Hydrography , 

Navy  Department,  Richmond. 


Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commander  Tucker ,  C.  S.  Navy, 
commanding  C.  S.  S.  Patrick  Henry,  to  proceed  on  an  active  cruise. 

CONPEDERATE  STATES, 

Navy  Department,  Richmond ,  July  13,  1861. 
Sir  :  It  is  deemed  important  that  the  steamer  Patrick  Henry,  under 
your  command,  shall  leave  James  Eiver  at  the  earliest  practicable 
moment  and  make  an  active  cruise  at  sea  against  the  enemy. 

The  Department  is  unwilling  by  any  instructions  to  limit  your  dis¬ 
cretion  as  to  the  time  and  manner  of  running  the  blockade,  your  cruising 
ground,  or  your  return,  confiding,  as  it  does,  in  your  good  judgment; 
but  it  is  evident  that  your  success  will  be  greatly  promoted  by  your 
escape  from  the  river  without  the  enemy’s  knowledge. 

Should  a  doubt  at  any  time  arise  as  to  the  course  to  be  pursued,  it 
may  be  solved  by  the  consideration  that,  in  accordance  with  the  rules 
of  Christian  warfare,  you  are  to  inflict  upon  the  enemy  the  greatest 
injury  in  the  shortest  time. 

It  is  believed  that  the  speed  of  the  Patrick  Henry  is  greater  than 
that  of  any  of  the  ships  of  the  United  States,  and  that  her  battery  will 
enable  her  to  engage  such  vessels  as  the  Harriet  Lane  and  the  char¬ 
tered  steamers  of  the  enemy’s  Navy  generally,  thus  affording  you  the 
means  of  escaping  from  his  first-class  ships  and  of  capturing  those  of 
the  second  class.  The  possession  of  one  of  the  enemy’s  cruisers  of  this 
class,  with  her  signal  book,  might  enable  you  to  capture  some  of  his 
heavier  vessels. 


Not  found. 


ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


813 


Steam  propellers  are  important  to  us,  as  are  all  ordnance  and  military 
stores;  and  captures  of  this  class  you  will  endeavor  to  send  safely  into 
port. 

Should  you  find  it  impracticable  to  leave  the  river,  you  will  cooperate 
with  the  military  forces  against  the  enemy,  keeping  watch  by  day  and 
night  upon  his  movements,  attacking  and  annoying  him  to  the  utmost 
of  your  power. 

Should  circumstances  render  it  important  to  land  your  crew  to  coop¬ 
erate  with  the  land  forces,  you  will  secure  your  ship  under  the  guns  of 
the  Jamestown  battery,  keeping  her  ready  for  instant  service. 

You  will  impress  upon  your  officers  the  importance  of  establishing 
and  maintaining  good  discipline,  and  of  inciting  every  man  to  do  his 
duty;  and  you  will  specially  report  to  the  Department  the  name,  place 
of  birth,  age,  character,  and  qualifications  of  every  man  under  your 
command,  whose  good  conduct,  particularly  in  action,  or  in  moments  of 
peril  or  excitement  may  merit  your  commendation. 

You  will  keep  this  Department  advised  of  your  movements,  and  you 
will  endeavor  to  prevent  all  publications  thereof,  not  authorized  by 
yourself,  as  tending  to  defeat  your  objects. 

With  my  best  wishes  for  yourself  and  your  command,  I  am,  respect 
fully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  E.  Mallory, 

/Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Commander  John  E.  Tucker, 

Commanding  C.  8.  8.  Patrick  Henry ,  Richmond ,  Va.
